exp.0:1:
The Lord answers the people's question: the tribe of Judah will be the first to go up to fight. God affirms that he has already handed the land into their hands, as a sure promise. "Shall go up" refers to going up into the highlands of Canaan. "Delivered" means giving the victory.

After Joshua died, Israel was left without its main leader. The Israelites did well to ask God before acting. God himself speaks and points to Judah. Afterward, Judah invites his brother Simeon to help him, and together they win the victory. Some scholars see here a good beginning, although the book later shows the people's failures.

For today: before making important decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer and in his Word. Then act with courage and seek the help of brothers and sisters, as Judah did with Simeon.
exp.0:2:
It says that Judah invited his brother Simeon to join him in fighting against the Canaanites. "Lot" refers to the land that each tribe received by drawing lots. Judah proposes: "Help me take my portion, and I will help you with yours." Simeon agreed and went with him.

After the death of Joshua, Israel asked God who should go up first to fight, and God pointed to Judah. Judah is the one speaking. Instead of going alone, he looks for Simeon, whose land lay inside the territory of Judah (Joshua 19:1). It was a partnership of mutual help between sister tribes.

For today: even when God gives us a task, we do not have to do it alone. We can ask other believers for help and offer our own help too, generously and without selfishness.
exp.0:3:
The explanation says that the tribe of Judah went out to fight, and that God gave them victory over the Canaanites and the Perizzites, peoples who lived in the land. In Bezek they struck down ten thousand men.

After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel asked God who should fight first against the Canaanites. God chose Judah and promised to give them the land. Judah invited his brother Simeon to help him, and together they went into battle. The book of Judges tells how Israel took possession of the promised land little by little.

For today: God often guides us when we ask him, and he also invites us to work as a team. Before facing a challenge, pray and seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters.
exp.0:5:
Adoni-bezek, king of Bezek, tried to escape from the battle, but the men of Judah chased him down and caught him. They captured him, and then they cut off the thumbs and big toes of his hands and feet, a punishment that left him badly limited in fighting or walking firmly.

This is part of the account of how Judah, one of the tribes of Israel, began to take possession of the land of Canaan after the death of Joshua. Here it is not a character who speaks; the narrator tells what happened. The next verse explains that this same king had done this to seventy kings, and he acknowledges that he received what he had done. The text reports it, but it does not say that every human punishment is a model to imitate.

For today: our actions leave a mark, and cruelty or abuse eventually catches up with us. We can choose to treat others with mercy, remembering that God treats us that way.
exp.0:6:
Adoni-bezek, a Canaanite king, acknowledges that what happened to him was the same as what he had done to others. He says that seventy kings, with their thumbs and big toes cut off, used to gather scraps of food under his table. Then they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.

Adoni-bezek speaks after being captured by Judah and Simeon, while Israel was conquering Canaan. He had humiliated and left disabled the enemies he had defeated. He himself sees his punishment as a just repayment from God. The text does not say that God approved his cruelty or anyone else's; it only records his acknowledgment.

For today: our actions have consequences, and sometimes life gives them back to us. It is wise to treat others with compassion and mercy, especially when we have power over them, remembering that one day we will give an account to God.
exp.0:8:
This verse tells that the tribe of Judah went out to fight the Canaanites who lived in three areas: the mountains, the south (the region that the Hebrew text calls the Negev, the dry region of the south), and the valley (the lowlands to the west). The word "Canaanites" refers to the peoples who inhabited that land before Israel.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges, who is not named. After the death of Joshua, Israel asks God who will go up first, and Judah goes at the front. It had already won at Jerusalem, and now it extends the conquest to other regions. Some scholars understand that Jerusalem later returned to enemy hands, and the text does not make this clear here.

For today: when God gives us a big task, it is wise to move forward step by step, with prayer and perseverance, not leaving halfway what He has entrusted to us.
exp.0:16:
Judah went with his brother Simeon, and together they attacked the Canaanites who lived in Zephath. They completely destroyed the city and changed its name to Hormah, a name connected with the idea of being utterly destroyed or devoted to destruction.

This is part of the book of Judges, which tells how the tribes of Israel took possession of the promised land after the death of Joshua. Judah and Simeon had agreed to help each other in the conquest (Judges 1:3). The text does not say who is speaking; it is the narrator showing that, at the beginning, obedience and unity brought victories.

For today: we do not move forward alone. God gives us brothers and sisters in the faith to help us face our battles. Find someone with whom you can pray and walk together in what is hard for you today.
exp.0:19:
It says that Hebron was given to Caleb, just as Moses had promised, and that Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, a people of very tall and feared men. The word "gave" in the verse means that Judah handed the city over to him, and the word "drove out" means that he removed them from his territory.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, and he does not identify himself. He tells how the tribes began to conquer the promised land after the death of Joshua. The promise to Caleb appears in Numbers 14 and Joshua 14. The text shows that God gave victory, but also that other peoples were not completely driven out.

For today: God keeps his promises, even when many years pass. Caleb trusted God and faced giants without giving up. We can pray and act with faith in the face of our own challenges, knowing that God is faithful.
exp.0:23:
The spies sent by the house of Joseph were keeping watch over Bethel. They saw a man coming out of the city, and they asked him to show them how to get in. In return, they promised to treat him kindly, which means they would protect his life.

The ones doing the watching were from Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph. After the death of Joshua, each tribe was fighting to take the land that had fallen to it, and Bethel, formerly called Luz, lay within their territory. The text says that the LORD was with them. The man helped them and was spared, along with his family.

For today: the kindness we promise must be carried out. The spies kept their word, and that invites us to be people whose word can be trusted, even toward those who are not of our own people.
exp.0:24:
He showed them the way into the city of Bethel. Joseph's men attacked the city with the sword, meaning with violence and without pity, but they let the man and all his family go free.

The author of the book of Judges is the one telling this, describing how the tribes of Israel were taking over Canaan after Joshua's death. The spies had promised mercy in exchange for help, just as Israel had done earlier with Rahab. The Bible does not say whether that man believed in God. Afterward, he founded another city called Luz, in the land of the Hittites.

For today: keeping what we promise is part of living with integrity. Also, the mercy we give to others reminds us of the mercy God has given us.
exp.0:28:
This verse says that the tribe of Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in the city of Gezer. Instead of removing them, they let them live alongside them. Here "drive out" means to expel or remove from the land, and "Canaanites" refers to the ancient inhabitants of that region.

Context: the one telling this is the narrator of the book of Judges, not a character in the story. He records it as part of a list of tribes that did not complete the conquest of the promised land. Before this passage, Manasseh had done something similar. Afterward, Zebulun and Asher also fail. The book thus shows a pattern of partial obedience, which later brings trouble to the people.

For today: sometimes we allow habits or attitudes to remain among us that we know do not please God, thinking they do no harm. Today you can ask God for strength to face one concrete thing honestly and not leave it half done.
exp.0:30:
This verse says that the tribe of Asher did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in several cities: Accho, Zidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob. The verse's wording refers to them as the inhabitants of those cities.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks (we do not know for certain who wrote it). He describes how, after the death of Joshua, the tribes did not finish the conquest. God had commanded them not to live alongside those peoples, and here we see only partial obedience. This prepares the account of the spiritual problems that come later in the book. Some of these cities lay on the northern coast, near Zidon.

For today: What we leave unresolved can grow and affect us. Let us ask God for the courage to face honestly whatever we know we must let go of, rather than getting used to living with it.
exp.0:31:
The explanation says that the tribe of Asher did not drive out the Canaanites from the land that had been allotted to it. On the contrary, the Israelites stayed to live among them. The sense of the verse is that the Asherites did not dispossess the Canaanites; instead they dwelt alongside them. The land that should have been theirs was now shared with the peoples God had commanded them to drive out.

Context: The book of Judges tells, in the narrator's voice, how Israel failed to complete the conquest. God had commanded that these peoples be removed so that they would not lead Israel into idolatry. Here several tribes are listed who gave way one after another. The text notes that Asher did so even more clearly: it does not say they made the Canaanites pay tribute, but that they lived among them. This prepares the cycles of disobedience that follow in the book.

For today: When we allow something into our lives that God asked us to remove, such as a habit or a harmful influence, sooner or later it begins to take charge. Ask God for the courage to obey completely, not halfway.
exp.0:32:
This verse says that the tribe of Naphtali did not drive out the people of Beth-shemesh or of Beth-anath. Instead of driving them out, Naphtali lived among the Canaanites who were already in the land. Still, those towns paid tribute to them, that is, labor or taxes.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, reviewing what happened after the death of Joshua. He lists the tribes that did not finish the conquest God had entrusted to them. He wants to show how Israel fell short in obeying, and that prepares the problems that will come later in the book.

For today: when we leave what God asks of us half done, and settle for what we should have changed, that small compromise can grow. Let us ask God for the courage to obey him fully, without settling for what is comfortable.
exp.0:33:
The Amorites, a people who lived in that region, pressed the tribe of Dan hard and forced them to stay in the hill country. They did not allow them to come down to the plain, that is, the lowland, which was more fertile and better for planting and living. The word "forced" here means that they cornered them or dominated them.

The book of Judges tells how the tribes of Israel did not fully take the promised land. We do not know for certain who wrote the book, but the account shows that Dan was not able to occupy what had been assigned to it. The nearby verses speak of other tribes who also lived alongside the Canaanites instead of driving them out. Later on, Dan moves north (Judges 18).

When we leave a task half-finished or put up with what we should have confronted, those problems can grow and limit us. Today we can ask God for courage and perseverance to deal in time with what hinders us, trusting that He gives us strength.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that God, because of Israel's disobedience, would no longer drive out the peoples who lived in Canaan. Those peoples would be a constant irritation to them, like a pain in the side. And their gods would be a trap, a snare in which Israel would fall when tempted to worship them.

The speaker is the angel of the LORD, a messenger who speaks on God's behalf. He comes to Bochim and confronts the people because they did not tear down the altars or avoid alliances with the inhabitants of the land, as God had commanded them. The consequences of that disobedience become real.

For today: what we tolerate and do not remove from our lives, even when it seems small, can end up binding us. Yet the people's weeping shows that God still receives a repentant heart. Today we can obey Him from the start and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that Joshua had already sent the people away, and that each family of Israel had gone to its own share, the land it was given to receive. There they were to live and take possession of it.

The book of Judges here looks back again, to the end of Joshua's life (see Joshua 24). After the weeping at Bochim, the narrator explains how the people came to that situation. First he recalls a time of faithfulness: while Joshua and the elders who had seen the works of God were alive, Israel served the LORD. In this way he prepares the story of what happened when that generation was gone.

For today: God gives us things that we are to hold on to with effort and faith. But the faith of others is not inherited automatically. Take care of your own relationship with God, and share with your children what He has done for you.
exp.1:6:
The people of Israel served God as long as Joshua lived, and also as long as the elders who outlived him remained. Those elders had seen with their own eyes the great works that God did for Israel. Their service meant obeying God and worshiping Him alone. The elders who outlived Joshua were those who lived on after him.

The narrator of the book speaks here, and the author is not known for certain. After recounting the weeping at Bochim, he looks back and explains what Israel was like before. He prepares the reader for verse 10, where it says that a generation arose that did not know God.

For today: faith is strengthened by remembering what God has done. Tell your children and friends how God has helped you, so that others may also come to know Him.
exp.1:7:
It says that Joshua, son of Nun, died at the age of 110. He is called "the servant of the Lord," a title of honor that Moses also received. It is a way of saying that his whole life was devoted to obeying and serving God. The name "the Lord" stands in this translation for God's personal name.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He is summarizing how the time of Joshua came to an end. As long as he and the elders lived, the people served the Lord, because they had seen his works. But the text immediately tells us that another generation came along that did not know the Lord. This sets up the cycle of disobedience that dominates the book.

For today: faith is not passed on by itself. We can tell our children and others what God has done in our lives, and live with steadiness, so that the next generation also comes to know him.
exp.1:9:
It says that the whole generation that lived with Joshua died and was gathered to their fathers, that is, they died and were buried. Afterward another generation arose that did not know the Lord, nor the works he had done for Israel. The phrase about being gathered to their fathers is an old way of saying that they died. Here "know" means more than knowing facts; it means having a real relationship with God and remembering his works.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Judges, whose identity is not known for certain. It explains why Israel fell into idolatry after Joshua. This new generation did not experience the departure from Egypt or the entry into the land, and the next verse shows the result: they served the Baals and forsook the Lord.

Today it reminds us that faith is not inherited on its own. Tell your children and others what God has done in your life, and live in a way that they too come to know him personally.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the people of Israel did what displeases God, that is, they did evil in the sight of the Lord. The Lord is the name of God. To serve the Baals means to worship Baal, a Canaanite god, in his various local forms. The plural form is used because he was worshiped in many places.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Judges, who is not known with certainty. He explains that, after Joshua and his contemporaries died, a generation arose that did not know God or what He had done. Thus begins a sad cycle: Israel turns away, suffers the consequences, and then cries out to God.

For today: our faith needs to be nurtured and passed on. Tell at home and at church what God has done, and maintain a personal relationship with Him every day.
exp.1:12:
This verse says that the people of Israel abandoned the Lord, their God, and began to worship Baal and Ashtaroth. "Forsook" means that they turned away from Him, and "served" means that they gave to other gods the honor that belonged to Him alone. Baal and Ashtaroth were gods of the neighboring peoples, commonly linked to rain and the fertility of the land.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after the death of Joshua. A new generation had not lived close to God's works, and they let themselves be drawn into the customs of their neighbors. Because of this, God allowed them to suffer at the hands of their enemies, just as He had warned.

For today: it is easy to trust in things that seem to give us security, such as money or success. Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our heart, and return to God with simplicity.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel did not even listen to the judges God sent them. Instead of obeying, they went after other gods, that is, they were unfaithful to God and bowed down to idols, like someone who betrays a spouse. They turned away quickly from the path their ancestors had followed when they obeyed God.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks (tradition is not certain about who wrote it). He explains why Israel lived in cycles of sin, oppression, and rescue. The judges were leaders whom God raised up to deliver the people from their enemies, but the people's hearts did not truly change.

For today: it is not enough for help or relief to arrive; we need to obey God with steadiness. Ask yourself what things you have allowed to take the place of God, and ask Him to help you return to Him today.
exp.1:19:
God was greatly angered with Israel. The anger of the Lord burned hot against them, meaning that his displeasure was very strong. The reason is that the people broke faith with the covenant, that is, they violated it or disregarded it, and did not obey his voice. That covenant was the commitment God had made with Israel's forefathers.

God speaks. Israel was already living in a repeated cycle: the people turned away from God, suffered oppression, cried out, and God sent a judge who delivered them. But when the judge died, they went back to worshiping other gods. That is why God speaks with firmness. He then explains that he will no longer drive out the nations that remained, in order to test whether the people would remain faithful to him.

For today: let us not let our faith depend on good moments or on leaders who encourage us. Let us cultivate a daily obedience to God, and when we fail, let us return to him quickly and humbly.
exp.1:20:
It says that God will no longer keep driving out of the land the nations that Joshua left unconquered when he died.

The speaker is the LORD, the Lord. He speaks to Israel through his angel, after the people had repeatedly broken their covenant and worshiped other gods. Because they broke the agreement, God decides not to remove those remaining nations. The verses that follow explain that these nations would be a test to see whether Israel would return to following the way of the Lord.

For today: God sometimes allows trials or struggles to remain in our lives, and does not always remove them right away. We can ask ourselves whether there is something God is asking us to leave behind or correct, and answer him with sincere obedience, trusting that he remains close and is patient with us.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues the list of the peoples that God left in the land of Canaan. It mentions the five lords of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians (from Sidon, a Phoenician city), and the Hivites who lived in Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon to the entrance of Hamath, a region in the north.

The book of Judges is told in the voice of a narrator, and it is not known with certainty who its author was. It explains why these peoples were left: to test Israel and to teach war to a generation that did not know the wars of Canaan. It then says that the test was whether they would obey the commandments given through Moses.

For today: the trials of life reveal whether we trust God and obey him. When you face a difficulty, ask yourself how you can respond with faithfulness.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that the people of Israel lived mixed in with the nations that were already in the land. Six peoples are named: Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

The book of Judges tells this as narrative. God had left these nations in the land to test whether Israel would obey his commands. Instead of living apart in faithfulness, Israel stayed and lived alongside them. The next verses show what followed: they intermarried with them and ended up serving their gods.

Today we also live alongside people who think differently, and that is not wrong in itself. But we must be careful that our customs and relationships do not gradually pull us away from God. It is worth asking ourselves honestly: who influences my heart more, God or my surroundings?
exp.2:5:
They say the Israelites married into the peoples who lived in the land: they took the daughters of those peoples as wives for their sons, and gave their own daughters to the sons of those peoples. And in the end they ended up worshiping the gods of those peoples.

The book of Judges tells the story of Israel after Joshua. The narrator (tradition says it may have been Samuel, though this is not known for certain) explains that God left those peoples in the land to test whether Israel would obey the law given through Moses. That law warned against marriages that would turn the heart away from God. This verse shows how the fall that follows began.

For today: close relationships influence us a great deal. Take care with your friendships, your courtship, and your important decisions, so that they draw your heart closer to God and do not pull it away little by little.
exp.2:7:
This verse says that God became very angry with Israel because of their unfaithfulness. The phrase "sold them into the hand of" means he handed them over, letting them fall under the power of another. So Israel was ruled over for eight years by Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia.

The book of Judges tells this moment in the voice of a narrator. Israel had mixed with the peoples of Canaan, married among them, and worshiped the Baals, false gods of that land. Because of this, God allowed this oppression. But the account goes on: when the people cried out, God sent Othniel to deliver them. About the king mentioned here we do not know much more than what the Bible says.

For today: our choices have consequences, and turning away from God leaves us enslaved to other things. But we can always cry out to Him, for He hears and rescues. Today you can return to God with sincerity.
exp.2:10:
After the victory that God gave through Othniel, the land had peace for forty years. Then Othniel died. The phrase "the land had rest" means there was calm, without wars. "Forty years" may be an exact number or a way of saying a full generation; the Bible does not make this clear.

The narrator of the book tells the story of the judges. Israel had disobeyed, suffered oppression, cried out to God, and God sent Othniel as a deliverer. This verse closes that cycle. But the text that follows shows that, once Othniel was gone, the people went back to doing evil. The peace depended greatly on his leadership.

For today: thank God for times of peace and do not take them for granted. Let your faith not depend only on one person, but on your own relationship with God, so that it stays firm even when circumstances change.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that the Israelites again did what was evil, that is, they disobeyed God. Then God gave Eglon, king of Moab, the power to rule over Israel.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. After the death of the judge Othniel, there were forty years of peace, but the people fell again into the same pattern: sin, punishment, and crying out to God. The text explains that God allowed that oppression as a consequence of their wickedness. Afterward, Moab, together with Ammon and Amalek, dominated Israel for eighteen years.

For today: let us not easily forget what God has done for us in times of peace. When everything goes well, it is easy to become careless. Let us make a habit of giving thanks, praying, and obeying every day, and if we fail, let us return to Him quickly.
exp.2:13:
The explanation says that the people of Israel were under the rule of Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years. The word "served" here means that they were subjected and forced to obey him and pay him tribute. "Eighteen" is simply eighteen.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks. He explains that Israel returned to doing evil, that is, to turning away from God, and that God allowed Eglon to grow strong against them. Eglon allied himself with the Ammonites and the Amalekites and took the city of palms, which many identify with Jericho, though this is not certain. Afterward, the people cried out to God, and he sent Ehud as their deliverer.

Turning away from God almost always brings consequences that weigh heavily for a long time. But the account also reminds us that God hears the sincere cry. If today you feel trapped by your mistakes, you can return to him in prayer, without waiting to be perfect.
exp.2:14:
After eighteen years under King Eglon, the people of Israel cried out to God for help. God raised up a deliverer for them: Ehud, the son of Gera, from the tribe of Benjamin. He is described as a man lefthanded, which is usually understood to mean he was left-handed, though this is not known for certain. The people of Israel sent a gift with him, which was the tribute they were required to pay to Eglon.

The narrator of the book of Judges explains that Israel had done evil in the sight of God, and for that reason they were brought under the rule of Moab and its allies. Here we see the pattern that repeats through the book: sin, oppression, crying out, and rescue.

For today: when you feel trapped by your mistakes or by a difficult situation, cry out to God with sincerity. He can use unexpected people and means to help you.
exp.2:15:
Ehud made himself a dagger with two edges, a cubit long (about 45 centimeters, though the exact Hebrew measure is debated). The phrase about Ehud fastening it at his waist, hidden under his clothing on the right side, is what the verse describes.

The one who tells the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel had been oppressed for eighteen years by Eglon, king of Moab, and had cried out to God. God raised up Ehud as a deliverer. He was left-handed or had limited use of his right hand, and so a weapon on that side might not raise suspicion. The text describes what happened; it does not tell us we should imitate it.

For today: God can use someone who has limitations and does not fit what is expected. When you feel you are not enough, cry out to God, prepare yourself with wisdom, and trust that He can work through you.
exp.2:18:
Ehud, after delivering the tribute, turned back from the quarries near Gilgal and told King Eglon that he had a secret message for him. The king answered by telling everyone to be quiet, and he ordered all his attendants to leave. So Ehud was left alone with the king.

Ehud was a deliverer whom God raised up for Israel, since the people had been under the rule of Moab for years because of their sin. Using the excuse of carrying the tribute, Ehud looked for a way to get close to the king without arousing suspicion. Scholars do not fully agree on what those stone quarries near Gilgal were; some believe they were stones or carved images.

For today: Ehud was patient and knew how to wait for the right moment. Often God works through people who act with prudence rather than haste. We can ask Him for wisdom to know when to speak and when to wait.
exp.2:25:
The explanation describes how, while the servants of King Eglon waited outside, unwilling to open the door, Ehud used that time to escape. He passed beyond the place of the carved stones (some understand these to have been carved images or boundary stones near Gilgal; the Hebrew term is interpreted in several ways) and reached Seirath safely, a place whose exact location is not known, in the hill country of Ephraim.

The narrator tells how God used Ehud to deliver Israel from Moab, which had oppressed them for eighteen years. The servants assumed the king was in private, so the waiting gave Ehud an advantage. His escape opened the way for the call to arms that follows.

For today: trust that God works even in small details, such as a delay, and then act with decision, rather than freezing when he opens the way.
exp.2:26:
That verse tells how Ehud, after escaping, came to the hill country of Ephraim and blew a trumpet. It was a signal to call the people to war. The Israelites came down from the mountain with him, and Ehud went at their head.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had been under the rule of King Eglon of Moab for eighteen years. Ehud had killed Eglon by cunning and escaped. Now he takes advantage of the confusion among the Moabites and gathers the people to win their freedom. He says that God has already given their enemies into their hands.

For today: God often uses people who are willing to take the first step. If He puts something good on your heart, do not wait for others to begin. Encourage others by your example, trusting that God goes before you.
exp.2:27:
Ehud tells the Israelites to follow him, because God has already given them victory over Moab. They go down after him and take the fords of the Jordan, that is, the shallow places where the river could be crossed on foot. In this way they block Moab's escape, and not one man gets through.

The one speaking is Ehud, the judge whom God raised up to deliver Israel. Moab had ruled over them for eighteen years. Ehud had just killed King Eglon and fled. Then he blew the trumpet to gather the people. His confidence was not in his own plan, but in the fact that the Lord had already acted.

For today: when God gives you a sign that he is at work, do not just stand and look. Take the step of faith and do your part with courage and order. Trusting God does not remove action; it drives it forward. Today you can ask yourself: what concrete step is mine to take?
exp.2:29:
That day Moab was defeated and brought under the power of Israel. The phrase "subdued" means brought under control, placed under authority. The phrase "the land had rest" means there was peace, without wars or oppression, for eighty years. Some understand that number as a long period of calm, and others as an exact count.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier, Ehud, the judge whom God raised up, had killed King Eglon and called the people to follow him, trusting that the LORD was giving them the victory. Israel had suffered for years under Moab because they had turned away from God. Now the account shows that God delivers his people and gives them rest.

For today: when you face something that weighs you down, do not trust only in your own strength. Act with courage and obedience, but remember that true victory and peace come from God. Give him thanks when rest arrives.
exp.2:30:
After Ehud, Shamgar the son of Anath defeated six hundred Philistines using an ox goad. The ox goad was a long stick with a metal tip that farmers used to guide oxen while plowing. The verse also says that Shamgar delivered Israel as well.

This is a brief note from the narrator of the book of Judges, who does not say who wrote it. It appears between the story of Ehud and the story of Deborah. Shamgar is mentioned as another deliverer whom God used when Israel was threatened. Little is known about him; his origin and exact occupation are not clear, and it is debated whether he was an Israelite.

God can use what we have on hand, even when it seems common or unimpressive. Shamgar used a working tool. Ask yourself what skill, time, or simple resource you can offer today to help others.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the people of Israel again did what God considered evil, after Ehud had died. The word "again" shows they had returned to their old ways, and "in the sight of the Lord" means what displeased God.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Ehud had been a judge who rescued Israel from their oppressors, and while he lived there was peace. The book shows a cycle that repeats: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, cry out for help, and God sends them a deliverer. Who wrote Judges is not known with certainty.

For today: it is not enough to have lived a good season of faith. If our steadfastness depends on a person or a period, we may fall when that is gone. It is wise to put down roots of our own in God and to keep seeking him every day.
exp.3:1:
And the Lord gave Israel into the hand of Jabin, a Canaanite king who ruled from Hazor. The verse says that God handed them over, leaving them under the power of another. Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles.

The narrator tells the story of Israel after the death of the judge Ehud. The people again turned away from God, and the text presents the oppression as the result of that disobedience. Soon after, Israel cries out to God, and He responds by raising up Deborah. In this way, the verse shows the problem before the help.

For today: the choices we make have consequences, and sometimes we must live with their effects. But we can always cry out to God sincerely. He hears, and in the middle of the trouble He can begin to prepare a way out.
exp.3:2:
The explanation says that the Israelites asked God for help with cries and pleas, because King Jabin, through his army, had been oppressing them harshly for twenty years. The verse speaks of nine hundred chariots of iron, which were war chariots reinforced with iron, a military force greatly feared. The verse says he mightily oppressed them, meaning he treated them cruelly and mistreated them.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks. He shows a cycle that repeats: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, and then cry out. The text does not say that their cry was a perfect return to God, but it does say that they turned to Him. Later Deborah will come, used by God to guide them.

For today: when you feel crushed by a problem that seems bigger than you, do not wait until you have strength or answers. Cry out to God sincerely, and if you have drifted away from Him, return. He listens.
exp.3:4:
She lived under a palm tree, called the palm of Deborah, in a place between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim. The people of Israel would go up to her to have their disputes settled.

The phrase about going up to her is explained as follows: they went to her to have their disputes resolved and to be told what was right. The hill country of Ephraim refers to the area of hills belonging to the tribe of Ephraim.

The narrator then describes Deborah just after saying that Israel had been oppressed for twenty years by an enemy with many chariots of iron. She was a prophetess and she ruled over Israel. Her open and simple place shows that the people could come near to her. Later she will call Barak to give him the word of God.

For today: God uses people who are approachable and trustworthy. We can be someone others turn to for wise counsel, and we can seek out people who will guide us according to the Word of God.
exp.3:6:
God himself says he will bring Sisera, the commander of King Jabin's army, to the river Kishon. Sisera will come with his chariots and all his soldiers. There God promises to hand him over into Barak's hands.

The speaker is Deborah, a prophetess and judge of Israel. She passes on to Barak what God had already commanded him: to gather ten thousand men on Mount Tabor. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, and his iron chariots caused great fear. Deborah reminds Barak that the victory would come from God, not from Israel's own strength.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, obey the step that God shows you, even if you cannot see the whole path. He can go before you and fulfill what he promised, so trust him and take that step in faith.
exp.3:7:
Barak tells Deborah that he will go into battle only if she goes with him. If she does not accompany him, he will stay behind.

Deborah was a prophetess and a judge of Israel. She had passed on to Barak a clear command from God, with the promise of victory over Sisera. Barak does not reject the command, but he sets a condition. Some see here a lack of trust; others see that he valued the presence of God's prophetess. The text does not say exactly what he was thinking. Deborah agrees, but she warns him that the honor will not be his.

For today: When God has already spoken to us and promised his help, let us trust in him without demanding further guarantees. Even so, it is wise to seek the company of people of faith who encourage us to obey.
exp.3:8:
Débora accepts going with Barak into battle, but she gives him an important warning. Because of the way he is acting, the credit for the victory will not be his. "Honor" here means glory or recognition, and the verb about selling means that God will hand Sisera, the enemy commander, over into the hand of a woman. Then Deborah gets up and goes with Barak to Kedesh.

Deborah, prophetess and judge of Israel, speaks here. God had commanded Barak to fight against Sisera, but Barak set a condition: he would go only if she went with him. Her reply is not a punishment but a warning. Many think the "woman" is Jael, although the text does not say so yet.

For today: when God asks something of you, obey with confidence and without conditions. And if you do what is right, do not seek applause, because God can use whomever he chooses to give the victory.
exp.3:15:
Barak pursued the chariots and the enemy army as far as a place called Harosheth of the Gentiles. There all of Sisera's army died by the sword, and not a single man survived. Only Sisera, the commander, escaped on foot.

The narrator of Judges tells how God delivered Israel from twenty years of oppression under Jabin, the Canaanite king. Deborah, a prophetess and judge, encouraged Barak to fight, assuring him that the LORD was going out before him. The text credits the victory to God, not to Israel's own strength.

For today: when God calls you to obey, take the step even when the challenge seems enormous. Trust that He goes before you, and finish what you started without stopping halfway.
exp.3:16:
This verse tells how Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army, fled on foot after losing the battle and came to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber, a Kenite. Sisera sought refuge there. He chose that place because there was peace, that is, an alliance or good relations, between Jabin, king of Hazor, and Heber's family.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel had been oppressed by Jabin for years, and God had just given the victory through Barak and Deborah. Sisera believed he would be safe with allies, but his trust in that political friendship proved mistaken, as the rest of the story shows.

For today: human alliances and places that seem safe can fail. It is wise to place our trust in God, who truly sustains and protects us.
exp.3:17:
Jael goes out to meet Sisera, the commander of the enemy army, and invites him to come into her tent. She tells him not to be afraid. He enters, and she covers him with a mantle.

Jael speaks here as the wife of Heber the Kenite. Sisera flees on foot after losing the battle against Israel, and he seeks refuge in a home he believed was friendly, since there was peace between his king and Heber's family. His trust leads him to lower his guard. The text does not explain all of Jael's reasons, but the account that follows shows that she acted in favor of Israel.

For today: kind words can be sincere or deceptive. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern, and let us take care that our words of welcome and peace are always honest.
exp.3:18:
Sisera, the commander of the enemy army, flees exhausted and asks Jael for a little water because he is thirsty. She does not give him water but milk, which was kept in a bottle, that is, a container made of animal skin. Then she covers him again.

Sisera speaks, having just lost the battle against Israel and now seeking shelter. Jael receives him with apparent kindness, and he trusts her because there was peace between her family and King Jabin. Many understand that the milk would help him fall asleep, although the text does not say so clearly.

For today: the story reminds us that not every kind gesture shows true intentions. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern, and let us strive for our own kindness to be sincere, without deceit.
exp.3:20:
This verse tells how Jael, the wife of Heber, took a tent peg and a hammer, approached Sisera quietly while he was sleeping from exhaustion, drove the peg through his temple into the ground, and so he died. A hammer is a heavy hand tool used to strike, and the temples are the flat areas on each side of the forehead.

It is part of the account in Judges 4. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, king of Canaan, and Sisera was his commander, who fled after being defeated. Jael offered him shelter and trust, and then killed him. The text says that God subdued Jabin that day, but it does not approve of every detail of the action. Some see courage here and others note the deception; the Bible simply narrates what happened.

For today: God can work even in violent and confusing times, and his justice does not depend on our strength. Trust in him, and seek to resolve conflicts with integrity, without deceit.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that it was God who humbled or defeated Jabin, king of Canaan, that day, in the sight of the people of Israel. The word for "subdued" means to bring down, lower, or overcome.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He summarizes what happened: Israel had been oppressed by Jabin, and his military commander, Sisera, died at the hands of Jael. Although Deborah, Barak, and Jael all acted, the account credits the victory to God. The following verse shows that Jabin's downfall was a process, since Israel kept growing stronger until it destroyed him.

For today: when you accomplish something difficult, recognize that God works even through people and unexpected circumstances. Give thanks, stay humble, and trust that He continues to act in long processes.
exp.3:23:
The explanation says that Israel's power grew and became firmer against Jabin, king of Canaan, until they wiped him out completely. The phrase "the hand of" is an old way of speaking about strength or power.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, who closes the story of Deborah and Barak. Israel had been oppressed for about twenty years by Jabin, and his general Sisera had died at the hands of Jael. The verse before this one says it was God who brought down Jabin. So Israel's growth is not presented as its own achievement, but as the fruit of what God did.

For today: when God gives you a victory, do not expect everything to change overnight. Keep moving forward with steadiness and trust, and thank God for each step, because he is the one who gives the strength.
exp.4:0:
That same day, Deborah and Barak, the son of Abinoam, sang a song together. "That day" refers to the day of Israel's great victory over its enemies. What follows is the song itself, which praises the LORD.

Deborah was a prophetess and judge in Israel, and Barak was the military leader who led the battle against the army of Sisera, captain of Jabin, the Canaanite king (Judges 4). After God gave them the victory, they both sang to give thanks. Many scholars regard this poem as one of the oldest texts in the Bible, though not all agree on its exact date.

When God helps us, it is good to pause and thank Him clearly and publicly, not only in silence. Telling what He has done encourages others to trust Him. Today you can write down, or share with someone, a recent answer to prayer.
exp.4:1:
This verse opens a song of praise. Deborah and Barak invite everyone to bless the Lord for two reasons: God brought justice for Israel's wrongs and sufferings, and the people offered themselves freely, presenting themselves willingly and by their own choice. The first phrase in the Hebrew can be translated in several ways, and some versions say that the leaders took command.

Deborah, a prophetess and judge, and Barak, the military leader, are the ones speaking. They sing after the victory over Sisera's army, following years of oppression by the Canaanites. They recognize that the triumph came from God, and they also honor those who willingly offered to fight.

For today: serve God and others with joy, not out of obligation. And when you see his help, do not keep it silent; thank him and tell others about it.
exp.4:6:
It says that in Israel the villages ceased to exist, meaning that life in the open towns faded and declined. This lasted until Deborah arose as a mother in Israel, someone who cares for, guides, and protects her people. Some understand the word for "villages" as referring to the farmers or the people living in areas without walls; the Hebrew here carries some uncertainty.

Deborah speaks in her song of victory, together with Barak, after defeating the army of Sisera. She describes the earlier time: there was fear, the roads were unsafe, and people hid. She recognizes that God used her to rouse the people and restore peace.

For today: when everything around you seems dim or filled with fear, do not wait for someone else to take the step. God can use your courage and your care to encourage your family, your church, or your community.
exp.4:7:
They chose new gods, the explanation says, meaning that when Israel left the LORD to follow idols, war came right up to the gates of their cities. And in that moment of danger, not a single shield or spear could be seen among forty thousand men. The gates were the place of a city's defense and its government. Some understand this to describe a people without weapons; others, a people without the courage to fight.

Deborah, a prophetess and judge, speaks in a song of victory together with Barak. She recalls how badly things stood for Israel before she rose up: unsafe roads, empty villages. She points out that the root of the problem was spiritual: abandoning God left the people weak and defenseless.

For today: when we put other things in the place of God, money, success or fear, we lose our inner strength. Let us return to Him every day, and He will sustain us.
exp.4:9:
This verse is an invitation to speak. It is addressed to three groups: those who ride on white asses (people of good standing, since the white or light-colored donkey was a distinguished mount), those who sit in judgment, and those who simply walk along the way. To all of them it says: speak, that is, tell what God has done.

The one singing is Deborah, together with Barak, after Israel's victory over the army of Sisera. Before this there was fear and injustice, and the roads were unsafe. Now, with the deliverance, everyone must proclaim the works of the LORD. Some details of the Hebrew text allow different interpretations.

For today: do not keep silent about what God has done in your life. Whatever your place, at work, at home, or on the road, tell with humility and gratitude how God has helped you.
exp.4:13:
The verse names several tribes of Israel who answered the call to fight. From Ephraim came warriors who went out after Benjamin, together with their people. From Machir, of the tribe of Manasseh, came leaders. From Zebulun came those who handled the scribe's stylus, a rod or tool used by someone who recorded or directed the people. The phrase about Amalek is difficult, and scholars explain it in several ways.

Deborah speaks, along with Barak, in a song of victory over the Canaanites. She remembers who joined the battle and who did not, as Reuben does later on.

For today: God uses people of every kind, from warriors to scribes. Ask yourself what gift you have, and offer it gladly to serve in your church or community.
exp.4:14:
The explanation says that the princes of Issachar went with Deborah to the war. Barak also went down on foot into the valley to fight, without horses or chariots. On the other hand, among the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts of heart, that is, many doubts and deliberations, but apparently they did not go out to fight.

This is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, after they defeated the army of Sisera. They praise God and remember who helped and who stayed behind. Reuben appears as a tribe that stayed thinking for a long time, but without acting. Some scholars understand the text this way; others see it as a milder rebuke.

For today: thinking and praying before deciding is good, but we should not remain in mere doubts when God calls us to serve. Let us ask for courage to take the concrete step.
exp.4:16:
This verse names three tribes that did not go to the battle. Gilead, the region east of the Jordan, stayed there. Dan stayed near the ships, and Asher stayed along the coast, in its harbors and landing places. The questions sound like a reproach.

Deborah, together with Barak, speaks in a song of victory over the Canaanites. She praises the tribes that risked their lives and points out those that did not help. Some think they stayed because of their work or comfort; the text gives no further reasons.

For today: when others need help, it is easy to retreat into our own occupations. Ask God for the courage to serve, even when it costs you.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, is highly blessed, more than all the women who live in tents. "Blessed" here means praised and favored by God. "Kenite" refers to a nomadic people who lived in tents.

The one speaking is Deborah, together with Barak, in a song of victory after Israel defeated Sisera's army. Deborah celebrates that Jael brought down the enemy commander, while others, such as those of Meroz, did not help. Some scholars point out that the way Jael acted, with deception and violence, is a difficult account, and the text does not say that God approves all of her methods, but that it praises her courage.

For today: God calls us not to stay silent or passive when what is right needs defending. Ask him for wisdom to act with courage, but with integrity and love.
exp.4:25:
This verse describes how Jael took a tent peg and a workman's hammer, and with them struck Sisera on the head until she pierced his temples. The peg was the stake that held the tent in place.

It is part of the Song of Deborah and Barak, a victory song after the battle against the Canaanite army. Sisera, their commander, had fled and arrived at Jael's tent. She welcomed him with hospitality, and then killed him while he slept (Judges 4). The song celebrates this act as a deliverance for Israel. The Bible tells the story, but it does not explain whether everything Jael did is an example to follow.

Today we can learn that God can use unexpected people to deliver his people. Let us ask him for courage to act with justice and wisdom, without resorting to violence.
exp.4:27:
This verse shows the mother of Sisera, commander of Israel's enemy army, looking out of a window. She peers through the lattice, which are wooden grilles that let her see without being seen. Anxiously she calls out, asking why her son is taking so long to return with his war chariots.

This is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, which celebrates Israel's victory. We already know that Sisera died at the hands of Jael. While his mother waits expecting a victory, the reader knows that her son will not return. Scholars see some irony here; others also notice a human touch of a mother's grief.

For today: it is easy to trust our own plans and take the outcome for granted, as she and her ladies did. Let us learn to place our plans in God's hands, and to treat with compassion even the grief of those on the other side.
exp.4:28:
This verse says that the wisest and most sensible women of the court would answer the mother of Sisera when she wondered why her son was taking so long to return. But she herself ended up answering her own question, repeating what she wanted to believe.

This happens within the song of Deborah and Barak, which celebrates Israel's victory. Sisera's mother waits for her son at the window and imagines that the delay is because he is dividing the plunder. She does not know that Sisera is already dead. The text contrasts her false sense of security with reality.

Today it reminds us that we can comfort ourselves with answers that merely repeat our own desires. It is wise to seek the truth with humility, and to place our trust in God, not in comfortable assumptions.
exp.4:30:
This verse closes the song of Deborah and Barak with a prayer: that all of God's enemies would perish, and that those who love him would shine like the sun when it rises in full strength. The text then says that the land had peace for forty years.

Deborah and Barak speak after the victory over Sisera and the Canaanite army. Earlier, the song showed Sisera's mother and her ladies waiting for a plunder that never arrived. With that contrast, the song ends by asking that God's justice be fulfilled and that his people flourish. The forty years can be understood as an exact number or as a long period of peace.

For today: loving God is not only a feeling, but a life that is visible, like the light of a sunrise. Today you can ask him to give you strength to live with faithfulness and hope.
exp.5:0:
The explanation says that the people of Israel again did what God considered evil. Because of this, God allowed the Midianites to rule over them for seven years. The phrase "delivered them into the hand of" means that he let them fall under the power of another people.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel lived in the promised land, but again and again it turned away from God and followed other religious customs. The book shows a cycle: the people turn away, suffer the consequences, cry out to God, and He sends them a deliverer. The verses that follow describe how the Midianites ruined their harvests and how the people lived hidden in caves.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and turning away from God leaves us vulnerable. But this passage also invites us to return to Him, for in Judges God always hears the cry of those who repent.
exp.5:1:
The verse tells how the people of Midian grew stronger than Israel and took control over them. Out of fear, the Israelites left their homes and hid in dens in the mountains, in caves, and in strong places.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Judges. He explains that this happened because Israel did evil in the sight of God, and God allowed Midian to oppress them for seven years. The Midianites, together with other peoples, would come and destroy the harvests, and so the people lived hidden away and hungry.

For today: when we live in fear or in trouble, it is wise to ask ourselves humbly whether we have drifted away from God. Not all suffering comes from sin, but sometimes pain wakes us up to return to Him, who hears and rescues, as we will see later in this story.
exp.5:2:
They did not wait for the harvest to grow; they arrived just in time to wipe it out.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He explains that Israel had turned away from God, and that God allowed seven years of oppression. The people lived hidden in caves and strongholds, and they were left without food. Some understand this as God's discipline, meant to bring them back to him.

For today: when we feel that everything we sow is being lost, we can stop and pray honestly. God does not delight in our distress, but he can use it to draw us closer to him. Crying out to him is a good first step.
exp.5:3:
They camped against them and ruined the crops across the land, all the way to the city of Gaza in the southwest. They left nothing to eat, neither animals nor food. The phrase "camp" here means to set up camp, and the animals meant are donkeys.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges, who tells the story of Israel. Every time Israel planted, the invaders came and took everything. The text has already said that the people were suffering this oppression because they had done what was evil before God. That is why they lived hidden in caves. This suffering prepares the way for the people's cry to the LORD, and then for Gideon's call.

For today: when you feel that everything is running out and you have no way out, do not hide your need. Like Israel, you can cry out to God sincerely. He listens, even when the difficulties seem enormous.
exp.5:4:
This verse describes how the Midianites invaded Israel. They came with their livestock and their tents, and they were so numerous that they are compared to locusts, that is, to a plague of insects that devours the fields. Neither they nor their camels could be counted.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He explains the hard situation of Israel, which suffered these attacks year after year just when the harvest was coming in. The book had already said that Israel did evil in the sight of God, and for that reason the people were left in the hands of Midian. But the people eventually cried out to the LORD, and that prepares the way for the calling of Gideon.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by problems that seem like a plague too great to count, do not stay silent or alone. Cry out to God with sincerity. He hears, even when we have arrived at that situation through our own mistakes.
exp.5:5:
This verse says that Israel was left very poor and weak because of the Midianites, who were taking their crops and their animals. Then the people cried out, that is, they asked for help loudly, to the LORD. The word "impoverished" in the verse means they were left without resources, and "greatly" means very much.

It is part of the book of Judges. The narrator tells that Israel had turned away from God, and for that reason spent seven years under the oppression of Midian. The Midianites came like a plague of locusts, with so many camels that they could not be counted. After their cry, God sent a prophet to remind them that He had brought them out of Egypt.

For today: when you feel weak or without resources, do not wait until you hit bottom to pray. Speak to God honestly, and let Him also remind you of His faithfulness in the past.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel asked God for help with cries and pleas because of the Midianites. The word "cried" means calling out with force, out of pain. The verse is incomplete, because the sentence continues into the next verse.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells how Midian kept invading Israel's harvests and left them in poverty, like a plague of locusts. Here Israel was already desperate. What stands out is that God does not first respond by sending a deliverer, but by sending a prophet who reminds them how he brought them out of Egypt. In this way he shows them that their suffering was connected to having left him.

For today: when you are in trouble, cry out to God without waiting until you are perfect. And let him also speak to you, not only to take the problem away, but to heal what is twisted in your heart.
exp.5:10:
The explanation tells how the angel of the Lord came to a town called Ophrah and sat down under a large tree, which some translate as oak or terebinth. That tree belonged to Joash. His son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, which was normally a pit for treading grapes, in order to hide the grain from the Midianites.

Israel was oppressed by Midian, which took away their harvests. Before this verse, God reminded them through a prophet that He had brought them out of Egypt, but they had not obeyed Him. Even so, God does not abandon them: He sends His angel to seek out Gideon.

For today: God can call us in the middle of fear and of our daily tasks. Gideon was working in hiding, but God saw him. If you feel small or afraid today, remember that God sees you and can use you where you are.
exp.5:18:
Gideon goes into his house and prepares a young goat and unleavened cakes made with an ephah of flour (about twenty liters, though the exact measure is debated). He puts the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, and takes it out to the visitor, who is waiting for him under an oak, a sturdy kind of tree.

Gideon is a young Israelite whom the angel of the Lord has just called to deliver Israel from the Midianites. He hesitates and asks for a sign so that he can be sure God is speaking to him. That is why he prepares this offering, which was an act of hospitality and worship. Then the fire from the rock consumes the food, and this confirms to him that the message comes from God.

For today: when God calls you to something great and you have doubts, do not stay frozen. Bring Him honestly what you have, even if it seems little, and let Him confirm and guide the next step.
exp.5:20:
He says the angel of the Lord stretched out the staff he carried in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread with its tip. Then fire came up out of the rock and consumed everything. After that the angel left, and Gideon no longer saw him.

Gideon was a fearful Israelite, and his people were suffering under the oppression of Midian. The angel had told him that God would use him to deliver Israel. Gideon asked for a sign and prepared an offering. The fire confirmed that the message truly came from God. Some believe this angel represents God himself, since the text also calls him Jehovah; others see him as a special messenger.

For today: when God calls you to something that frightens you, you can bring your doubts to him honestly. He knows how to confirm his word and to give you the peace to obey.
exp.5:24:
God tells Gideon that very night to take two bulls from his father's herd: one ordinary bull and another that is seven years old. With them he is to pull down his father's altar to Baal and cut down the sacred pole beside it. That pole was probably a wooden post or tree dedicated to a pagan goddess, called Asherah in Hebrew.

The Lord speaks just after Gideon saw him and received peace. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had fallen into idolatry. Before giving him the military victory, God first wants to cleanse Gideon's own household. The verses that follow show that he obeyed at night, out of fear, yet he did obey.

For today: before attempting great things for God, ask him what idols or bad habits are in your own home and heart. Obey even when you are afraid; God values the sincere step, even when it is small and trembling.
exp.5:25:
God tells Gideon to build an altar to the LORD on the top of this rock, in a suitable place. Then he is to take the second bull and offer it whole as a burnt offering, a sacrifice that was burned up completely. For the fire he would use the wood of the grove that he cuts down, which in other versions is rendered as the Asherah, a pole or sacred tree of pagan worship that Gideon was to cut down.

The LORD speaks the same night that Gideon is called. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had given itself over to idolatry. Before freeing the people, God wants to clean out Gideon's household: first to tear down the altar of Baal that his father had, and then to worship the true God.

For today: before asking God for great victories, it is wise to ask ourselves what things have taken his place in our hearts. Obeying in the small, nearby matters, even when it is frightening, as Gideon did, opens the way for God to work.
exp.5:27:
It says that when the people of the town got up in the morning, they found the altar of Baal torn down. The wooden pole beside it had also been cut down; here it refers to a post or tree used in pagan worship (some versions call it Asherah). Also, the second bull had been offered as a burnt offering, that is, burned completely, on a new altar.

God had commanded Gideon to do this. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had fallen into idolatry. Gideon obeyed, but he did it at night because he was afraid of his family and the people. His fear did not keep him from obeying.

For today: sometimes obeying God frightens us. God does not ask us to feel no fear, but to take the step of faith in spite of it. Do today what you know God is asking of you, even if it is a little at a time.
exp.5:29:
The men of the city demand that Joash hand over his son Gideon so that they can kill him. They accuse him of having torn down the altar of Baal and of having cut down the grove beside it, which here is the wooden post or tree dedicated to the goddess Asherah.

The people of the town of Ophrah speak in anger after discovering what happened during the night. God had asked Gideon to destroy that altar, which belonged to his own father. For them, attacking Baal was a serious offense that deserved death. Joash, however, challenges them: if Baal is a god, let him defend himself.

Obeying God can bring rejection, even from people close to us. But God cares for those who are faithful to Him. Ask Him for courage to leave behind whatever competes with Him, even when others do not understand.
exp.5:30:
Joash tells the angry men that it makes no sense to stand up for Baal. He asks whether they are going to take up Baal's cause, that is, plead for him, and whether they are going to save him. He warns that whoever pleads for him will be put to death early, in the morning. And he concludes: if Baal is a god, let him plead for himself against the one who pulled down his altar.

Joash, the father of Gideon, is speaking. The people of the town wanted to kill his son for tearing down the altar of Baal. It is striking that Joash, whose altar it was, now protects Gideon. We do not know everything that was going on in his heart, but his words show how weak that idol was. That is why Gideon received the name Jerubbaal.

For today: what is truly God does not need us to defend him with violence or with fear. Examine the things in which you trust too much, and rest in the living God.
exp.5:34:
This verse tells how Gideon sent messengers throughout the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, and the people there gathered to follow him. He also sent messengers to the tribes of Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they came up to meet them.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. The Midianites, the Amalekites, and other peoples from the east had camped in the valley of Jezreel to attack Israel. God had put his Spirit upon Gideon, and he began to gather his people. Shortly afterward, Gideon would ask God for a sign with the fleece of wool.

For today: when God calls you to a difficult task, you do not have to carry it alone. Ask for help, bring other believers together, and walk with them, trusting that God is the one who gives the strength.
exp.5:36:
Gideon tells God that he will put a fleece, that is, a piece of sheep's wool, on the threshing floor, which is the open-air place where wheat was beaten out. If in the morning only the fleece is wet with dew and all the ground is dry, he will understand that God will indeed save Israel through him, just as he promised.

Gideon is the one speaking. God had already called him and had promised to free Israel from its oppressors. Now the enemy armies are drawing near, and Gideon has gathered people from several tribes. Even so, he feels fear and asks for a sign to confirm the promise.

For today: God invites us to trust what he has already told us in his Word. Gideon asked for a sign because of his weakness, and God was patient with him. But we do not need to keep asking for signs over and over. We can pray with sincerity, admit our fears, and move forward in faith, relying on the promises God has already given us.
exp.5:38:
Gideon speaks to God carefully and asks him not to be angry with him for asking once more. He wants to make another test with the fleece, which is the wool of a sheep. Now he asks for the opposite of the first time: that only the fleece be dry, and that the dew, that is, the moisture of the night, fall upon all the ground.

Gideon is the one speaking, the man whom God called to deliver Israel from the oppression of Midian. He had already received promises from God, but he still felt fear and uncertainty. God, with patience, answered his request. Some see here a weakness of faith; others see an example of God's kindness toward someone fragile.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them to God with honesty and humility. But do not keep asking for signs; seek guidance in his Word, in prayer, and in the counsel of wise people.
exp.5:39:
This verse tells us that God did that night what Gideon had asked of him. The fleece, which is a sheep's wool, was dry in the morning, while all the ground around it was wet with dew. It is the reverse of the first sign.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Gideon, called by God to deliver Israel from the Midianites, felt fear and doubt. He had already asked for a sign with the wet fleece and the dry ground. Then he asked for a second one, begging God not to be angry for asking again. God answered him with patience. Some see here a weakness of faith, and others see God's kindness toward him.

For today: if you have doubts, bring them honestly and humbly to God. But do not keep asking for signs; seek to confirm his will in his Word, in prayer, and in the counsel of wise people, and then obey with confidence.
exp.6:5:
This verse tells how only three hundred men were left. They took the water in their hand and brought it to their mouth. All the others knelt down to drink straight from the water.

God speaks to Gideon before the battle against Midian. Israel had a large army, and God wanted to reduce it so that no one would think the victory came from their own strength. It is not known for certain why this way of drinking made a difference; some think it showed greater alertness, but the text does not say so.

For today: God does not depend on our abundance, but on our willingness to trust Him. When you feel small or short on resources, remember that God can work with the little you have.
exp.6:8:
God speaks to Gideon at night and commands him to get up and go down to the enemy camp. He assures him that he has already given the Midianites into his hand.

Here it is God himself who speaks. Gideon had already been left with only three hundred men, a very small group facing an enormous army. This made it clear that the victory would come from God and not from human strength. God knows that Gideon is afraid, and that is why, in the verses that follow, he offers that Gideon go down with his servant Purah to listen to the enemy and be encouraged.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, God is not angry at your fear. He encourages you to take the step you are able to take, and to trust his promise. Obey today in what is asked of you, even if you feel afraid.
exp.6:9:
God offers Gideon a gentle way out: if he still feels fear about attacking, he may first go down to the enemy camp, accompanied by Purah, his servant or attendant. The word "go down" means to go down, and the camp refers to the Midianite encampment, which was in the valley.

God is the one speaking, and He addresses Gideon at night. Gideon had just reduced his army to three hundred men, and even so God had promised him the victory. God knows Gideon's fear and does not scold him. He suggests that Gideon listen to what the enemies are saying so that his courage may be strengthened. The verses that follow show that Gideon did go down.

For today: when you feel fear before a great challenge, do not hide it. Bring it honestly before God, and take the next step, even if it is small and taken with someone you trust. He knows how to strengthen those who come to Him with humility.
exp.6:10:
God tells Gideon that, if he is still afraid, he should go down to the enemy camp and listen to what they say. By this, his hands will be made strong, meaning he will regain courage and strength. The "armed men" are the soldiers carrying weapons. The "servant" is an attendant or helper. Gideon goes down with Phurah (as it is spelled today) to the edge of the camp.

The LORD speaks to Gideon at night. He had already promised him victory, but He knows Gideon's fear and does not scold him. He gives him a concrete step to strengthen his faith. The Midianites were very numerous, and Gideon had only three hundred men, so his fear was understandable.

For today: when you are afraid, do not hide it. Bring it honestly before God. He can give you signs and support to take the next step. Obey even if it is with fear, and seek the company of someone, as Gideon had with Phurah.
exp.6:11:
This verse describes the enormous enemy camp. Midian, Amalek, and the peoples of the east (groups who lived east of Israel) were spread out across the valley. They are compared to locusts because of their great number, and their camels to the sand on the seashore, too many to count.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. God had offered Gideon the chance to go down by night into the enemy camp, together with his servant Phurah (called Phara in this version), so that he could listen and be encouraged. Gideon was afraid, and the text shows how great the challenge was: a few men of Israel facing a multitude.

For today: sometimes our problems seem like an endless army. God does not deny that they are great, but he invites us to come to him with our fear, and he knows how to give us courage at just the right moment.
exp.6:12:
This verse tells how Gideon went down to the enemy camp and overheard a Midianite soldier telling his companion about a dream. In the dream, a loaf of barley bread rolled into the camp, struck the tents, and knocked them down completely. The soldier's words for "struck" and "overturned" are clear in the verse itself: the bread hit the tent and turned it over until it lay flat.

God had told Gideon to go down to the camp with his servant Purah, because there he would hear something that would encourage him. Gideon was afraid, and the enemy army was enormous. The barley bread was humble and simple food, and the companion interpreted it as Gideon's sword. In this way, God used an enemy to confirm his promise.

For today: when you feel small before a large problem, remember that God can use what is humble to accomplish great things. Ask him for encouragement and trust his guidance.
exp.6:13:
This verse tells how a Midianite soldier explains his dream of the barley loaf to his companion. He says that the loaf is nothing other than the sword of Gideon, and that God has already given the Midianites and their whole camp into Gideon's hand. Being given into his hand means God has granted him the victory. A man of Israel simply means an Israelite man.

Gideon had gone down at night into the enemy camp, afraid, because God had directed him to. There he heard one soldier tell his dream and another interpret it. The barley loaf was humble food, just like Gideon and his small army of three hundred. God used an enemy to encourage Gideon, and Gideon responded by worshiping.

For today: when you feel small or afraid before a great problem, remember that God can encourage you in unexpected ways. Respond as Gideon did: give thanks, trust, and take the next step.
exp.6:14:
This verse tells how Gideon, after hearing a Midianite soldier's dream and what his companion said it meant, bowed down to worship God. Then he returned to the Israelite camp and gave the order to get up, because God had already handed the enemy camp over to them.

Gideon had gone down into the Midianite camp at night, along with his servant Purah, to strengthen his courage. There he heard the dream of a barley loaf that tumbled into the tents. The companion understood it as a sign that Gideon would win. The text does not explain how God used those words, but Gideon received them as confirmation from God.

Before acting, Gideon first worshipped. When God gives you encouragement or answers a prayer, take a moment to thank him. That thankfulness strengthens your confidence to take the next step with courage.
exp.6:15:
This verse tells that Gideon divided his three hundred men into three groups. He gave each man a trumpet (a horn, usually made from an animal's horn) and an empty clay jar with a burning torch inside it.

The one acting here is the narrator, who describes Gideon. He had just secretly overheard the dream of a Midianite soldier, which foretold their defeat. This encouraged him, and he worshiped God. Now he prepares a simple plan: at first they will not use swords, but sound and light, to confuse the enemy. The jar hid the fire until the moment they broke it.

For today: God can use small and fragile things, like a jar, when we obey Him with trust. Before taking a difficult step, stop to worship and remember that God goes before you.
exp.6:18:
This verse tells how Gideon and his hundred men came to the edge of the enemy camp, just as the middle watch of the night was beginning, when the guards had only just changed shifts. Then they blew the trumpets, and they broke the clay jars they were carrying in their hands. Inside those jars, according to the account, they had hidden the torches.

It is part of the story of Gideon, whom God called to rescue Israel from the Midianites. God reduced his army to only 300 men so that it would be clear the victory came from Him. Here Gideon sets the example, and his men follow it, carrying out the plan God had given him.
