For today: God can work through small resources and plans that seem strange, when we follow them with obedience. Do today, in faith, what He asks of you, even when it seems like very little.
exp.6:22:
This verse tells how, after the Midianites fled in fear, the men of Israel from the tribes of Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh gathered together and went out to pursue them. "Pursued" here means they went after them in order to catch up with them. Before this, only three hundred men had been with Gideon.

Context: This is the account in the book of Judges; the narrator is telling what happened, not a character speaking. God had reduced Gideon's army so that Israel would know the victory came from Him. With trumpets, torches, and shouting, the enemy camp fell into panic. Now, with the enemy in flight, other Israelites join in and take advantage of the victory.

For today: God can begin a work with a few people and then encourage others to join. If He gives you a step of faith, take that step without waiting for crowds, and when others come alongside, work together with humility and give God the credit.
exp.6:23:
Gideon sent messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim. He asked them to come down to fight against the Midianites and to cut off their escape by taking the crossing points of the water, from Beth-barah as far as the Jordan River. Taking the waters means holding those passages so the enemy cannot get away. The men of Ephraim gathered together and did so.

Gideon, the judge of Israel, spoke after God had given the victory with only three hundred men. The Midianites were fleeing, and Gideon needed more people to close off their way out. The exact location of Beth-barah is not known with certainty.

For today: God can begin a work with a few, but He also wants others to take part. When He gives you an advance, invite others humbly to help and to finish what He has started.
exp.7:1:
Gideon asks the men of Ephraim what he has done in comparison with what they have done. He uses an image from the field: the gleaning is what is left in the vineyard after the harvest, and the vintage is the grape harvest. He says that the little Ephraim gathered is worth more than the whole harvest of Abiezer, which was Gideon's clan.

The men of Ephraim were upset because Gideon did not call them at the beginning to fight against Midian. Gideon, who is the one speaking, answers with humility. Then he reminds them that God put the Midianite leaders Oreb and Zeeb into their hands. With those words, their anger was calmed.

For today: a humble answer can put out an argument. Before defending yourself, acknowledge the good that others have done. Valuing others helps to protect peace and keeps unity.
exp.7:2:
Gideon tells the men of Ephraim that God gave them the greater victory: they captured Oreb and Zeeb, the leaders of Midian. Then he asks, "What was I able to do in comparison of you?" With those words, their anger was calmed.

Gideon speaks to the tribe of Ephraim, which was upset because he did not call them at the beginning of the battle. They felt ignored and complained harshly. Gideon does not argue or defend himself; he acknowledges what they did and honors it. Ephraim probably also cared about its pride, although the text does not say this clearly.

For today: a humble and kind answer can calm an argument. When someone feels hurt or ignored, instead of fighting, we can recognize the good they have done and give them their place. As Proverbs 15:1 says, a soft answer turns away wrath.
exp.7:7:
He went up from there to Penuel and made the same request to them. The men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had answered him, meaning they also refused to help him.

Gideon was pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, with three hundred men who were tired and hungry. These cities belonged to his own people, but they did not want to risk supporting him, out of fear of the Midianites' revenge if Gideon failed. Their refusal was selfish and disloyal. The following verses show that Gideon responded with threats.

For today: when God works through someone, let us not be among those who stand by and watch out of fear or comfort. Let us support those who serve with generosity and faith, even when the result is not yet visible.
exp.7:9:
This verse tells us where the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, were. They were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand soldiers, all that was left of the huge army of the peoples from the east. Earlier, one hundred and twenty thousand men who drew the sword, that is, armed warriors, had been killed.

The narrator is speaking. Gideon had been pursuing the Midianites with three hundred weary men, and two cities, Succoth and Penuel, had refused to give them bread. This detail shows how hard the task was: the enemy still far outnumbered them. Even so, God had already given great victories. The Bible does not explain the exact location of Karkor, and scholars do not fully agree on it.

For today: do not give up halfway through the road just because what remains looks large. If God has helped you this far, you can keep going with faith and patience, taking the next step with Him.
exp.7:10:
Gideon went up by the way of those who lived in tents, that is, nomadic people who wandered through the desert, to the east of Nobah and Jogbehah. There he attacked the enemy camp by surprise, for the army was secure, that is, confident and not expecting any danger.

This is what the narrator of the book of Judges tells us. Gideon pursued the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, who had fled with about fifteen thousand men. He had already warned the people of Penuel that he would return. The exact location of his route through the desert is hard to pin down, and scholars do not fully agree on the details.

For today: Gideon finished what he had started, even when he was tired and the pursuit was difficult. May God give us perseverance to faithfully carry out what He has entrusted to us, and may we not lower our guard by trusting ourselves too much.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that Gideon, son of Joash, returned from the battle before the sun was up. In other words, he came back from the fight very early, while it was still dawn. Some modern translations understand the phrase differently: that he returned by the ascent of Heres. The Hebrew can be read in either way, so there is no complete certainty.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Gideon had just surprised a Midianite camp that was overconfident, and he had captured the two kings, Zebah and Zalmunna. Now he returns, and the account sets up his encounter with the men of Succoth, who had earlier refused to give bread to his weary people.

For today: finishing well what God has given us to do requires perseverance. Gideon did not stop when he was tired; he pressed on until he brought the matter to its close. Let us ask for strength to persevere and to carry out our responsibilities to the end.
exp.7:13:
Gideon seized a young man from the city of Succoth and questioned him. The young man wrote down for him the names of the town's leaders: the princes and the elders, seventy-seven men in all.

The narrator tells how Gideon was pursuing the kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna. Earlier, when he and his men were tired and hungry, the leaders of Succoth refused to give his men bread and mocked him. Now Gideon returns and wants to know exactly who was responsible. We do not know why a young man knew those names, but it served to identify them.

For today: when someone needs help and we have the chance to give it, let us not refuse out of fear or selfishness. God sees our decisions, and refusing support to those who serve a good cause has consequences.
exp.7:16:
This verse tells that Gideon, after punishing the leaders of Succoth, tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of that city. The tower was probably a strong place for defense.

Gideon was pursuing the Midianite kings, Zebah and Zalmunna, while his men were exhausted. The people of Succoth and Penuel refused to give him bread and mocked him, as if the victory were not certain. He had promised to return and answer them. The text narrates what he did, but it does not say that God commanded him to do it, so many read it as a personal revenge.

For today: when someone refuses us help or mocks us, revenge can lead us too far. It is better to help the one who is tired and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.7:17:
Gideon asks Zebah and Zalmunna, the two kings of Midian whom he had captured, what kind of men they were whom they killed at Tabor. They answer that the men were like him, with a noble appearance, "each one resembled the children of a king."

Gideon has been pursuing the Midianites. He had already punished Succoth and Penuel because they had not helped him. With his question, he discovers that those men who were killed were his own brothers. The Bible does not tell us here how that killing happened. That is why his next answer sounds like grief and personal revenge.

For today: when pain or anger takes control of us, it is easy for justice to become mixed with revenge. Before we act, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask God to guide our hearts. And remember that He calls us to trust in His justice.
exp.7:19:
Gideon orders Jether, his firstborn son, to get up and kill the two captured Midianite kings. But the young man did not draw his sword, because he was afraid. He was still just a youth.

Gideon is the one speaking. Zebah and Zalmunna had killed his brothers at Tabor, and he seeks justice for that family blood. In asking his son to do it, he may have meant to honor or prepare him, though the text does not explain this. Jether's fear is understandable given his age. Then Gideon himself kills them.

For today: not all of us are ready for every task. If something intimidates you, acknowledge your limits with humility and ask for help. As for young people, let us give them responsibilities little by little, without shaming them when they are not yet prepared.
exp.7:20:
Zebah and Zalmunna, the two captured kings of Midian, ask Gideon to kill them himself, because a man is measured by his strength. Gideon does so and takes the ornaments that were on their camels' necks, which were crescent-shaped pieces hanging from the necks of the camels.

Gideon had pursued these kings because they had killed his brothers at Tabor. First he asked his son Jether to execute them, but the young man was afraid. That is why the kings ask Gideon himself to do it. It is a scene of justice and revenge in a time of war. Afterward, Gideon refuses to be king, saying that only God should rule.

Today, this passage invites us not to let pain dominate us, and to remember that God is the one who holds the highest place in our lives. Gideon knew how to reject the power that was offered to him. We can ask God for humility so that we do not seek our own honor.
exp.7:21:
The men of Israel ask Gideon to be their ruler, and that after him his son and his grandson should rule as well. They want a dynasty, meaning that the leadership would pass from father to son. Here the idea of ruling means being king or a leader with authority.

The people of Israel speak, grateful that God saved them from Midian through Gideon. They have just seen a great victory and want to secure their protection with a human leader. Gideon answers in the following verse that only the LORD should rule. However, the Bible does not say that their request was entirely wrong, and later Gideon does something that becomes a snare for the people.

For today: when God gives us a victory, let us give Him the glory and not put a person in the place that belongs only to God.
exp.7:22:
Gideon refuses to be ruler or governor over Israel, and he also refuses to let his son rule. He says that the true Lord of the people is the LORD, that is, God. The word "rule" means to govern or have authority over others.

The Israelites, grateful because Gideon had delivered them from Midian, ask him to be their ruler, and then to let his son and grandson rule after him. Gideon answers with humility, acknowledging that the victory came from God. However, the account goes on to show that Gideon later asks for gold and does something that becomes a snare for the people, so his life is a mixture of faith and failure.

For today: when you receive praise or success, give the glory back to God. Remember too that no one, neither you nor others, should take the place that belongs to Him alone in your life.
exp.7:23:
Gideon asks the Israelites for a favor: that each one give him the gold earrings he took from the spoils of war. "Earrings" here means the same thing as the earrings or pendants we wear today. The text explains that the defeated enemies wore gold earrings because they were Ishmaelites, a name used here for those desert peoples.

Gideon had just refused to be king and had said that only the LORD would rule over them. But now he asks for gold. Later, with that gold, he makes an ephod, and the people end up worshiping it as something sacred (Judges 8:27). The Bible does not state clearly what his intention was; many think he wanted a reminder of the victory, but it ended up becoming a trap.

For today: a good work can be damaged by a poorly considered decision. Let us ask God for wisdom so that our good desires do not become a stumbling block for others.
exp.7:24:
The people of Israel gladly accept Gideon's request. They spread a cloak or garment on the ground, and each soldier throws into it the earrings, that is, the gold earrings he had taken from the spoils.

Gideon had just defeated the Midianites. The Israelites wanted to make him king, but he said that only the LORD should rule. Then he asked for the gold. Afterward he made from it an ephod, a sacred garment, and the people ended up worshiping it. That is why the Bible calls it a snare. Gideon's motives are not explained with certainty.

A good decision can be twisted by one step taken without careful thought. Let us take care that what we do with good intentions does not take the place of God in our hearts.
exp.7:25:
The gold earrings that Gideon asked for weighed one thousand seven hundred shekels, about 19 kilos by common calculations. That did not include the ornaments, the pendants, the purple clothing of the kings of Midian, or the collars on their camels. "Earrings" are the rings worn in the ears, and the small hanging jewels are the ornaments that dangled from them.

Gideon speaks after defeating Midian. He asks his soldiers for part of the spoil, and they give willingly. The text shows how much wealth there was. Then Gideon makes an ephod from that gold, and the people worship it. Scholars debate exactly what that ephod was, but the text says it became a snare.

Today: a victory or a blessing can become a trap if we turn what God gave us into a symbol of pride. Give thanks to God, and do not place your trust in what you have achieved.
exp.7:31:
This verse tells us that Gideon, son of Joash, died at an advanced age, after a long life. He was buried in the tomb of his father, in Ophrah, the town of the family of the Abiezrites.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges sums up the end of Gideon's life. He had delivered Israel from the Midianites. But just before this, his large family is mentioned, his many wives, and his son Abimelech, something that will later bring trouble. After his death, the people forgot God and worshiped Baal.

For today: a successful life does not guarantee that others will keep following God once we are gone. It is good to teach the faith steadily, at home and at church, so that it does not depend on just one person.
exp.7:33:
This verse says that the people of Israel forgot the LORD their God. It is not only that the thought slipped their minds: they stopped keeping Him present in their lives. And they forgot Him even though He had rescued them from all the enemies that surrounded them. The word "delivered" in the verse means saved or rescued.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He explains what happened when Gideon died, the leader who had led the people to defeat their enemies. Without their leader, Israel returned to idolatry and took Baal-berith as their god. The text shows that ingratitude toward God also led to ingratitude toward Gideon's family.

For today: remembering often what God has done for us helps us remain faithful, especially in times of change. We can thank Him every day and tell others how He has helped us.
exp.8:3:
The people of Shechem gave Abimelech seventy pieces of silver, taken from the temple of Baal-berith. With that money he hired men who were idle and worthless, that is, people without a trade, without direction, and ready for anything. These men followed him.

The narrator describes how Abimelech, son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) and of a woman from Shechem, seeks to become king. He had already won over his mother's relatives and the people of Shechem. Now he uses money from the temple of a false god to form his small band. The next verse shows what for: to kill his seventy brothers.

For today: power gained with tainted money and people without convictions ends in violence. Before following a leader or an opportunity, let us ask where their support comes from and what they really want.
exp.8:4:
Judges 9:5 tells how Abimelech went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon). There were seventy of them, and he slew them on one stone. Only Jotham, the youngest son, survived, because he hid himself.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how Abimelech, using money from Shechem and violent men he hired, sought to take power for himself. His relatives on his mother's side supported him in Shechem. To secure his rule, he eliminated those who could compete with him. Some scholars think that "seventy" is a rounded number, but the text presents it as a great family massacre.

For today: unlimited ambition destroys those closest to us. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that does not use people or money to climb, and that cares for family instead of harming it.
exp.8:5:
All the men of Shechem and all the people of Beth-millo gathered together and went and made Abimelech king, beside the oak or pillar that stood in Shechem. The phrase about the plain of the pillar probably refers to a well-known place in the city, perhaps next to a tree or a standing stone.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. Abimelech, son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), had paid reckless men with silver from the temple of Baal-berith and had killed his seventy brothers. Only Jotham escaped. So this kingship is born out of violence, ambition, and the support of people willing to stay silent about injustice.

For today: it is not enough that something is popular or gains support for it to be good. Before we follow a leader or back a decision, let us ask how it came about and whether it honors God and respects people's lives.
exp.8:8:
Here the olive tree refuses the offer to become king over the trees. It says it will not leave its rich, abundant oil, which serves to honor God and people. For the olive tree, giving up that work to rule over the others is not worth it.

Jotham, the son of Gideon, speaks from Mount Gerizim to the men of Shechem. He tells them this fable because they made Abimelech king, and Abimelech had killed Jotham's brothers. The olive tree stands for those who serve well and do not seek power. Many understand that oil was used in offerings and to honor people, which is why it is said to honor God and men.

For today: value the good gift God has given you to do, and do not trade it for a position or fame. Faithful service is worth more than rising at any cost.
exp.8:10:
The explanation says that the fig tree does not want to give up its sweetness or its good fruit to go and rule over the other trees. She prefers to keep giving what she knows how to give.

It is part of a fable that Jotham, son of Gideon, tells to the people of Shechem. The trees look for a king: first the olive, then the fig tree and the vine refuse the position. Jotham speaks because Abimelech, his brother, made himself king by killing almost all his brothers. The fable criticizes that desire for power.

For today: value the fruit that God has given you to serve, even when no one applauds you. Serving with humility and kindness is worth more than seeking a position only to stand out.
exp.8:11:
In this verse, the trees have gone looking for a king, and they approach the grapevine with a simple request: "Come and reign over us." The olive tree and the fig tree have already turned them down, so the trees now try the vine.

This is part of a fable that Jotham, the son of Gideon, tells the people of Shechem. They had made Abimelech king, a man who had killed his own brothers to seize power. Jotham uses the trees to show that the good and fruitful people did not want to rule, and that in the end someone harmful took the throne, pictured as the bramble, a thorny plant.

For today, let us value those who serve with humility and produce good fruit, and be wary of anyone who seeks power at any cost. Before choosing a leader, let us look at their character, not only their ambition.
exp.8:12:
The explanation says that the vine, when the trees ask her to be their queen, refuses. She values her new wine, that is, the juice of the grape, which brings joy to God and to people. She does not want to trade that useful task for a position of power over the other trees.

Jotam, the youngest son of Gideon, tells this fable to the people of Shechem. They had made Abimelech king, and he had killed his brothers to reign. Jotam uses the trees to show that good and fruitful people did not seek the throne, and that the one who did want it was someone who knew only how to harm.

For today: value the good gifts God has given you to serve, even if they bring you no fame or authority. Being useful and faithful is worth more than rising in position at any cost.
exp.8:13:
The explanation says that after the other trees turned down the offer, all the trees go to the bramble and ask it to be their king. The bramble is a thorny shrub, of little value and without useful fruit.

It is a parable told by Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). Abimelech had killed his brothers to make himself king of Shechem. Jotham uses the story to say that the good trees, like the vine, did not want to reign, and that only the thorny shrub accepted. Many understand that the bramble represents Abimelech, although the text gives no further details about the exact plant.

For today: before following a leader, do not look only at his ambition or his promises. Look at his character and at the fruit of his life. And if you are the one who must lead, do it with humility and service, not out of pride.
exp.8:15:
This verse is the start of a pointed question. Jotham tells the people of Shechem: if you really acted with sincerity and integrity in making Abimelech king, and if you dealt well with Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon) and his family, then all is well. Giving Gideon back the good he did is what it means to repay him according to what his hands had done.

Jotham, the only one of Gideon's sons who survived, speaks from Mount Gerizim after Abimelech has killed his brothers. He has just told the parable of the trees. With this "if" he shows them, ironically, that their action was unjust and treacherous. He warns that it will bring consequences.

For today: before supporting a leader or making an important decision, ask yourself whether you are acting with truth, gratitude, and justice. God looks at the heart and at the consequences of our decisions.
exp.8:17:
This verse accuses the men of Shechem of a grave wrong. It says they rose up against the household of Gideon (Jerubbaal), killed seventy of his sons on one stone, and made Abimelech, the son of Gideon's female servant, king over them, only because he was their relative.

The one speaking is Jotham, the only son of Gideon who escaped with his life. From Mount Gerizim he shouts this to the people of Shechem after telling them a parable. He wants them to see that their treatment of Gideon's family was betrayal, not gratitude or justice.

For today: loyalty and gratitude matter. If someone has done us good, we should not repay them with harm, nor support violence out of convenience or because of family ties. Let us ask God for the courage to act with truth and integrity.
exp.8:19:
It says that, if the people of Shechem and Abimelech did not act with truth and integrity, God would let fire come out from Abimelech and burn up the men of Shechem and the house of Millo, and also let fire come out from them and burn up Abimelech. The house of Millo seems to be a house or stronghold of Shechem; its exact meaning is not entirely certain. The fire is a way of speaking about destruction and mutual conflict.

The speaker is Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). He escaped when Abimelech killed his brothers. From Mount Gerizim he told a parable, and now he ends with this warning: if they did wrong in making Abimelech king, that wrong would turn back against all of them. Then he fled to Beer out of fear.

For today: alliances built on violence or injustice do not last, and in the end they harm everyone. Before we support a leader or a plan, let us ask whether it is based on truth and integrity.
exp.8:20:
Jotham ran away and fled, and went to live in a place called Beer. He stayed there, far from his family, because he was afraid of his brother Abimelech. Nobody knows for certain where Beer was; we only know it was a remote place.

Jotham was the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). Abimelech, his half-brother, had killed the other sons of Gideon in order to become king in Shechem. Jotham escaped, climbed Mount Gerizim, told a parable to the people of Shechem, and warned them with a curse. Afterward he fled, since Abimelech would have killed him too.

For today: sometimes it is wise to step away from danger and leave justice in God's hands. Jotham did not take revenge on his own; he trusted that God would see what had been done, and the account shows that this is what happened.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years. The word "reigned" means that he gave orders and held power, and it sounds more like forcing one's way to control than like serving. It is a short phrase that sets up what comes next.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book of Judges. Abimelech had come to power by killing his brothers, and Jotham, the only one who escaped, had warned that this fire of violence would turn back on him and on Shechem. These three years seem to be a time of calm before that warning comes true. The verses that follow say that God sent an evil spirit between them, and the Bible does not explain in detail how that happened.

For today: power gained through injustice may seem firm for a time, but it does not go unanswered. Let us seek to act with justice and trust that God sees everything.
exp.8:23:
God allowed the conflict between Abimelech and the men of Shechem so that the wickedness committed against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal (Gideon) would receive its answer. The injustice done to them would be repaid. The men of Shechem who backed him were guilty too.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Abimelech had killed his brothers to become king, and the men of Shechem supported him. Three years later the relationship breaks down. The text says that God sent an evil spirit between them, and that expression is understood in several ways. What is clear is that the account shows the crime did not go without consequences, both for the one who committed it and for those who helped him.

For today: it is not enough to avoid doing evil; we are also responsible if we back it or make it possible. Let us ask God for the courage to refuse to support injustice, even when it would be convenient for us.
exp.8:24:
This verse tells that the men of Shechem set ambushes on the tops of the mountains. Those men attacked everyone who passed along the road. People who lie hidden and wait to attack are described here as ambushers, and the verse says they robbed travelers. In the end, someone told Abimelech what was happening.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Abimelech had killed his seventy brothers in order to rule, and the people of Shechem had supported him. The text says that God sent an evil spirit that set the two sides against each other. It is usually understood as a mistrust and hostility allowed by God, as a judgment for so much blood that had been shed. The people of Shechem now rebel against him.

For today: evil built on violence and betrayal does not bring lasting peace. Let us ask God to keep us from seeking power or advantage by doing harm, and let us trust that he is just.
exp.8:28:
Gaal, speaking with pride, says that he wishes all the people were under his command. He then challenges Abimelech: to gather more soldiers and come out to fight.

Gaal, son of Ebed, speaks during a grape harvest festival in Shechem. The people were resentful toward Abimelech, who had ruled with violence. Gaal takes advantage of the people's anger by eating and drinking in the temple of their gods to gain power. His speech sparks a rebellion, and Zebul, the city's officer, warns Abimelech.

For today: beware of bold words spoken in the heat of the moment, especially when we are seeking power. True strength rests on God and on humility, not on pride or on the anger of the crowd.
exp.8:34:
This verse tells how Gaal, the son of Ebed, went out and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city of Shechem. At that moment, Abimelech and all his people rose up from where they had been hidden.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Zebul, the ruler of the city and loyal to Abimelech, had advised the attack. Gaal had rebelled against Abimelech and boasted before the people. Now he goes out without noticing the danger, and Abimelech's plan begins to take effect.

For today: big words and self-confidence can blind us. It is wise to be humble, to watch carefully, and to seek God's wisdom before facing any situation.
exp.8:35:
Gaal sees people coming down from the highest points of the mountains and tells Zebul about it. Zebul answers him that it is only the shadow of the mountains, which looks to him like people.

Gaal is the one who had risen up against Abimelech and was leading the men of Shechem. Zebul, the governor of the city, also speaks; he was secretly on Abimelech's side. Zebul wants Gaal not to take the danger seriously and to stay confident, while Abimelech draws near. Afterward Zebul confronts him for his proud words.

For today: let us not downplay clear warnings, nor trust someone who reassures us while hiding their own interests. Let us be humble, look at reality carefully, and seek sincere counsel, above all from God, before it is too late.
exp.8:38:
This verse tells how Gaal, pushed on by Zebul's words, goes out at the head of the men of Shechem to fight against Abimelech. "Went out before" means that he was leading them toward the battle. "Shechem" is the city of Shechem.

Here the narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Gaal had spoken proudly against Abimelech, but Zebul, the governor of the city and loyal to Abimelech, threw his words back at him. He challenged Gaal to prove his courage. The Bible does not say that Gaal wanted to fight at that moment; what it shows is that his boasting left him with no way out. The result, as the story goes on, was his defeat.

For today: let us be careful about what we say in pride or anger, because afterward we will have to answer for it. It is better to speak with humility and seek peace than to promise what we cannot fulfill.
exp.8:43:
This verse describes a military strategy. Abimelech and his company rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the city gate, to keep the people from getting back in. Meanwhile, the other two companies attacked everyone who was out in the fields and killed them.

It is part of the account in Judges, where the narrator describes the war between Abimelech and the people of Shechem. Abimelech had made himself king through violence and murder, and Shechem had supported him. Now that alliance breaks apart, and both suffer the consequences, just as Jotham had foretold earlier (Judges 9:20).

For today: this passage does not present Abimelech as an example to follow, but as a warning. What is built through violence and deceit ends up destroying those who built it. Let us seek relationships and achievements grounded in truth and justice.
exp.8:48:
This verse tells that all the people with Abimelech each cut a branch, followed him, and piled them against the stronghold of Shechem. Then they set it on fire, and about a thousand men and women who were inside the tower died.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Abimelech had made himself king by killing his brothers, and the people of Shechem had supported him, but later they rebelled against him. Judges presents this outcome as the consequence of that betrayal and violence (Judges 9:56-57). The text recounts what happened and does not approve of the cruelty.

For today: the evil that is sown often comes back. For that reason it is wise to seek power and agreements through justice, not through violence or deceit.
exp.8:50:
The verse tells that Abimelech took the city of Thebez, and all the people took refuge in a strong tower in the center. Men, women and leaders went inside, shut the doors and climbed to the upper floor, the roof or the top part of the tower. They were looking to be safe from an attack.

It is part of the story of Abimelech, who made himself king by killing his brothers. Here it is not a character speaking, but the narrator. Shortly before, Abimelech had burned the tower of Shechem. Now he repeats the same method in Thebez, but the next verse shows that this time something turns out differently: a woman strikes him with a millstone.

For today: violence and pride may seem to succeed for a while, but they do not have the last word. God sees injustice. Trust that he acts in his own time, and seek refuge in him, not only in human towers.
exp.8:52:
The passage says that a woman, from the top of the tower, dropped the upper part of a millstone onto Abimelech and crushed his skull. The word "skull" here refers to the bones of the head. The millstone was the stone used at home to grind grain.

This is part of the story, not a speech by a character. Abimelech had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. Later he attacked a city that had rebelled and tried to burn the tower where the people had taken refuge. The narrator presents this ending as God's justice for his violence (Judges 9:56-57). His pride shows when he asks his armor-bearer to kill him, so that people will not say that a woman killed him.

For today: violence and pride sooner or later turn against the one who practices them. God can use the person we least expect. Let us seek to be humble and not to live guarding our reputation.
exp.8:53:
Abimelech, struck on the head by a woman, calls to his armourbearer, the young man who carried his weapons. He orders him to kill him with the sword so that people will not say that a woman killed him. The young man runs him through, and Abimelech dies.

Abimelech is the one speaking. He had made himself king by killing his seventy brothers. He attacked the tower of Thebez, and a woman dropped a millstone on him. He cared more about his reputation than about his life. But the account says that his pride did not save him: God repaid him for the evil he had done. Moreover, the story is remembered just the same.

For today: caring about how we look can become more important than being honest with God. It is better to live with humility and justice than to seek to look good before others.
exp.8:54:
This verse says that when the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home. The soldiers had followed him for a purpose, and once he was gone, they had no reason to keep fighting. With the death of their leader, the conflict ended, and the men scattered.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells of the end of Abimelech, who had made himself king by killing his seventy brothers. His death, brought about by a woman and by his own armor-bearer, closes a story of violence and ambition. Without their leader, the men no longer had a reason to keep fighting. The following text makes clear that God brought justice for that wrong.

For today: power gained through violence and pride does not last. We can seek to lead and to live with humility and justice, trusting that God sees everything and that in the end he puts things in their place.
exp.8:55:
This verse says that God paid Abimelech back for the evil he had done. He killed his seventy brothers in order to keep power for himself, and in the end he died in a shameful way.

The narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. After describing Abimelech's death, when a woman dropped a millstone on him and his armor-bearer finished him off, the author explains what happened: it was not simple chance, but God's justice. This fulfilled the curse that Jotham, the only brother who survived, had spoken earlier.

For today: do not lose heart when evil seems to go unpunished. God sees everything and is just. So instead of taking revenge, trust in Him, and make sure you do not gain anything through violence or deceit.
exp.9:0:
This verse tells us that, after Abimelech, God raised up Tola to defend Israel. He was the son of Puah and grandson of Dodo, from the tribe of Issachar. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim.

The book of Judges covers the period before the kings, when Israel repeatedly fell into disobedience. The narrator, whose identity is not known with certainty, introduces Tola right after the violent rule of Abimelech. The text does not tell us how he saved Israel, since it gives very few details. The verses that follow say that he judged Israel for twenty-three years.

For today: God also uses ordinary, little-known people to bring stability and good to others. You do not need fame to be useful; steady faithfulness in your own place and time counts before God.
exp.9:1:
Judges 10:2 says that Tola led Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir, the town where he lived.

"Judged" means that he guided the people, settled disputes, and protected them, not merely that he handed down verdicts. The word "buried" in the verse is the same as "was buried" in the verse text itself.

The narrator of the book of Judges is the one speaking. Tola comes right after the violent rule of Abimelech, which had left much suffering. God raised up Tola to bring Israel deliverance, that is, to give the nation stability. The text does not recount battles or great deeds of his; it gives only brief facts. After him comes Jair, and then the people return to idolatry.

For today: not all service to God is showy. Tola was faithful quietly, and his life helped others live in peace. We can value and practice steady service, even when almost no one notices it.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that Jair had thirty sons, and that each one rode on a young donkey. They also had thirty towns, which were still called Havoth-jair when the book was written. They were in the region of Gilead. Here "towns" means small settlements, and "donkeys" means the animals that carry people and loads.

It is one detail within the list of judges, and the narrator does not say who wrote it. Riding donkeys was usually a sign of high social standing, so the sons seem to have had authority or wealth. No deed of Jair is recorded. After his death the people return to idolatry, which shows that a leader's prestige did not guarantee the faithfulness of the nation.

For today: a family's success, name, or possessions do not take the place of a life given to God. Let us ask him that our faith be sincere and not depend on what we have or on who our family is.
exp.9:4:
Judges 10:5 says that Jair, the judge of Israel, died and was buried in a place called Camon. It is a simple ending for a man who governed for twenty-two years.

The book of Judges is a narrative, so there is no one speaking in it; the narrator is telling the story of Israel. This verse closes the brief summary of Jair. Right after, the text shows that, with the judge gone, the people returned to idolatry. As for where Camon was, it is thought to have been in Gilead, east of the Jordan, but this is not known for certain.

For today: good leaders are not enough; each person needs their own faithfulness to God. We should not depend only on others for our faith. Let us cultivate a personal relationship with Him today, so that our faith remains firm even when the people around us change.
exp.9:11:
This verse continues God's question to Israel. He reminds them that the Zidonians, the Amalekites, and the Maonites also oppressed them, and that when they cried out to God, He delivered them from their hand.

God speaks here, answering Israel's cry. The people said they were sorry, but they had served the Baals. God reminds them of his faithfulness in the past to show that their abandonment of him was unjust and ungrateful. His words that follow are harsh, but they aim to make their repentance sincere.

For today: let us not remember God only when there are problems. Let us recall the times he helped us and respond to him with gratitude and faithfulness, not only with words, but with a life that truly follows him.
exp.10:0:
This verse introduces Jephthah, a man from the region of Gilead. It describes him as a mighty man of valour, that is, a strong and capable warrior. It also says that he was the son of an harlot, a term for a prostitute, and that his father was named Gilead. Here "Gilead" may refer to the father or to his family line; the text does not fully clarify this.

The narrator of the book of Judges speaks here. Israel was going through a difficult time, and God was raising up unexpected leaders. The verses that follow tell how his half-brothers drove him out of the house because he was the son of another woman. So Jephthah's story begins with him as one who was rejected, before he is called to lead.

For today: our origins or the rejection we suffer do not define our worth before God. He can use people who are wounded or looked down upon. If someone made you feel less, remember that your story does not end there, and that God is still at work in you.
exp.10:2:
This verse tells how Jephthah, rejected by his half-brothers, fled and went to live in the land of Tob. There men gathered around him and went out with him. The explanation says these were men without a steady job, probably adventurers or people with few resources, and the verse itself gives no further detail. They likely went out with him on armed expeditions, though the text does not say more.

It is the narrator who speaks. Jephthah was the son of a woman of poor reputation and was driven out of his father's house with no inheritance. Later, when the Ammonites attack Israel, the elders of Gilead will look for him precisely because he was a brave man. God had not forgotten him, even though his family had.

For today: if you have been rejected or looked down on, your past does not decide your future. Place your gifts in God's hands, be careful about who you associate with, and trust that He can use you in His time.
exp.10:6:
Jephthah calls out to the elders of Gilead. He reminds them that they hated him and drove him out of his father's house. That is why he asks them why they have come to him now, just when they are in trouble, that is, in a time of anguish and need.

He is speaking as a man of Gilead. His half-brothers had driven him out because he was the son of another woman, and he went to live in the land of Tob. Now the Ammonites are making war against Israel, and the leaders who rejected him need a military commander. His question expresses pain and distrust, and it also serves him as a way to negotiate.

For today: when someone who wounded us comes looking for us only because they need us, it is healthy to be honest about the hurt without letting bitterness take charge. We can ask God for wisdom to decide whether to help, and how to do it, with clarity and with grace.
exp.10:7:
The elders of Gilead answer Jephthah that this is exactly why they have come back to look for him. They ask him to go with them, fight against the Ammonites, and be their head, that is, their leader and chief, over all who live in Gilead.

The leaders of Gilead, who had earlier driven Jephthah out of his family, are now speaking. Ammon is threatening them and they are in trouble. That is why they need Jephthah, a brave warrior. He points out their rejection of him, and they offer him more than a commander's role: they offer him rule. Even so, they seek his help out of necessity, and the verse does not say here that there was any deep repentance.

For today: if someone hurt you and later seeks you out for their own convenience, you can speak honestly about the pain and ask God for wisdom. And if you have failed someone, asking for their help is not enough; it is also wise to acknowledge the wrong and seek sincere reconciliation.
exp.10:12:
Here the king of the Ammonites answers Jephthah's messengers. He says that when Israel came up out of Egypt, they took away his land, the land that stretches from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan. For that reason he demands that the land be returned to him without a fight.

The king of Ammon speaks here because Jephthah had asked him why he had come to make war. Jephthah, newly chosen as leader of Gilead, first tries to settle the conflict with words. The king gives his reason, but in the next verse Jephthah will answer that this accusation is not true, and the history of Israel that he then recounts will show it.

For today: before fighting or responding in anger, it is worth asking questions, listening to the other side's reasons, and checking the facts honestly. Many conflicts calm down, or at least come to be better understood, when people seek peace through honest dialogue.
exp.10:15:
It says that when Israel came out of Egypt, they traveled through the desert to the Red Sea, and after that they came to Kadesh, a place in the wilderness.

The speaker is Jephthah, a judge of Israel. The Ammonites were attacking and claiming that Israel had taken their land. Jephthah sends them a message and goes over the history of the people. He wants to show that Israel did not take territory from Moab or Ammon, but went around them with respect. Some scholars point out that Jephthah summarizes the events, and that the details can be read more fully in Numbers.

For today: when someone accuses you or misunderstands you, answer with the truth and with calm. Remembering honestly what happened, and how God guided you, helps you speak with firmness and without hatred.
exp.10:18:
This verse tells how Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who ruled from Heshbon. They asked for permission to pass through his land on the way to the place where they were going to settle. "Messengers" are men sent to speak on behalf of a people. Their request was made with respect, asking politely.

The one speaking is Jephthah, judge of Israel. He reminds the Ammonites how Israel came to that land after leaving Egypt. He wants to show that Israel did not seek a fight: first they asked for passage peacefully, as they had done with Edom and Moab. Sihon distrusted them and attacked, and the account says that God gave Israel the victory.

For today: before entering a conflict, try to speak with respect and seek peace. Asking humbly does not guarantee that the other person will agree, but it leaves the conscience at rest.
exp.10:19:
It says that King Sihon did not trust Israel and for that reason did not let them pass through his land. Instead, he gathered all his army, camped at Jahaz, and attacked Israel.

The speaker is Jephthah, judge of Israel. He is answering the king of the Ammonites and explaining how Israel came to possess that land. According to his account, Israel asked for passage in peace, respected the borders of Edom and Moab, and fought only when Sihon attacked them first. Jephthah wants to show that Israel did not take the land out of greed.

For today: distrust can lead us to shut doors and start conflicts that could have been avoided. Let us seek peace and speak with clarity. And if others attack us without cause, we can place our cause in God's hands.
exp.10:20:
It says that God handed Sihon and his army over into the hands of Israel, and that the Israelites defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who lived there.

The speaker is Jephthah, a judge of Israel. He sends a message to the king of Ammon, who was claiming that land. Jephthah reminds him that Israel asked for passage peacefully, Sihon distrusted them and attacked, and that is why there was war. He tells the story to show that Israel did not seize that territory unjustly. Some scholars debate details of that land dispute, but Jephthah's argument is clear.

For today: before fighting for something, seek dialogue and the truth. And when you receive something good, recognize that it comes from God and not from your own strength.
exp.10:24:
Here Jephthah asks the king of the Ammonites whether he considers himself better than Balak, a king of Moab. Jephthah reminds him that Balak never fought against Israel to claim those lands, and that he himself has no reason to do so now.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, answers the king of Ammon by messengers. The king was demanding territory east of the Jordan. Jephthah argues from history: Israel received those lands after defeating the Amorites, and no one had claimed them for centuries. Some scholars debate the details of the dates and of who owned the territory, but Jephthah's point is clear.

For today: before entering a conflict, it is wise to look at the facts honestly and seek dialogue. And when someone makes a claim against us, we can respond with calm and truth, letting God be the final judge.
exp.10:26:
Jephthah tells the king of Ammon that Israel did him no harm, and that it is he who is acting wrongly by declaring war on them. Since they cannot agree, Jephthah asks that the LORD, the righteous judge, decide today between the two peoples. Asking for a decision means asking God to pass the verdict.

Jephthah is a leader of Israel in Gilead. Before fighting, he sends messengers to the Ammonite king and explains why the disputed lands belong to Israel, which had occupied them for three hundred years. In the end, the king does not listen to him, and then the Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah.

For today: before entering a conflict, try to speak calmly and truthfully. Then place your cause in the hands of God, who is the righteous judge, and do not let yourself be carried away by pride or by revenge.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and he traveled through Gilead and Manasseh to gather people. Then he passed through Mizpeh of Gilead and from there advanced toward the Ammonites, ready for battle. The word "passed" in the verse means that he went across or through the land, and the name "the Lord" refers to God.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Jephthah, a man from Gilead, had first tried to settle the conflict with words, but the Ammonite king would not listen to him. Then the Spirit of God empowers him to lead Israel. What follows, Jephthah's vow, is not presented as a command from God, and the Bible lets us see how painful it was.

For today: seek peace and dialogue first, and when you must act, ask for God's guidance. Do not add hasty promises that He has not asked of you.
exp.10:29:
It says that Jephthah, before going into battle, made a solemn promise to God. A "vow" was a commitment someone made before the Lord, promising to give something if God granted what they asked. Here Jephthah asks that God deliver the Ammonites into his hands, that is, that God give him victory over them.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, had already tried to settle the conflict with words, but the king of Ammon would not listen. The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and even so he added this vow. The text does not say that God asked for it. What Jephthah promised afterward has been much debated, and interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: when we ask something of God, let us do it with confidence, but with humility, and think carefully before making promises in haste. God does not need us to bargain for his help; we can trust in his grace.
exp.10:30:
Before going into battle, Jephthah makes a promise to God: whatever comes out of the door of his house to meet him when he returns victorious will belong to the Lord, and he will offer it up as a burnt offering, meaning an offering burned up completely.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, speaks here as a warrior called to defend his people against the Ammonites. The text says that the Spirit of the Lord was already upon him, yet he still made this vow. It is not made clear whether he had in mind an animal or a person; scholars interpret this in different ways. What follows in the story is painful.

For today: before promising something to God, let us think calmly. God was already with Jephthah without any need for that vow; we should not bargain with Him or speak in haste.
exp.10:32:
He defeated the Ammonites with a very great slaughter. The defeat stretched from Aroer to near Minnith, about twenty cities, and reached as far as the fields of the vineyards (probably a place called Abel-keramim). The Ammonites were brought low before Israel.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had made a vow to God before the battle. God gave him the victory, but the verse that follows shows the painful cost of that vow. Scholars discuss how to understand what happened to his daughter, and it is good to recognize that difference.

For today: God may give us victories, but we should speak with Him carefully and humbly. Let us not make hasty promises that God has not asked for. We can trust His help without trying to buy it with impulsive vows.
exp.10:34:
Jephthah sees his daughter come out to meet him, and he tears his clothes, which was a sign of deep grief. He tells her that she has left him crushed, because he made a promise to God and cannot take it back.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, speaks right after defeating the Ammonites. Before the battle he had promised God that he would offer whatever came out of his house first to meet him (Judges 11:30-31). He did not expect it to be his only daughter. Scholars debate what happened next: some believe he offered her as a sacrifice, others that he dedicated her to the service of God for life, unmarried.

For today: before we speak, let us think carefully about what we promise, especially before God. Words spoken in haste can bring pain to those we love most. Let us ask for wisdom and trust that God guides us without the need for rushed promises.
exp.10:36:
She asks her father for a favor before fulfilling the vow: two months to go up and down the mountains with her friends and mourn that she would never marry or have children.

The speaker is Jephthah's daughter. He had made a vow to God before fighting against the Ammonites, and she was the first to come out to meet him. She accepts her father's word. Scholars debate whether she was offered as a sacrifice or dedicated for life to service at the sanctuary, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: promises made carelessly can cause great pain. Think carefully before you promise, and comfort with tenderness anyone who suffers a loss, as her friends did.
exp.10:37:
Jephthah let his daughter go for two months, as she had asked. She went off with her friends to the mountains and wept there because she would never marry or have children. Her unlived life is what the word translated here as "virginity" refers to. Her friends are her companions.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had made a vow to the LORD before fighting against the Ammonites. His daughter was the first to come out to meet him. She accepts her father's vow and asks only for time to mourn with her friends. The text does not explain everything clearly: some understand that she was offered as a sacrifice, others that she was dedicated to remain unmarried in God's service. Those who study the Bible do not agree.

For today: let us think before making a promise in haste, because our words can affect others. And let us accompany with tenderness the one who grieves a loss.
exp.11:2:
Jephthah tells the men of Ephraim that when they did not come to help him, he risked his life and went out to fight against the Ammonites. The Lord gave them into his hand. Then he asks them why they have now come up to fight against him.

Jephthah, judge of Gilead, is speaking. The men of Ephraim, a proud tribe, were angry because they had not been invited to share in the victory, and they threatened to burn his house. Jephthah defends himself by saying that he did call them and they did not answer. This ended in a war between brothers, as the following text shows.

For today: when a conflict arises, do not let wounded pride lead you into fighting. Speak calmly, seek the truth, and work for peace before a small offense becomes a great harm.
exp.11:4:
The explanation says that the men of Gilead, the group of Jephthah, took the crossing points of the Jordan River to cut off the escape of the Ephraimites. The fords are shallow places where a person could cross on foot. When a fugitive asked to pass, they asked him whether he was an Ephraimite, that is, from the tribe of Ephraim. If he answered that he was not, came the test that follows in verse 6.

The narrator recounts a civil war between tribes of Israel. Ephraim complained that Jephthah had not called them to fight against Ammon. Jephthah replied that he had already asked for their help and they did not come. Then there was battle, and the Gileadites won. The text only relates what happened; it does not say that God approved of so much violence.

For today: wounded pride and harsh words can grow until they cause enormous harm. Let us seek to resolve conflicts with humility and dialogue, and not divide anyone by their accent, origin or group.
exp.11:7:
After Jephthah's death, this verse says, a man named Ibzan, from Bethlehem, became the next judge of Israel. To judge here means that he governed, guided, and settled matters for the people. Bethlehem is the town of Ibzan's origin. No deed of his is recorded here.

Context: the book of Judges describes a time when God raised up leaders to guide Israel. Here the narrator speaks, giving a brief bridge after the painful war between Gilead and Ephraim. The text does not explain why Ibzan is mentioned so briefly. Some think the Bethlehem named here is the one near Nazareth, and others think it is the one in Judah, but this is not certain.

For today: not all faithful service to God is famous or dramatic. You can be faithful in your family, your work, and your church, even when few notice. God does see it.
exp.11:8:
This verse is about Ibzan, who was a judge of Israel. He had sixty children: thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters in marriage to people from outside his own family or clan, and he brought in thirty wives from outside for his sons. He ruled for seven years. The word "judged" here means that he led and governed the people.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, who gives a brief report between longer stories, such as that of Jephthah. It does not say why Ibzan arranged his children's marriages this way. Some think he was seeking alliances or showing his wealth and influence, but the text does not make this clear. It also does not say whether he did well or badly.

For today: our lives also leave a mark on our families and on others. Let us make our decisions with prayer and wisdom, thinking about how they help others know and follow God.
exp.11:9:
He says that Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem. It is the brief close of his time as a judge of Israel, which lasted seven years. The explanation notes that the verse is a short summary, and that the word "buried" means laid to rest in the ground.

The book of Judges tells the story of Israel after Joshua, when the people were led by judges, leaders whom God raised up at different moments. Here the narrator records Ibzan very briefly. He does not recount any battles or feats of his. It is not certain whether this Bethlehem is the one in Judah or a town in Zebulun; scholars debate it.

Today it reminds us that every life ends and that God continues to work through different people and generations. Even when our work seems small or little known, God sees the faithfulness of each day. We can serve with humility, without needing applause.
exp.11:11:
Elon of the tribe of Zebulun died and was buried in Aijalon, within the territory of his tribe. "Was buried" means that they put him in the ground.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is recording the leaders whom God allowed in Israel. About Elon we are only told that he judged for ten years; no deeds are recounted. This Aijalon is not the same one near Jerusalem, since here it is located in Zebulun, in the north. Its exact location is uncertain.

For today: not everyone leaves a famous story, but a faithful and steady life also counts before God. Serve where you are, without worrying about applause.
exp.11:13:
This verse speaks of Abdon. It says he had forty sons and thirty grandsons, and that they rode on seventy donkeys (asses). He also judged Israel for eight years, that is, he was a leader who guided and governed the people.

The narrator of the book of Judges gives here a brief summary of a little-known judge. He tells of no battles and no miracles. Many understand that having so many sons and donkeys showed wealth and importance in that time, although the text does not explain this. We also know no further details about his rule.

God also works through ordinary people who are not famous. Perhaps no one will remember your name, but your faithfulness in your family and in your community has value. Serve God today where you are, without needing applause.
exp.12:1:
This verse introduces a man named Manoah, who lived in Zorah and belonged to the tribe of Dan. His wife was barren, meaning she could not have children, and had never borne a child, that is, had never given birth.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Israel had once again turned away from God and was under Philistine rule for forty years. In the midst of that dark situation, the account begins with an ordinary family and a deep need. Later God will act through them, and from them Samson will be born.

For today: when your situation seems closed or without a way out, remember that God can begin something important in ordinary places and with ordinary people. Keep trusting Him and obeying Him, even when you cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord appeared to Manoah's wife and told her that, though until then she had been unable to have children, she was now going to become pregnant and would have a son.

The people of Israel had long turned away from God, and for that reason they were under the rule of the Philistines for forty years. Even so, God takes the initiative and draws near to this woman, whom the Bible does not name here. The child who would be born would be a Nazirite, set apart for God, and he would begin to deliver Israel.

For today: God can act even where there seems to be no hope. When you feel there is no way out, remember that he sees your situation and can act in his own time and in his own way. Trust and keep seeking him.
exp.12:4:
She is told that a woman who could not have children will become pregnant and have a son. His hair will never be cut (the phrase about no razor coming on his head says this), because he will be a Nazirite, that is, someone set apart for God from before he is born. That son will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. The word "conceive" here simply means to become pregnant.

The angel of the Lord speaks to the wife of Manoah, at a time when Israel was oppressed by the Philistines. God chooses to act through a woman without children. The child is Samson. His Nazirite vow included not drinking wine and not cutting his hair. Notice that it says he will "begin" to save: his work would not be complete.

For today: God can start great things in situations that seem closed. Trust that your life has purpose, even if you see only the beginning.
exp.12:5:
Here the wife of Manoah tells her husband what happened to her. A man of God appeared to her, and his appearance was terrible, that is, so awe-inspiring that it brought great respect and fear. She did not ask him where he came from or what his name was, and he did not tell her.

The wife of Manoah was from the tribe of Dan. She could not have children, and the messenger announced that she would have a son who would be a Nazirite, set apart for God. She tells this so that her husband may know what God said. This son would be Samson, at a time when the Philistines ruled over Israel.

When God speaks to us or gives us a responsibility, it is good to share it with those closest to us, such as a spouse or family. In this way we walk together, with humility and reverence.
exp.12:6:
Here the wife of Manoah tells her husband what the visitor said to her. She will have a son, and while she is expecting him she must not drink wine or strong drink (a fermented drink), nor eat anything unclean, that is, what the law considered impure. That child will be a Nazarite, someone set apart for God, from before birth until his death.

It is the wife of Manoah who speaks, repeating the angel's message. Israel was under the rule of the Philistines, and God prepares a deliverer, Samson. The Nazarite vow was normally temporary; here it is for life, which was uncommon.

For today: God calls us to live set apart for Him, and that can begin in everyday life, in what we eat, say, and decide. Ask Him today to show you one area where you can live more fully devoted to Him.
exp.12:7:
Manoah speaks to God with respect and humility. He asks that the man of God who appeared earlier come again. He wants him to teach them how they should raise the child who is going to be born.

Manoah is the husband of a woman who could not have children. She told him that a messenger of God announced the birth of a son, who would be a Nazarite, that is, set apart for God. Manoah did not see the visitor, so he prays to receive direction. The text does not say that he doubted his wife, although some readers interpret it that way.

When we receive a great responsibility, such as raising children or serving in something important, it is wise to pray first and ask God for guidance. Recognizing that we need direction is not weakness, but wisdom and humility.
exp.12:14:
Manoah asks the angel of the Lord to stay a little longer. His request is polite and courteous, something like asking him to let them hold him there for a while. Manoah wants to prepare a young goat, which is a kid, and offer it to him as a meal.

Manoah is the husband of the woman who would become the mother of Samson. The angel had already announced to them the birth of a son. Manoah did not yet know that he was an angel; he took him for a man of God and wanted to honor him with hospitality, as was the custom. The angel redirects that gesture toward the Lord through a burnt offering.

For today: generosity is good, but we should ask to whom the honor is directed. Serve and be hospitable, but let every gesture end up pointing to God, not to people.
exp.12:15:
Here the angel of the LORD refuses the food that Manoah offers him. He tells him that, even if Manoah insists on holding him back, he will not eat his bread. But if Manoah wishes to offer a burnt offering, a whole offering burned completely, he must offer it to the LORD. The text makes clear that Manoah still did not understand that this visitor was an angel of the LORD.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel announced to them that they would have a son, Samson, set apart for God from his birth. Manoah, out of his custom of hospitality, wanted to honor the visitor, without knowing who he was. The angel directs attention toward God, not toward himself.

For today: when God acts in our lives, let us give Him gratitude and worship. And let us be attentive, because sometimes God works in the midst of everyday life, and we are slow to recognize Him.
exp.12:16:
Manoah asks the angel of the Lord what his name is. He wants to know it so that he can honor him when the promise he gave them comes true.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel told them they would have a son, Samson. Manoah still did not understand that he was speaking with a messenger of God. That is why he treats him as a visitor and wants to thank him. The angel answers that his name is secret, and he directs attention toward the Lord through the sacrifice.

For today: when God gives us something, it is natural to want to give thanks. But gratitude should reach God himself, not stop at the messenger or at the gift. We can take a moment to thank him directly.
exp.12:18:
Manoah takes a young goat with a grain offering and offers them to the Lord on a rock, which served as an altar. Then the angel does something wonderful, a miracle, before the eyes of Manoah and his wife.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a son, Samson, and the angel had given them instructions for raising him. Manoah wanted to know the visitor's name so he could honor him, but the angel answered that his name was secret. The text does not fully explain the wonder; the next verse tells how the angel rose up in the flame.

For today: when God shows us his goodness, let us respond with gratitude and worship, even when we do not understand everything about him. We can trust what he reveals, without demanding that we have all the answers.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah or to his wife.

The narrator goes on to describe what happened after the angel announced the birth of Samson. Manoah had offered a sacrifice, and the angel rose up in the flame of the altar. Until that moment, Manoah had not understood who he was. His wife, by contrast, seems to have trusted more from the beginning. Some scholars see in this angel a messenger sent by God; others think it is a special appearance of God himself. The Bible does not make this entirely clear here.

For today: sometimes we only understand late how God has been at work. It is fitting to respond with worship and humility, and to remember that he is faithful even when we did not recognize it right away.
exp.12:22:
Here the wife of Manoah answers her husband calmly. She tells him that if the Lord had wanted to kill them, he would not have accepted their burnt offering and their meat offering from their hands. Nor would he have shown them all these things or told them such things as these.

Manoah was afraid to die because they had seen the angel of the Lord. At that time it was believed that seeing God brought death. His wife reasons with faith: God had dealt with them in favor and with promises, not in anger. Afterward Samson was born, and God blessed him.

When you feel fear before something of God that you do not understand, remember how he has been good to you and what he has promised you. His past dealings can give you calm to trust him today.
exp.13:1:
Samson returns from Timnah and tells his parents that he has seen a young Philistine woman. He respectfully asks them to get her for him as his wife. Philistines were a neighboring people who dominated Israel.

The one speaking is Samson, an Israelite set apart for God from his birth. In those times parents often arranged marriages. His parents object, because God had asked Israel not to intermarry with neighboring peoples. The text says that God used this situation against the Philistines, but it does not say that he approved of Samson's choice. Some see it as an example of God working in spite of human mistakes.

For today: before making an important decision, do not be guided only by what attracts you. Seek God's voice and listen to the counsel of wise people who love you.
exp.13:4:
This verse tells that Samson went down to Timnath together with his father and mother. When they came to the vineyards, a young lion came roaring toward him. The word "young lion" here refers to a young and strong lion, not a helpless cub. The roaring is the sound the lion made as it charged at him.

The one who narrates this is the writer of Judges. Samson was going to ask for a Philistine woman as his wife, something his parents did not approve of. Yet the text says that God was using that situation to act against the Philistines, who ruled over Israel. The lion appears suddenly, and afterward the Spirit of the LORD gives strength to Samson.

For today: God can work even in confusing or imperfect situations, but that does not justify our bad decisions. When we face unexpected trials, let us trust that God is the one who gives strength, not ourselves.
exp.13:5:
This verse tells how Samson, when a young lion attacked him, received a special strength from God. The phrase "the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him" means that God empowered him in a powerful way. With nothing in his hand, he tore the lion apart as one would tear apart a young goat. Afterward, he told neither his father nor his mother what he had done.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel was under the rule of the Philistines, and the text says that God was looking for an opportunity against them. Samson was on his way to Timnah, where the woman who had pleased him lived. His parents did not know that God was at work in all of this.

For today: true strength comes from God, not from ourselves. And when He helps us overcome something, we can acknowledge it with humility, without boasting about it.
exp.13:8:
Samson takes the honey in his hands and keeps eating as he walks. When he arrives at his father and mother, he gives them honey too. But he does not tell them that he took it out of the dead body of the lion.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Samson had killed a lion and, on returning, found bees and honey inside the carcass. According to the law of Moses, touching a dead body made the one who did it unclean (Numbers 19:11), and Samson was a Nazirite. That is why his silence stands out. Some see it as carelessness and others as a way of hiding what he did. The text does not explain it.

Today, this passage invites us to consider whether we are sharing with others something that is neither clean nor honest. Let us ask God for help to be truthful and not to hide what we ought to acknowledge.
exp.13:10:
When the people of the place saw Samson, they chose thirty young men to accompany him during the wedding feast.

Samson was in Timnath, at his wedding banquet, following the custom of young men in those days. The text does not say why they surrounded him with thirty men. It may have been a gesture of courtesy, or it may have been distrust toward a foreigner. Some older translations suggest they were afraid of him, but this is not certain. These thirty men will be the ones who hear Samson's riddle.

For today: companions matter. Before entering a gathering or celebration, it is wise to ask ourselves who surrounds us and what influence they will have on us. Let us ask God for wisdom to choose our friendships well and to act with prudence.
exp.13:11:
Here Samson proposes a riddle to the thirty companions at the wedding. If they can solve it during the seven days of the feast, he will give them thirty sheets (fine linen garments) and thirty changes of clothing (festive garments). It is a challenge with a prize.

He speaks during the celebration of his wedding to a Philistine woman. It was customary to hold a feast, and the Philistines had assigned him thirty companions. Scholars do not know the exact reason, but Samson takes the occasion to set the challenge. Later it will become clear that the game brings serious consequences.

For today: before making a bet or a promise, think about what it might lead to. A seemingly harmless game can produce conflict, pressure, and resentment. Let us ask God for wisdom to speak with prudence.
exp.13:12:
Samson goes on with his wager at the wedding feast. He says that if the thirty young men cannot solve his riddle, they must give him thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes for festive wear. They agree and ask him to put forth his riddle, that they may hear it.

Samson, a judge of Israel, speaks during the seven-day wedding banquet of his marriage to a Philistine woman. The thirty companions were Philistine guests. Samson uses the riddle as a game, but the account shows that the wager soon brings pressure, deception, and violence. The text does not justify every action of Samson; it only tells what happened.

For today: think before making wagers or promises lightly, even in jokes or celebrations. What seems like a game can hurt relationships and bring consequences you did not expect.
exp.13:13:
Samson poses a riddle to the guests at his wedding. He says that out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. He is referring to the honey he found in the body of the lion he had killed. The guests could not solve it in three days.

Samson speaks during the seven-day wedding feast with a Philistine woman. The guests were thirty young men, and he made a wager with them over clothing. Only Samson knew the story of the lion and the honey, so the riddle was nearly impossible to solve without help. Afterward they pressured his wife with threats.

For today: clever words and games with wagers can end in pressure and conflict. Before making a bet or sharing a secret, think about who will be affected. Care for your relationships with wisdom and sincerity.
exp.13:14:
On the seventh day of the wedding feast, the Philistine guests pressured Samson's wife. They told her to coax her husband into revealing the answer to the riddle, and they threatened to burn her and her father's house with fire. Coax means to persuade or win over. To take what is ours here means to leave us without our belongings, that is, to strip us of them.

Speaking here are the thirty companions who accompanied Samson at the banquet. They had wagered thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing, and in three days they had not been able to solve the riddle. So they turned to fear and violence, and accused the woman of having invited them in order to leave them with nothing.

For today: pressure and threats can push us to betray someone's trust. Before giving in to fear, it is wise to seek help and act with honesty, caring for the relationships God has given us.
exp.13:16:
She wept before Samson the whole seven days of the wedding feast. On the seventh day he gave in and explained the riddle to her, because she pressed him hard, she kept at him and would not let up. Then she told the answer to her own people.
