Samson had set a riddle for the Philistine guests. They could not solve it, and they threatened his wife, who was from that people. She used her tears and her complaint that he did not love her to get the answer out of him, and so she betrayed his trust.

Today, constant pressure can push us to give in on things we know we should not. Let us ask for wisdom to keep what has been entrusted to us, and take care not to manipulate others with guilt or tears to get what we want.
exp.13:17:
The men of Timnah gave Samson the answer to his riddle just before the seventh day, the deadline of the agreement, came to an end. They answered him with a question of their own: "What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?" With these words they showed that they already knew the secret: the honey and the lion that Samson had seen before.

The speakers are the thirty guests at the wedding. They had pressured Samson's wife with threats to get the secret out of her. She wept for seven days until he gave in and told her. She then passed it on to her people, and so Samson was betrayed.

For today: constant pressure and tears can wear down our defenses. We should take care with whom we share what matters most, and look for relationships built on trust rather than manipulation.
exp.14:0:
After a while, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife and brought her a young goat as a gift. He wanted to go into her room, but her father did not allow him to. The phrase about going into the room means being with her as her husband.

This is a story about Samson, a judge of Israel. Earlier, in Judges 14, he had left the wedding angry. As the story goes on, her father thought Samson had rejected her, and he gave her to another man. So Samson comes with good intentions, but he finds that the situation has already changed.

For today: when there are conflicts, let us not let time pass without speaking. Silence and misunderstandings can cause harm that is later hard to repair. Let us seek dialogue and reconciliation in good time.
exp.14:3:
Samson catches three hundred foxes. He ties the animals in pairs by their tails and puts a torch between each pair. Some scholars think the original word could also refer to jackals, but the text does not make this clear.

Samson has just learned that his father-in-law gave his wife to another man. He feels wronged and declares that he will now be blameless before the Philistines if he harms them. His plan aims to destroy their crops, which were their livelihood. The account shows that revenge produces more violence, since the Philistines later burn the woman and her father.

For today: when we are hurt, it is easy to respond with anger and revenge. This story warns us that getting even almost always harms others too. Ask God for wisdom and calm before you react.
exp.14:4:
He says that Samson set fire to the torches (firebrands) and let the foxes loose in the fields of the Philistines. The fire burned the shocks (piles of cut grain), the standing corn (grain not yet harvested), the vineyards and the olive groves. It was a hard blow to their food and their livelihood.

It is the narrator who tells what Samson did. Shortly before, his father-in-law had given his wife to another man, and Samson decided that now he would bear no guilt if he harmed them. The Philistines responded by burning the woman and her father, and Samson took revenge again. The Bible shows here a cycle of violence, though it also says that God used these conflicts against the Philistines (Judges 14:4).

Today: revenge begins with a wound and almost always ends in more pain. Before responding in anger, let us ask God for wisdom to seek justice without destroying others or ourselves.
exp.14:5:
The Philistines ask who caused the burning of their crops, and they are told: it was Samson, the son-in-law of the man from Timnah, because this man took his wife and gave her to his companion (the friend who had accompanied him at the wedding). The phrase "were told" means the answer was given to them. Then the Philistines burn the woman and her father.

The Philistines speak in anger over the loss of their fields. Earlier they had threatened to burn that woman and her family (Judges 14:15). Now, instead of punishing Samson, they carry out that threat against them. The Bible shows here a chain of revenge, without presenting it as an example to follow.

For today: revenge almost always grows and harms people who are not at the center of the conflict too. When someone wrongs us, we can stop, pray, and seek justice without repaying evil with evil. As Romans 12:19 says, let us leave room for God.
exp.14:10:
They say that three thousand men of Judah went to the cave in the rock of Etam, where Samson was. They confronted him: "Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why have you done this to us?" Samson answered that he had only repaid them in the same way they had treated him.

The Philistines had invaded Judah to capture Samson, because he had caused them great harm. The men of Judah speak out of fear: they prefer peace with their oppressors to facing them. Samson defends himself by saying that he acted in revenge. We note that Israel, accustomed to oppression, did not expect God to deliver them.

For today: be careful about growing used to what oppresses us out of fear of conflict. And Samson's revenge reminds us that repaying evil with evil does not bring peace; it is better to trust God and seek what is good.
exp.14:11:
Here the men of Judah tell Samson that they have come down to tie him up and hand him over to the Philistines. Samson does not resist right away; instead, he asks them for a promise: that they themselves will not attack him.

The three thousand men of Judah speak, frightened because the Philistines were ruling over them. They prefer to hand Samson over rather than face a conflict with their oppressors. Samson, for his part, wants to make sure his own people will not harm him. Later it will be seen that God acts with power in him.

For today: sometimes fear leads us to give in to pressure and let go of the one God has used. Let us pray for the courage to act with justice and to trust God, instead of seeking comfort alone.
exp.14:12:
The men of Judah assured Samson that they would not kill him. They would only tie him up and hand him over to the Philistines. They bound him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock.

The men of Judah speak here, about three thousand of them. They lived under Philistine rule and were afraid. They chose to hand Samson over rather than face their oppressors. Samson agreed to be tied up, but asked that they not be the ones to kill him. The text does not explain why he let himself be bound. Some think he trusted that God would deliver him, although the Bible does not say this directly.

For today: sometimes fear leads us to choose the easy way out instead of the brave one. The people of Judah could have sought help from God, but they preferred to give in. Let us ask God for the courage not to give up what is right merely out of fear of trouble.
exp.14:14:
It says that Samson found a donkey's jawbone that was still fresh, that is, recently dead and not dried out or brittle. He took it in his hand and with it defeated a thousand men. The word for "struck" here means that he hit them or killed them.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Samson had just been handed over by his own people from Judah to the Philistines, bound with new ropes. But the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, the ropes fell off, and with no other weapon at hand, he used what he found. The text credits the strength to God, not to the jawbone.

For today: God can use what you have at hand, even when it seems small or improvised. Instead of waiting until you have better resources, offer him with faith what you have today, and trust that his power works through you.
exp.14:15:
Samson composes a short song or verse about his victory. There is a play on words: in the original language, the words for "donkey" and "heaps" sound very similar, and for this reason some translate it as "with the jawbone of a donkey, I have piled them in heaps." The jawbone is the bone of the lower jaw. He says that with that bone he defeated a thousand men.

He speaks after the Philistines came to Lehi to capture him. His own countrymen from Judah had handed him over, bound. Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, the ropes fell off his arms, and he fought with whatever he found at hand. The following verse shows that he acknowledges the deliverance came from God.

For today: God can use the little and the common things we have. But let us not forget to give Him the credit and to depend on Him, because Samson soon admitted his thirst and cried out to the LORD.
exp.14:19:
This verse says that Samson judged Israel for twenty years, while the Philistines dominated the region. "Judged" here does not mean only pronouncing sentences, but also guiding and defending the people.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Judges, who summarizes Samson's life. Earlier, Samson had defeated many Philistines and, exhausted and thirsty, cried out to God, who gave him water. This verse closes that part of his story. Samson was a man with great flaws, but God kept working through him. Some scholars think the twenty years came before his final fall; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when you feel weak, cry out to God with sincerity. He can sustain you and use your life, even with your weaknesses.
exp.15:1:
This verse tells that someone warned the people of Gaza that Samson was in their city. So they surrounded him and posted watchers at the city gate all night. They stayed quiet, waiting for the light of morning to kill him.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Gaza was a Philistine city, and the Philistines dominated Israel at that time. Samson, a judge of Israel, had gone there and got involved with a prostitute. The people of Gaza saw their chance to finish off their enemy. Even so, the following text shows that Samson escaped.

For today: Samson put himself in danger by neglecting his life and his holiness. God can rescue us from our mistakes, but it is wise not to play with them. Let us watch our steps and seek to live with integrity.
exp.15:2:
According to the passage, Samson lay there until midnight, then got up. He tore up the doors of the city of Gaza, along with their two posts and their bar (the crossbar that held them shut), put them on his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the mountain that faces Hebron.

The narrator tells us that the people of Gaza had surrounded him, planning to kill him at dawn, while he was with a woman of loose morals. Samson, a judge of Israel, escapes the trap by the strength God had given him. Many see here a sign of his power, but also a contrast with his conduct, because the text does not present him as a moral example.

For today: God can sustain us and deliver us even when we get ourselves into dangerous situations, but we must not take advantage of his grace. If we have received his help, let us value that mercy and seek to live with more wisdom and purity.
exp.15:3:
Samson falls in love with a woman named Delilah, who lived in the valley of Sorek, after what happened in Gaza. The text does not say that she was a Philistine or that she loved him; the explanation does not clarify this here.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells the story of Samson, a judge of Israel endowed with extraordinary strength. He has just shown his power by carrying off the gates of Gaza. Now the story changes direction: his physical strength stands in contrast to his weakness in relationships. Soon the Philistine rulers will seek out Delilah to discover the secret of his strength.

For today: love and emotions are powerful, but they need wisdom. Before we give our heart or our trust to someone, it is wise to pray, seek counsel, and notice whether that relationship draws us closer to God or pulls us away from Him.
exp.15:4:
This verse tells how the rulers of the Philistines went to Delilah. They asked her to trick Samson so they could find out the secret of his great strength, and then be able to tie him up and make him suffer. In return, each of them would give her eleven hundred pieces of silver.

The ones speaking are the Philistine lords, rulers and enemies of Israel. Samson had humiliated them again and again, and they wanted to stop him. The Bible says that he loved Delilah, but it does not clearly say whether she was a Philistine or whether she loved him. That is left open to interpretation.

For today: money and pressure can push us to betray the trust of others. Let us be careful about whom we open our hearts to, and let no gain lead us to hurt someone who trusts us.
exp.15:6:
Samson tells Delilah that if they bind him with seven fresh bowstrings, that is, flexible branches freshly cut that have not yet dried out, he will lose his strength and become like any other man.

Samson, judge of Israel, speaks to Delilah. The Philistine lords had offered her money to discover the secret of his strength. Samson does not tell the truth; this is the first of several false answers. The verses that follow show that it was a trap, and that he frees himself easily. Even so, he plays with fire by continuing in that relationship.

For today: when we toy with temptation, believing we can control it, sooner or later it catches up with us. It is wise to step away in time from whatever puts our faith at risk and to guard what God has entrusted to us.
exp.15:7:
This verse tells how the Philistine rulers brought Delilah seven fresh green willow branches, that is, flexible and moist twigs that had not yet dried out. With them she tied up Samson, just as he had told her to do.

Delilah asked Samson to reveal the secret of his strength. The Philistine leaders wanted to defeat him, and she was working with them. Samson answered with a deception: he said that fresh green branches would weaken him. There were spies hidden in the room, but he snapped the branches easily. The Bible does not explain in detail why he kept playing this game with her.

For today: toying with temptation and with people who do not look out for you is dangerous, even when you believe you have everything under control. Seek wise boundaries and surround yourself with people who help you stay faithful to God.
exp.15:9:
Delilah accuses Samson because he gave her a false answer about the secret of his strength. She says that he deceived her and told her lies. Then she asks him again to tell her how he could be tied.

Delilah, whom Samson loved, is speaking. The Philistine lords had offered her money to find out the source of his strength. She had already tried once with the fresh bowstrings, and there were spies hidden in the room. She pretends to feel hurt and trust, but in reality she seeks to hand him over to his enemies.

For today: let us take care about who and what we allow into our hearts. A relationship that presses us again and again to give in on what God has entrusted to us should alert us. Let us ask for wisdom to set boundaries in time.
exp.15:10:
Samson tells Delilah that if they bind him tightly with new ropes that have never been used, he will lose his strength and be like any other man. The verse says the ropes must be new and never used. He is speaking to Delilah, who kept asking him to reveal the secret of his strength. She was working with the Philistines, who wanted to overpower him. He had already lied to her before with the fresh branches. This second answer is also false, and the Bible shows this when he easily breaks the ropes. Samson is playing with fire, and he comes closer and closer to revealing the truth.

For today: do not play with temptations or with those who seek your harm. Each small concession brings you closer to a greater fall, so set clear limits in time.
exp.15:11:
Delilah took new ropes, the ones Samson had told her about, and tied him with them. Then she shouted that the Philistines were coming against him. Some men were waiting in hiding in a room, that is, in an inner chamber. Samson snapped the ropes from his arms as easily as if they were a thread.

The Philistine leaders had asked Delilah to find out the secret of Samson's strength. She keeps pressing him again and again. Samson gives her false answers, yet he keeps playing with her and stays close to danger. This is the third time she tests him, and she still does not know the true secret.

For today: playing with temptation is dangerous, even if so far we have come through unharmed. Samson escaped three times, but each time he came closer to the truth that would destroy him. It is wise to flee quickly from whatever drags us along, rather than seeing how far we can go.
exp.15:12:
Delilah accuses Samson that until now he has been lying to her, and she asks him to finally tell her how he could be tied up. This time he answers that if she weaves the seven locks of his head into the cloth, he would lose his strength. He is speaking of the seven locks of his hair being woven into the cloth on a loom.

Delilah speaks because the Philistine rulers had asked her to discover the secret of Samson's strength. She had already tried twice to tie him up, and both attempts failed. Samson plays with her, coming closer and closer to the truth, without realizing the danger. This is the third attempt.

For today: playing with what can harm us often slowly lowers our guard. If something or someone keeps seeking our downfall, it is not wise to flirt with the risk. It is better to keep our distance and ask God for wisdom.
exp.15:13:
Here, the account tells how Delilah once again got the secret of Samson's strength out of him, and once again he deceived her. She fastened the pin (a peg that held the loom in place) with Samson's hair woven into the cloth, and cried out that the Philistines were upon him. He awoke and pulled away the pin and the whole web.

The narrator recounts this third attempt by Delilah. The Philistine lords had asked her to discover the source of Samson's strength, and their spies waited in hiding. Samson was playing with her, but he was already very close to revealing the truth, since he had mentioned his hair.

For today: playing near danger usually ends badly. Samson believed he could control the situation, but each step brought him closer to his fall. It is wise to move away quickly from what tempts us, rather than testing how far we can go.
exp.15:16:
Samson tells Delilah his secret. He opened his whole heart to her, and the words describe a complete disclosure. The razor is the blade used to shave the head. A Nazirite was someone set apart for God by a special vow, which included never cutting the hair. Samson says that if his head is shaved, he will lose his strength and become like any other man.

Samson, judge of Israel, had been dedicated to God since before he was born. Delilah pressed him every day, and he, worn out, gave in. The Philistine lords had offered her money to discover his secret. His strength did not lie in the hair itself, but in his relationship with God, which the hair represented.

For today: let us guard what God has entrusted to us and not hand it over out of weariness or pressure. Let us set healthy limits with anyone who insists on pushing us to give in, and ask God for the firmness to say "no" in time.
exp.15:22:
This verse tells that the lords of the Philistines gathered to hold a great feast. They offered a sacrifice to Dagon, who was their god, and rejoiced. They said that Dagon had delivered Samson, their enemy, into their hands.

The ones speaking are the Philistine rulers. Samson, a judge of Israel, had caused them great harm. Now he was blinded, a prisoner in Gaza, and forced to grind grain. They credited their victory to Dagon, not knowing that God allowed it. The text mentions that Samson's hair was growing back, and this prepares what happens next.

We can celebrate a triumph and believe everything is settled, but only God sees the end. It is better to be humble and not to boast. And if today you feel defeated, remember that God can still act.
exp.15:25:
Samson asks the young man who is leading him by the hand to bring him close to the pillars that hold up the building. He wants to feel them and lean against them.

Samson speaks as a blind prisoner of the Philistines. They had brought him out of prison to mock him at a feast in honor of their god. His request seems simple, but it sets up what follows: his prayer to God for strength one last time. The Bible does not say whether the young man understood what Samson intended to do.

For today: even when we have failed and feel weak or humbled, we can return to God. He can use our last resort, and the best thing is to lean on Him with humility.
exp.16:2:
Here a mother says that she had dedicated the eleven hundred pieces of silver to the Lord, but she does so so that her son may have a carved image (carved from wood or stone) and a cast image (made of melted metal). Then she returns the money to Micah, whose name appears here as Micah. A shekel was a unit of weight used as money.

The mother is the one speaking. He had stolen the money, she had cursed it, and when he confessed, she blesses him. We are in a time when Israel had become disordered in spiritual matters. She mixes devotion to the Lord with making an image, something the law of Moses forbade (Exodus 20:4).

We may want to honor God with good intentions, but in our own way. A sincere promise does not make right what God has already said he does not want. It is worth asking ourselves whether we worship as God teaches in his Word or as it seems best to us.
exp.16:3:
This verse tells how Micah returned the money to his mother. She took two hundred shekels of silver (a quantity of silver measured by weight) and gave them to the founder, the craftsman who melts metal. With them he made a carved image and a cast image (made of molten metal), and they were placed in Micah's house.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes a time of spiritual disorder. The mother says she dedicated the silver to the LORD, yet she uses it to make an image, something the law of Moses forbade. In addition, the account notes that only part of the silver was used, and that there was no king in Israel. Each person did what seemed right to him.

For today: good intentions or using God's name is not enough to please him. It is wise to measure our customs and decisions by what God actually says in his Word, not only by what seems right to us.
exp.16:4:
The verse says that Micah had a house of gods, made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest. So the explanation tells us that Micah kept a shrine with idols in his home. He also made an ephod (a priestly garment) and teraphim (household figures used to seek guidance). Then he set apart one of his sons to be his priest.

The narrator of Judges describes a time without a king and without a clear direction. Micah mixes the name of the LORD with images and rites of his own invention, something the law of Moses forbade. The texts that follow show that the author tells this as a sign of spiritual disorder, not as an example to follow. Furthermore, a priest had to be of the tribe of Levi, and his son was not.

We can have good intentions and still worship God in our own way. It is worth asking ourselves whether we serve Him as He has revealed in His Word, or as is more comfortable for us.
exp.16:9:
Micah makes the Levite an offer: stay in his house and be like a father and priest to him. In return, he will pay him ten shekels of silver a year (a shekel was a unit of weight for silver), his usual clothing, and his food. The Levite agrees and stays.

This happens in the time of the judges, when, according to the book, "everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes." Micah already had his own shrine with idols. The Levites were meant to serve in the worship God had established, not in a private shrine. Here Micah hires the Levite to lend legitimacy to his religion, and the Levite lets himself be guided by convenience.

For today: let us be careful not to use God to back up what we already want to do. And if we serve God, let it not be only for comfort or gain, but out of obedience to his Word.
exp.16:12:
Micah says that now he is sure the Lord will bless him, because he has a Levite as his priest. The phrase about the Lord doing him good means that God will give him prosperity and favor. The word about it being done or settled means that it has been put in place, or has come to be.

Micah had made an idol of silver and had a shrine in his house. It was a disordered time, when everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes. On finding a Levite, from the tribe set apart for the service of God, he believes that his home religion is now complete. But he himself appointed him, and his worship remained mixed with idols. Many understand this passage as a warning.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we trust that God blesses us because we meet certain religious requirements, or because we truly obey him according to his Word. Having religious things does not guarantee God's favor; he looks for a faithful and sincere heart.
exp.17:0:
In those days Israel had no king. The tribe of Dan was looking for a territory where it could settle, because it had not yet taken possession of the land that had fallen to it.

The narrator of the book of Judges is the one speaking. This phrase appears several times in the book and sums up a time of disorder, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them. Dan had not managed to conquer the territory assigned to it, and so it was looking for another place. Later it sends out scouts, and on that journey they will arrive at the house of Micah.

For today: when we do not put God in the place of guide, we tend to settle things our own way and end up far from what He has given us. Ask Him today to help you finish faithfully what He has already placed in your hands.
exp.17:10:
Six hundred men of the tribe of Dan set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, two towns in their own territory. They went "armed with weapons of war", that is, ready to fight. This was the start of their journey to conquer a new place to live.

Earlier, five Danite scouts had looked over the region of Laish, in the north, and came back urging their brothers to take it. They said God had handed it into their hands. The account in the book of Judges shows a disordered time, and not everything they do here is presented as an example to follow. The Bible does not make clear that God commanded this advance.

We can learn not to act simply because others encourage us with confident words. Before taking a big step, it is wise to pray, to seek God's guidance in his Word, and to ask ourselves whether our decision is just.
exp.17:12:
These six hundred men of the tribe of Dan continued on their way from Kiriath-jearim. They passed through the hill country of Ephraim and arrived at the house of Micah, a man who had a shrine of his own.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Danites were looking for a territory where they could settle. Five scouts had already passed by that house before and had seen the ephod (a garment used in worship), the household idols, and the carved image. Now the group draws near, and the account prepares what follows: they will take those objects. Judges shows a time of spiritual disorder.

For today: let us not trust a religion made to suit ourselves. Before we move forward with our plans, let us ask God to examine whether what we follow comes from Him or only from our own convenience.
exp.17:14:
The explanation says that the Danites came to the house of Micah and went to the young Levite, who lived there. They greeted him and asked how he was.

This story is from the time of the judges, when there was no king in Israel and each person did what seemed right to him. Six hundred men from the tribe of Dan were looking for a place to settle. Their five scouts already knew about Micah's religious objects. The friendly greeting seems polite, but it was the first step toward taking those objects from him and carrying off the Levite.

Today, a kind word does not always show good intentions. Let us be honest in how we treat others, and not use religion to get what we want, but instead seek God's guidance.
exp.17:15:
This verse says that six hundred men of the tribe of Dan stood at the entrance of the gate, with their weapons of war ready. "Armed with their weapons of war" means they were equipped for fighting. The gate was the entrance to the city or the place where they were.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. The Danites were looking for a territory to settle, and five spies had already passed by the house of Micah. There they saw religious objects: an ephod, household idols, and images. While the six hundred armed men kept the young Levite busy at the gate, the spies went in and carried off everything. The account shows a time of spiritual and moral disorder.

For today: strength or cleverness does not justify doing wrong. The Danites acted as if they had a right to everything, but God does not approve of worship mixed with theft, or of shortcuts. Before you act, ask yourself whether your decision honors God.
exp.17:16:
The explanation says that the five men of the tribe of Dan, who had earlier gone out to explore the land, came back and went into Micah's house. There they took the religious objects: a carved image, the ephod (a priest's garment used to seek God's guidance), the teraphim (household figures or idols), and a cast metal image (made of molten metal). Meanwhile, the priest was standing at the gate with the six hundred armed men.

Here the narrator speaks. It is a disordered time in Israel, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The Danites were looking for territory and wanted to secure a religion of their own. They used force and distracted the Levite priest so they could take what was not theirs.

For today: let us not seek God by shortcuts, or by things we can control or take by force. Let us worship God as He has asked, and not use faith to justify what is unjust.
exp.17:17:
This verse tells how the five men from the tribe of Dan entered the house of Micah and took his religious objects: a carved image, the ephod (a garment used by priests), the teraphim (household figures used in religious practices), and a molten image made of cast metal. The priest, surprised, asked them what they were doing.

The one speaking is the young priest whom Micah had hired. The Danites were looking for a territory where they could settle, and they also wanted a priest of their own. This takes place in a disordered period of Israel's history, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The armed men waiting outside show that they were acting by force.

For today: it is not acceptable to worship God in our own way or according to what suits us. It is wise to examine whether our faith rests on the Word of God or on customs, objects, or personal interests. God deserves sincere obedience, not convenient religion.
exp.17:19:
It says the priest was glad. Then he took the ephod (a sacred garment used in worship), the teraphim (figures used for religious purposes in the home), and the graven image, and went in the midst of the people of Dan. His joy did not come from obeying God, but from receiving a better offer.

The men of the tribe of Dan were looking for territory, and they passed by the house of Micah. They took his religious objects and persuaded the Levite to go with them, offering him a more important position. Judges shows a disordered time, in which each person did whatever seemed right to them. Here worship and the priesthood are treated as a business.

For today: examine what makes you glad when you make decisions. A greater position or more benefits do not always mean God's will. Before deciding, ask yourself whether you are drawing closer to God or only to your own convenience.
exp.17:24:
The men of Dan tell Micah to stop shouting at them. They warn him that some men with a violent, angry temper might attack him, and that he would lose his life and the lives of his household.

The tribe of Dan speaks here. They are looking for land, and they have already taken Micah's idols and his priest. Micah protests, but they openly threaten him. He withdraws when he sees that they are stronger. The account shows a time of disorder, without law or justice, where force and manipulated religion are mixed together. The Bible only recounts this; it does not approve of it.

Today we can remember that having power does not make something right. Before we use our strength, our voice, or our influence, let us ask ourselves whether we are honoring God and treating others with justice.
exp.17:26:
The explanation says that the men of Dan took the idols that Micah had made and also carried off his priest. They came to Laish, a quiet and secure people, struck them with the edge of the sword, and burned the city with fire.

Here the narrator is telling the story, not speaking as a character. The tribe of Dan had not taken the land that had been assigned to it, so it went looking for another by force. The book of Judges shows a time of disorder, when everyone did what seemed right to them. The text describes what happened; it does not say that God approved of it.

For today: let us not confuse success with God's blessing. We can achieve what we want and still be far from his way. Let us ask him to teach us to seek what is right, not only what suits us.
exp.17:27:
This verse tells us that no one came to help the people of Laish when they were attacked. They lived far from Zidon, the nearest Phoenician city, and they had no dealings with other peoples. They were in a valley near Beth-rehob. After the Danites destroyed the city, they rebuilt it and settled there to live.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how the tribe of Dan, without having taken the land assigned to it, went looking for another place. They attacked a peaceful and unsuspecting people. The account shows the disorder of that time, when each person did whatever seemed right to them, and even stole the religious objects of Micah.

For today: security without connections is fragile. We should not live isolated lives; let us seek community and care for others. Moreover, it is not enough to succeed if we have taken the wrong path.
exp.18:3:
This verse tells how the Levite's father-in-law, seeing him arrive at Bethlehem, went out happily to receive him. He persuaded him to stay, and the Levite spent three days there, eating, drinking and resting.

It is part of the story in Judges, which takes place in a time of moral disorder in Israel. A Levite goes to bring back his concubine, who had gone to her father's house. The narrator speaks here not of reproach but of a very warm welcome. Some interpreters see in the father a sincere desire to reconcile the couple; others note that the insistence on keeping him there prepares the delay that brings serious consequences later.

For today: hospitality and the joy of reconciliation are valuable, but we should take care that comfort does not lead us to postpone what we ought to do in time.
exp.18:14:
It says that the Levite, his concubine, and his servant turned off the road to spend the night in Gibeah. When they arrived, they sat down in the square, which was the open space of the city, because no one offered them a place in their home.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He tells of the return journey of a Levite toward the region of Ephraim. Gibeah belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, that is, it was an Israelite town. Even so, no one received them. In that time hospitality was a very important duty, and this failure foreshadows the great wickedness that comes later in the story. Only an old stranger will help them.

For today: open your eyes to those who are alone or passing through, in your church, workplace, or neighborhood. A simple gesture, such as a meal or a place to rest, can be a real act of love.
exp.18:18:
Here a Levite says he needs nothing from the old man. He already has straw and feed for his donkeys, and bread and wine for himself, for his concubine, and for his servant. The word for the dry feed given to animals is what the verse calls straw and provender. Only a place under a roof is still missing.

The one speaking is a Levite from the hill country of Ephraim, traveling with his companion and his servant. He arrived in Gibeah, but in the square no one took him in. An old man asks who he is, and he explains that he is not asking for food or money, but for hospitality. This shows how harsh the lack of welcome was in that town, as the book depicts in those dark days.

For today: sometimes the person nearby does not need gifts, but a safe place and a gesture of welcome. Think of someone in your church, workplace, or neighborhood who is alone or passing through, and open your door to them or invite them to eat.
exp.18:20:
This verse tells that the old man brought the travelers to his house. First he gave food to the donkeys, and then the visitors washed their feet, ate, and drank. Donkeys are the animals meant here, and the verse's wording refers to them as the animals that were fed. Washing the feet was a common gesture of courtesy, because people walked along dusty roads.

A Levite was traveling with his concubine and his servant, and no one in Gibeah took them in at the square. An old man who was coming in from the fields offered them his house and took charge of everything they needed. The narrator shows his kindness just before telling of the terrible wickedness of the men of the city. In this way the contrast is visible between the hospitality of one man and the violence of many.

Today we can practice a simple and genuine hospitality: opening the door, sharing the table, and caring for someone who is far from home or has nowhere to stay. Like the old man, one can do what is good even when everything around is wrong.
exp.18:24:
This verse describes a terrible crime. Some men of Gibeah wanted to abuse the guest, and they would not accept the offer of the host. So the Levite brought out his concubine, a secondary wife, and they abused her sexually all night long until morning. At dawn they let her go.

Context: the narrator of Judges describes a time of great wickedness in Israel, when everyone did whatever seemed right in their own eyes. No one in this scene acts justly: not the attackers, not the host who offered his own daughter and the concubine, and not the man who handed her over. The Bible recounts this as a denunciation of the people's moral collapse, not as an example to imitate.

For today: violence against women is never acceptable. As Christians, we must protect the vulnerable, listen to them, and speak up when someone is suffering abuse.
exp.18:26:
This verse tells that the Levite got up early, opened the door of the house where he had stayed, and got ready to continue his journey. Then he saw his concubine (a secondary wife) fallen before the door, with her hands on the threshold, which is the lower part of the entrance. She had spent the night suffering a terrible abuse.

It is part of the closing account of the book of Judges, which does not give a speech but a narrative. It shows how far the wickedness in Israel had gone. The book repeats that there was no king and that each person did whatever seemed right to them. The text does not approve of what happened; it presents it as a sign of a broken society.

For today: let us not be indifferent to the pain of the vulnerable. Let us listen to the one who suffers, protect the one who is in danger, and not look the other way.
exp.19:0:
All of the people of Israel came out together, and the assembly gathered as one person, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, and also from the land of Gilead, on the other side of the Jordan. They gathered before the Lord, that is, in the presence of God, at Mizpah. An assembly means a group of people gathered together.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Before this, a terrible crime had happened in Gibeah, a city in the tribe of Benjamin, and the people gather to decide what to do. According to the text that follows, they want to hear how that wickedness happened. Interpreters debate whether their reaction was entirely fair or whether it went too far, since the situation later becomes very violent.

For today: when there is a serious problem, let us seek unity, prayer, and truth before acting. Listening calmly and placing everything before God helps us not to react only with anger.
exp.19:2:
The tribe of Benjamin heard that the other Israelites had gathered at Mizpah. Then the Israelites asked that they be told how this evil had come about, meaning this terrible crime.

The speakers are the Israelites who have gathered, and the question is addressed to all of them, so that they may hear the case. The Levite, whose concubine was mistreated and died in Gibeah, will be the one to tell what happened. Notice that Benjamin only heard about the gathering; the text does not say they attended it. Before acting, the people want to hear the testimony.

For today: before judging or reacting to an injustice, let us take time to hear the facts calmly and truthfully. Seeking justice calls for listening carefully, without being carried away by rumors or by anger.
exp.19:8:
This verse is part of a sentence that continues from the previous one. The Israelites say that they will not return to their homes until they do the following to Gibeah: cast lots to decide who will go up against it. Casting lots was a common way of making decisions fairly in those times, trusting that God guided the outcome.

The assembly of Israel is speaking, after a Levite has told them about the terrible crime committed against his concubine in Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin. The people unite as one man and organize the army: they choose by lot and gather supplies. Later the story shows that anger and hasty decisions led to much violence, so not everything they do is a model to imitate.

When faced with injustice, seeking unity and order is good, but it is wise to ask for God's guidance and to act with humility, without letting ourselves be carried away by anger.
exp.19:9:
The explanation says that Israel will organize its army and its supplies. From every hundred men they will take ten, from every thousand they will take a hundred, and from every ten thousand they will take a thousand. They will carry provisions, meaning food, for those who are going to fight against Gibeah of Benjamin. The reason is the terrible wickedness that was committed there.

The people of Israel, gathered together as one man, speak after the horrible crime against the Levite's concubine. Before they fight, they decide how to divide the work and cast lots. Note that they will first ask the tribe of Benjamin what happened, as the following verse shows.

For today: even when something is unjust and stirs our anger, it is wise to act with order, cooperation, and a search for the truth. A just cause is not defended with haste or anger, but with responsibility and wisdom.
exp.19:10:
This verse says that all the men of Israel gathered together against the city of Gibeah, united as one man. That is, they acted with one decision, without divisions. The explanation of the other words in the phrase is not needed here, since the verse above is what the reader sees.

After a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin, the tribes came together and decided to act jointly. They organized the response by casting lots and gathering supplies for the journey. Then they asked Benjamin to hand over the guilty men, but Benjamin refused. The account shows unity in facing evil, although Judges is a book of very chaotic times, and not everything the people do is approved by God.

For today: unity has great strength, but it needs to be guided by justice and humility. Before we join together to act, let us ask God for wisdom, so that our unity serves good and not anger.
exp.19:11:
This verse says that the tribes of Israel sent messengers to the whole tribe of Benjamin to ask what terrible evil had been committed among them. The word "men" in the verse refers to the men who were sent, and "wickedness" refers to a dreadful crime.

The tribes of Israel are speaking together here, after the horrible crime in Gibeah, where the concubine of a Levite was abused and killed. Before going to war, they seek an explanation and give Benjamin the chance to hand over the guilty. But Benjamin refused to listen and defended its own, which led to a war between brothers.

For today: when there is a serious injustice, the right response is to confront it with the truth and not cover it up, even if the guilty person belongs to our own group or family. Defending the guilty out of loyalty alone ends up harming everyone.
exp.19:14:
It says that the men of Benjamin were counted for war. Twenty-six thousand came out of the cities, all able to fight with the sword, and in addition seven hundred chosen men who lived in Gibeah.

The verse speaks of men who were able to fight, that is, skilled in battle. Men who were wicked and without moral worth are the ones the text describes as worthless and corrupt.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had asked the people of Benjamin to hand over the wicked men of Gibeah, who had committed a terrible crime, so that they could be punished. Benjamin refused to listen to their brothers and chose instead to prepare for war. So one tribe ended up set against the others.

For today: when someone points out a wrong that needs to be corrected, it is easy to defend our own group and trust in our own strength. But misplaced loyalty leads to ruin. It is better to listen, to admit the mistake, and to seek justice with humility.
exp.19:16:
This verse says that the men of Israel were counted, not including the tribe of Benjamin. There were four hundred thousand men who knew how to fight with the sword, that is, who were trained to use it. All of them were men of war, meaning soldiers prepared for battle.

The one counting is the narrator of the book, who describes how Israel organized itself to fight against Benjamin. This happens after a terrible crime in Gibeah, and the Benjamites refused to hand over the guilty men. Both sides prepare for a war between brothers, in a disordered time in which, according to the book, everyone did whatever seemed right in their own eyes.

For today: before facing a conflict, let us ask whether we truly seek justice and reconciliation, or only to win. Numbers and strength are not enough, and it is wise to seek God with humility and in time.
exp.19:18:
It says that the Israelites rose early in the morning and camped opposite Gibeah, the city of Benjamin. The phrase about setting up camp against it means they set up their camp in order to attack. Gibeah was the place where the terrible events of the previous chapter had happened.

Here the narrator tells the story. Israel had gathered together as one people, and God told them that Judah would go first. They wanted to punish the crime committed at Gibeah, since the tribe of Benjamin refused to hand over the guilty men. It is a difficult time, when everyone did as they saw fit. Notice that, although they consulted God, the battle that follows does not turn out as they expected.

For today: rising early and seeking God is good, but it does not guarantee that everything will go easily. When you face a problem, pray, act with humility, and do not assume the outcome. Keep seeking God even in the middle of difficulties.
exp.19:26:
Here the text says that the Israelites, after a harsh defeat, sought direction from God. It mentions that the ark of the covenant was there, in Bethel, as a sign that God had committed himself to his people. The phrase about asking the Lord means that they consulted him about what to do.

The narrator of the book explains this detail in parentheses. Israel had lost two days of battle against the tribe of Benjamin, with thousands dead. Before this, they had fought trusting in themselves; now they weep, fast and offer sacrifices. Then Phinehas, the priest, ministers before the ark, and God gives them an answer.

For today: when everything goes wrong, it is not enough to keep trying with our own strength. We can stop, humble ourselves and seek God sincerely before deciding the next step. He knows how to guide us.
exp.19:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel set ambushes around Gibeah. An ambush is a group of soldiers hidden in wait, ready to attack by surprise. Gibeah was the city of the tribe of Benjamin where a terrible crime had taken place.

At this point, the writer of the book tells how Israel prepared its third attack against Benjamin. They had already lost two battles. This time they asked God, and He promised them victory. After receiving that answer, Israel made a plan with strategy, not only with strength.

For today: trusting God does not mean ceasing to think or to plan. We can ask Him for direction and then act with wisdom, effort and patience, knowing that the outcome is in His hands.
exp.19:30:
Judges 20:31 tells how the men of Benjamin went out to fight against Israel and were drawn away from their city, Gibeah. They began to strike down some of the Israelites, as they had done at other times, along two roads: one that goes up to Bethel, and another that goes to Gibeah across the open country. About thirty men of Israel died.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. It is the third day of fighting. Israel had lost twice, and now it pretended to retreat while preparing ambushes. The Benjamites believed they would win again, without seeing the trap. The text does not justify all the violence; it describes a time of great disorder in Israel.

For today: past success can make us overconfident and blind. Before we take anything for granted, it is wise to ask God for wisdom and to examine our situation humbly.
exp.19:32:
At the agreed moment, the whole army of Israel left the place where it had pretended to flee and lined up for battle at Baal-tamar. At the same time, the men hidden in ambush (groups that wait in concealment to attack by surprise) came out of their hiding place, out of the open field of Gibeah.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin, which had protected the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah. Twice Israel had been defeated, so now it used a strategy: pretending to retreat in order to draw Benjamin away from its city. Some scholars note that the text summarizes the plan in a way that is somewhat hard to follow.

For today: even when we are right, fighting leaves pain behind. Before we act against others, it is wise to seek God with humility and to prepare ourselves with wisdom and patience.
exp.19:35:
This verse says that the men of Benjamin realized they were defeated. The Israelites had pulled back on purpose, making room for the Benjamites to advance. They did this because they trusted the ambush they had set up behind Gibeah. The ambushers are hidden groups who attack by surprise.

It is part of the account of the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed at Gibeah. The narrator describes the battle and says that the LORD struck Benjamin. Benjamin believed it would win, as in the previous days, but did not know that disaster was near.

Today we learn that confidence based only on appearances or past successes can deceive us. It is wise to examine our lives with humility and not to excuse the evil within us.
exp.19:37:
This verse says that the men of Israel and the men hidden in the ambush had agreed on a sign. The men in the ambush were to make a great fire, so that a large column of smoke would rise up from the city of Gibeah.

It is part of the account of the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The narrator explains Israel's plan: to make Benjamin believe it was winning, as it had the previous time, and then to surprise them. The smoke would signal that the city had already been taken.

For today: this passage reminds us how dangerous it is to trust in an apparent victory without looking at the whole situation. It also invites us to be humble and to ask God to show us what we cannot see.
exp.19:39:
This verse describes the key moment of the battle. When the flame began to rise up out of the city (Gibeah) with a pillar of smoke, the men of Benjamin looked back and saw that all the fire of the city was rising up to heaven.

It is part of the account of the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The author of the book is the one telling the story. The Israelites pretended to flee in order to draw Benjamin away from the city, while an ambush set it on fire. The smoke was the agreed signal. Benjamin believed it was winning, but it had fallen into the trap.

For today: confidence in oneself can blind us. Benjamin only looked at its apparent victory and did not see the danger behind it. It is good to stop, look with humility, and ask ourselves whether we have set aside justice and the guidance of God.
exp.19:40:
This verse describes the moment when the battle turns. The men of Israel, who had pretended to flee, turned around to attack. The men of Benjamin were filled with fear, because they understood that disaster had already come upon them.

It is part of the account in the book of Judges, which tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. This happened after a terrible crime in Gibeah, and the Benjamites protected the guilty. Israel set an ambush and sent up a great smoke from the city as a signal. When Benjamin saw the smoke, they realized they were surrounded. The narrator does not speak in a personal voice but simply reports the events.

For today: confidence in oneself can be deceiving. The Benjamites believed they were winning, but they did not see the danger behind them. It is wise to examine our decisions with humility, to turn back to what is right in time, and not to defend wrong out of pride or misplaced loyalty.
exp.19:44:
This verse tells of the end of the battle between the tribes of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. The Benjaminites, defeated, fled toward the wilderness, to a rock called Rimmon. Along the way, the Israelites overtook five thousand of them, and they pursued them as far as Gidom, where they killed two thousand more.

It is part of an account in the book of Judges, written by a narrator who does not identify himself. It tells of the punishment of Benjamin for protecting the guilty in a terrible crime at Gibeah. The book describes a time without order, when everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. It is an account of what happened, not a model to imitate.

For today: when injustice is tolerated, its consequences grow and wound many people. Today we can choose to act justly and humbly in time, before evil becomes larger.
exp.19:46:
This verse tells that, out of the whole tribe of Benjamin, only six hundred men managed to escape. They fled into the wilderness, to a rock called Rimmon, and stayed there for four months. The word "rock" in this verse means a high, rugged place that is hard to attack.

It is part of the civil war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, which had defended men guilty of a terrible crime in Gibeah. The narrator of the book recounts these events without fully approving of them; the book shows a time of great violence, when everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. These six hundred are the survivors who will later allow the tribe to continue.

For today: when sin is not corrected in time, its consequences can be very painful for everyone. We should seek justice with humility, and not let pride or misplaced loyalty lead us to defend what is wrong.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that the men of Israel had made a solemn vow at Mizpah. They promised that none of them would give his daughter in marriage to a man of the tribe of Benjamin.

The writer explains what had happened before. The other tribes had fought against Benjamin because of a terrible crime in Gibeah (chapters 19 and 20). Benjamin had nearly been wiped out. Now the people weep, because their own vow threatens to erase one tribe of Israel.

Today this teaches us to think before we make strong promises, especially when we are angry. Words spoken in haste can bring painful consequences. Before promising something, it is wise to pray and ask God for wisdom.
exp.20:2:
Here the people of Israel cry out to God in grief. They ask why something so serious has happened: that one of the twelve tribes, Benjamin, is about to disappear. The phrase about being incomplete means that the tribe is no longer whole.

The people have gathered at Bethel, the house of God, weeping since the evening. Shortly before, in a terrible war against Benjamin, they had nearly killed the entire tribe. They had also sworn at Mizpah not to give their daughters in marriage to the men of Benjamin. Now they see that their own oath and their violence led them to this loss. Their question is sincere, even though they themselves had a part in the problem.

For today: when we suffer the consequences of hasty decisions, it is good to bring our grief to God, but also to examine with humility what our own part was, before making promises or passing judgments on impulse.
exp.20:10:
The explanation says that the people of Israel ordered the killing of all the men of Jabesh-gilead and of every woman who had already been with a man. The phrase about a woman who had known a man means she had had sexual relations. The virgins would be kept alive.

This happens at the end of Judges, a time of great disorder, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them. The tribes of Israel had nearly destroyed Benjamin and had sworn not to give them wives. Later they regretted it and looked for a way out, but they committed more violence. The Bible records the event; it does not approve of it as an example.

For today: when we try to fix one wrong with another, the harm grows. Let us seek God's guidance and not rely on our own ideas.
exp.20:11:
It says that the Israelites found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young virgins, that is, women who had never been intimate with a man. They brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan. The narrator tells the ending of the book of Judges. The tribes of Israel had nearly destroyed Benjamin and had sworn not to give them their daughters as wives. Then they grieved over that tribe and looked for a way out. This solution is violent and tragic. The text does not approve it; it presents it as part of a chaotic time, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them (Judges 21:25).

For today: when we make hasty decisions or oaths without thinking, we sometimes try to fix one mistake with a bigger one. Before acting, let us seek God and his wisdom, and not let pride or anger guide us.
exp.20:14:
The explanation says that the people of Israel felt sorrow and grief over the tribe of Benjamin. They recognized that the Lord had made a breach in the tribes, that is, had left a gap or a wound: one of the twelve tribes was nearly gone.

This takes place at the end of the book of Judges, after a civil war between Israel and Benjamin. Almost the whole tribe died, and few men were left. The narrator describes how the people grieved, since they had made a vow that made it difficult to give wives to the survivors. They were looking for a solution, though the account shows a time of great disorder.

For today: when there is division and harm between brothers and sisters, grief can open the door to repentance and reconciliation. Before acting on impulse, it is wise to ask God for wisdom.
exp.20:15:
It says that Israel's leaders asked how they could get wives for the men of Benjamin who had survived. The word "destroyed" in the verse means wiped out or eliminated: almost all the women of that tribe had died.

The elders speak after the civil war against Benjamin. Israel had sworn not to give their daughters to that tribe, and now they grieved that a whole tribe might disappear. They had already been given women from Jabesh-gilead, but there were not enough. The elders look for a way out, and the book shows a nation in confusion, where each person did whatever seemed right to him.

For today: before making promises or taking hasty decisions, let us seek God's direction. Impulsive vows can bring painful consequences, and trying to fix them with human solutions often makes things more complicated.
exp.20:16:
They say that the survivors of Benjamin, those who managed to escape, must keep the land that belonged to their tribe. In this way Benjamin would not disappear from Israel.

The elders of Israel are speaking after the war against Benjamin, which left that tribe almost destroyed. They were grieved by what had happened, but they were also trapped by an oath not to give their daughters to the Benjamites. They were looking for a way for the tribe to survive. The book shows a time of great disorder, and not all of its solutions are examples to follow.

For today: when a conflict leaves wounds, it is worth seeking restoration and not merely winning the fight. But before promising something lightly, let us think carefully, because hasty vows can bring difficult problems that are hard to resolve.
exp.20:18:
This verse says that every year there was a solemn feast in honor of the Lord in Shiloh. Its location is given in detail: on the north side of Beth-el, on the east side of the highway that goes from Beth-el to Shechem, and on the south of Lebonah. The words "north" and "south" are the directions shown in the verse itself.

The leaders of Israel are speaking, after a terrible war against the tribe of Benjamin. They had sworn not to give them their daughters as wives, but they did not want the tribe of Benjamin to disappear. They were looking for a way out of their problem, and they point to this place and this feast as the opportunity. What they propose afterward is a violent and very questionable plan; the Bible does not present it as an example to follow. The book describes it as a time when each person did whatever seemed right to him.

For today: before making hasty promises, let us think carefully. And if we get it wrong, let us look for solutions that honor God and do not add more harm.
exp.20:20:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin were to hide among the vineyards near Shiloh and wait. When the young women came out to dance in circles, they would rush out, each seize one of them by force as his wife, and return to their own land. The word "catch" in the verse means to take by force.

It is spoken by the elders of Israel. After a war that had nearly wiped out the tribe of Benjamin, the Israelites had sworn not to give them their daughters. To avoid breaking their oath, they devised this violent plan. The book of Judges places it within a chaotic period, when "every man did what was right in his own eyes." The text does not approve of the act; it presents it as a sign of moral decline.

For today: a badly made promise is not fixed by another injustice. When we go wrong, the way forward is to repent and seek God, not to justify wrongdoing with clever solutions that harm others.
exp.20:21:
Here the elders of Israel tell the tribe of Benjamin what to answer if the fathers or brothers of the young women of Shiloh complain. They should ask for mercy. They argue that in the war they did not take wives for every Benjamite, and that, since the Israelites did not hand over their daughters of their own will (because of the oath they had made), they would not be guilty now.

The elders speak near the end of the book, in a chaotic time. Israel had nearly destroyed Benjamin and had sworn not to give them daughters. Now they look for a way out that keeps the oath only in appearance. The text does not approve the seizing of the women; it shows it as part of the disorder, for everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.

For today: let us not justify one wrong with another. When we have made promises or committed faults, let us seek honest and just solutions, not shortcuts that hurt others.
exp.20:23:
This verse tells that the Israelites, after settling the matter of the wives for the men of Benjamin, took their leave and returned home. Each one went back to his tribe, to his family, and to his inheritance, which is the land that fell to him as his share.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He closes a very painful story: a civil war among the tribes and a plan to keep Benjamin from disappearing. The verse that follows gives the background: there was no king, and each man did what seemed right to him. So the end of the scene sounds calm, but it leaves a sense of a people wounded and without direction.

For today: it is not enough that a conflict ends and each person goes back home. It is worth asking ourselves whether what we did was in line with God's will, and not merely with our own judgment.
exp.9:10:
God answers Israel's cry with a question that calls their own history to mind. He asks whether the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, and the Philistines had not mistreated them and ruled over them before. The question carries into the verses that follow, where God reminds them that he rescued them every time.

The LORD speaks. Israel had just admitted its sin: it had turned away from God to serve the Baals, false gods. But God does not respond right away with relief. First he shows them that he had already rescued them many times, and that they kept turning away from him. His answer aims to make them see how serious their unfaithfulness is.

For today: it is not enough to ask for help only when trouble arrives. God wants a heart that is faithful to him every day. Remembering how many times he has helped us invites us to return to him sincerely, not only out of need.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel did what displeased the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs. The Baals were false gods worshiped by the Canaanites, and the Asherahs were religious symbols connected with a Canaanite goddess, though experts debate the details.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He explains why trouble came: Israel mixed with the neighboring peoples, married them, and ended up adopting their gods. Then would come the punishment, the cry of the people, and deliverance through Othniel.

For today: forgetting God almost never happens all at once, but little by little. Guard your influences and keep your relationship with God alive. If you have drifted away, remember that he listens when you cry out.
exp.14:13:
When Samson arrived in Lehi, the Philistines came out to meet him shouting, sure that they already had him. Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon him with great power, and the ropes on his arms turned to something like burnt flax, and the bonds fell away from his hands. The shouting of the crowd describes a loud celebration, and the phrase "became like" means the ropes were left looking like burnt flax thread, no longer able to hold him.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Men of Judah, out of fear of the Philistines, had bound Samson in order to hand him over. Samson allowed it, but the strength did not come from himself. The text stresses that it was the Spirit of God who acted, not Samson's own muscles.

For today: when you feel bound or without a way out, remember that your true strength comes from God. Ask Him humbly for His help, instead of trusting only in your own abilities.
exp.7:32:
As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned away from God again. The Berean Standard Bible describes this as prostituting themselves with the Baals, which is a way of speaking about spiritual unfaithfulness: abandoning God to worship other gods. The Baals were Canaanite gods, and the name Baal-berith means "lord of the covenant." They set this god up as their own in place of the LORD.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Gideon had led Israel to a great victory and had encouraged them to follow God. But while he was alive, the faith of the people seemed to depend on their leader. When he was gone, they went back to their old habits. The verses that follow show that they forgot God and were not grateful to Gideon's family.

For today: do not let your faith depend only on one person or on a good season. Build your own relationship with God, remembering what he has done for you and thanking him every day.
exp.7:4:
Gideon arrives at Succoth with his three hundred men, exhausted from chasing the enemy. He asks the men of the town to give his troops some bread, meaning a little food, because they are worn out. He explains that he is still pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian. The word "troops" here refers to his soldiers.

Gideon, judge of Israel, is speaking. He has just defeated the Midianites with God's help, and now he is continuing the pursuit of their kings. The people of Succoth were Israelites, so he expected support from his own nation. They refused, perhaps out of fear of reprisal, though the text does not state this clearly.

For today: when someone is tired but keeps doing a good task, we can help them with something simple. And if we need to ask for help, let us do so with humility. A little bread shared in time can sustain others in their work.
exp.9:12:
It says that God reminds the Israelites that they abandoned him and worshiped other gods. That is why he tells them: "I will no longer save you."

God himself speaks here, answering the cry of Israel, which was suffering oppression from the Ammonites and the Philistines. He reminds them of the many times he rescued them, and yet they returned to idolatry. His words sound harsh, but they aim to shake them so that they recognize their sin. Then they confess and repent, and the account shows that God, moved by compassion, does not leave them entirely (v. 16).

For today: do not use God's kindness as an excuse for living far from him. If you have given your heart to other things, return to him sincerely, confess, and ask for his help.
exp.6:7:
Gideon sent the rest of the Israelites home to their tents but kept the three hundred men, who took charge of the others' provisions and rams' horns. Now the camp of Midian lay below him in the valley.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God had already reduced Gideon's army, first from 32,000 to 10,000 and then to 300, so that Israel would not think it had been saved by its own strength. The Midianites were very numerous and were oppressing Israel. Interpreters explain in different ways why those who lapped the water were chosen, but the clear point is that God made the decision.

For today: when you feel small or short on resources, remember that God can work through you. Obey step by step, and trust that the outcome will depend on Him.
exp.11:5:
Here the account tells how the men of Gilead guarded the fords of the Jordan River. Each man trying to escape from Ephraim was asked to say "Shibboleth." If he said "Sibboleth," because he could not pronounce it correctly, they recognized him by the way he spoke and killed him at the river crossings. The places named are the shallow spots where the river could be waded. The text gives the number of Ephraimites who died that day as forty-two thousand.

The writer of the book describes a civil war between tribes of Israel. Ephraim had taken offense at Jephthah and confronted him, and the fighting broke out. We are in the time of the judges, when the people lived in disorder. The account does not approve of the violence; it shows it as the fruit of that chaos.

For today: wounded pride and quarrels can grow until they cause enormous harm. Before responding harshly, let us seek to speak calmly and to be reconciled quickly. Jesus calls the peacemakers blessed.
exp.5:32:
The Midianites, the Amalekites, and the other peoples of the east joined together as one army. They crossed the Jordan River and camped in the Valley of Jezreel. The phrase about joining together describes the way their forces came together as one, and the idea of camping is simply that they set up their camp there.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Israel had been oppressed by these peoples for years. Gideon had just torn down the altar of Baal, and his father Joash had defended him. Now the real threat arrives: a huge enemy army. This is the moment when God is about to call Gideon to act, as the next verse shows.

For today: sometimes, right after taking a step of faith, the greatest trials arrive. This does not mean that God has abandoned you. It is an opportunity to depend on Him, who strengthened Gideon with His Spirit.
exp.18:4:
He says that on the fourth day, very early in the morning, the Levite got up and prepared to leave for home. But the young woman's father, his father-in-law, asked him to first refresh himself with a small bite of bread, and then he could go. A "son-in-law" is the husband of one's daughter, and to "refresh your heart" means to take in some food so you can regain your strength.

The young woman's father is the one speaking. The Levite had come to bring back his wife in order to make peace with her, and the father-in-law welcomed him with great warmth. In that time, taking good care of a guest was very important. Yet the father keeps stretching out the farewell, and that will end up affecting the journey.

For today: hospitality is good, but we also need wisdom to know when a kind invitation is delaying us from what we should be doing. Be grateful for the warmth, but act with prudence.
exp.8:16:
This verse recalls what Gideon (also called Jerubbaal) did. He fought for the people, risked his life, and rescued them from the power of Midian. The phrase "risked his life" means that he put his life on the line without thinking of himself.

Jotham, the only son of Gideon who escaped the slaughter, is the one speaking. From Mount Gerizim he tells the people of Shechem a fable. He wants to show them their ingratitude: they owed their freedom to his father, yet they killed his seventy sons and crowned Abimelech. This verse is part of his complaint.

For today: remember those who sacrificed themselves for you, such as parents, teachers, or brothers and sisters in the faith, and repay them with gratitude and respect. May the favors you have received never be forgotten.
exp.8:56:
This verse says that God brought back upon the men of Shechem the wickedness they had themselves committed. The phrase "brought back upon their own heads" means that they received the consequences of their own actions. The curse that Jotham had spoken against them also came true.

This is the narrator's comment closing the story of Abimelech. He killed his seventy brothers, and the men of Shechem supported him and made him king. Jotham, the only brother who escaped, had warned that this agreement would bring destruction (Judges 9:20). Abimelech died in battle, and the city of Shechem was also destroyed. The text presents this as the justice of God.

For today: we cannot support injustice and expect nothing to happen. God sees what we do and calls us to act with honesty. If we have taken part in something wrong, we can repent and ask for forgiveness.
exp.17:21:
Judges 18:22 says that after the men of the tribe of Dan had gone some distance from Micah's house, the men in the houses near Micah's home mobilized and chased after the Danites. The phrase "chased after" captures the sense here. The "houses near" were the homes of the neighbors in that place.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. The Danites, who were looking for land to settle, had just taken Micah's religious objects (the ephod, the household idols, and the carved image) and also his priest. The neighbors react to help Micah and recover what was his. The text does not approve the theft or the idolatry; it simply recounts a time of disorder.

For today: what we build with our own hands to feel secure can be taken from us in a moment. It is wise to place our trust in God, who cannot be stolen or made by human hands.
exp.9:7:
This verse tells that the Philistines and the Ammonites harassed and oppressed Israel for eighteen years. "Harassed and oppressed" means that they pressed hard on the Israelites and treated them cruelly. The suffering was hardest for the Israelites who lived on the other side of the Jordan River, in Gilead, a land that had once belonged to the Amorites.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, not with a personal voice but by summarizing the story. He explains that this oppression came after Israel forsook the LORD and served many false gods. The book shows a cycle: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, and then cry out asking for help.

For today: when we give first place to things that are not God, they end up enslaving us. If you are tired of burdens you have brought on yourself, you can return to God with humility and sincerity, because He still listens to those who cry out.
exp.2:16:
This verse tells us that Ehud brought the tribute to Eglon, king of Moab. It also tells us that Eglon was an obese man. The word "tribute" here means the payment that Israel had to give the king as a subject people.

The narrator of the book of Judges speaks here. Israel was oppressed by Moab because of its disobedience, and it cried out to God. He raised up Ehud as a deliverer. Ehud carried the tribute, but he also carried a hidden dagger. The detail about Eglon's great size sets up what happens next in the story.

For today: God can use people the world would overlook, such as a left-handed or limited man, to carry out his plan. When you feel you do not have what you need, cry out to God with confidence, and be willing to obey him with what you have.
exp.19:21:
It says that, after losing the first day of battle, the Israelite army took courage again and took up their battle positions once more in the same place where they had lined up the first day. The verse's "took courage" means to regain heart, and "took their battle positions" means they organized and prepared for the fight once more.

This is part of a passage from the book of Judges. The one speaking is not a character but the narrator. The tribes of Israel were fighting against Benjamin over a terrible crime committed in Gibeah. Israel had suffered a great defeat, with twenty-two thousand dead. Even so, they wept before the LORD and asked Him for guidance, and He told them to go up. The verses that follow show that this taking heart and returning to the place of defeat was joined to seeking God.

For today: when you fail or suffer a loss, do not stay paralyzed. Weep and pray sincerely, seek God's guidance, and with renewed courage take the next step.
exp.19:31:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin believed they would win again, just as they had in the two earlier battles. But the Israelites pretended to retreat. "Let us retreat" was a strategy: they wanted the Benjamites to chase them, pulling them away from the city and out onto the roads.
