The narrator recounts a war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin, after a terrible crime in Gibeah. Israel had already lost twice. Now it uses a trap: while some pretend to retreat, others wait hidden. The Benjamites trusted their past successes and did not see the danger close at hand.

For today: do not become overconfident just because things went well for you before. What worked yesterday does not guarantee tomorrow. Ask God for wisdom and humility to see what you are not seeing.
exp.4:10:
Now that the danger has passed, at the watering places where people draw water, they will recount the righteous acts and victories of the Lord. The verse speaks of the voices of singers there. "Villages" refers to the people of the open settlements of Israel. Then the people of the Lord will return to the city gates, where judgment was given and agreements were made.

Deborah, together with Barak, sings this song of victory over the Canaanites. Before this, the threat of enemies made the roads and the wells unsafe. Now there is peace to return to daily life.

Today we can make everyday conversations a place to remember what God has done. Tell someone this week, simply, how He helped you.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that the heavens themselves took part in the battle against Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite army. The stars are described as fighting from their places in the sky. It is poetic language: the verse does not explain how they fought. Some understand it as an image of God acting from on high; others take it to refer to forces of nature, such as the rain that filled the stream.

Here Deborah speaks in a song of victory, together with Barak. Israel had been oppressed by Jabin and Sisera. After the triumph, she praises those who risked their lives and acknowledges that the victory did not come by human strength alone. The next verse mentions the Kishon river, which swept the enemy away.

For today: when you face something greater than you, act with courage and do your part, but trust that God can work in ways you do not see. And when help arrives, give thanks for it.
exp.0:13:
This verse tells that Acsah, Caleb's daughter, was on her way to her new home with her husband Othniel. One day she came to him and urged him to ask her father for a field. When she got off her donkey, Caleb asked her what she desired.

Caleb is Judah's great warrior. He had offered his daughter as the prize to whoever conquered Kiriath-sepher, and Othniel succeeded. Now she, already married, approaches her father with respect to ask for something. Some believe it was Othniel who encouraged her; the text suggests this, but gives no further details.

For today: draw near with confidence to your heavenly Father and ask him simply for what you need. He listens and cares for you, just as Caleb listened to his daughter.
exp.16:6:
Here a young Levite is presented who was living as a foreigner in Bethlehem of Judah. "Residing" means that he was staying there for a time, without a home of his own. That he is described as "from Bethlehem in Judah" and as having lived "within the clan of Judah" may mean that he lived among the clan of Judah, since he was a Levite by birth. Some scholars explain it this way.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Judges. He has just told how Micah made his own shrine and set his son up as priest, at a time when everyone did what seemed right to them. The Levites were meant to serve God, and this young man wandered without direction. That emptiness prepares what comes next.

For today: it is not enough to feel good about what we do. Let us seek God's direction in his Word, and in his people, before we decide.
exp.0:25:
The explanation says that the man who helped the Israelites enter Bethel went to the land of the Hittites. There he built a city and called it Luz, the same name as the city he had left. The text adds that this name is still in use today, meaning at the time the book was written.

Here the narrator of Judges speaks. He tells how the tribes of Joseph took Bethel, which was formerly called Luz. That man showed them the way in exchange for mercy, and he and his family were saved. We do not know for certain where that land of the Hittites was.

For today: God cares for people even in the middle of difficult stories. We can recognize that mercy is remembered and leaves a mark. Let us ask him for help to be thankful and kind toward those who help us.
exp.20:1:
The explanation says that the whole people of Israel came to Bethel and sat there before God until evening. They were lifting up their voices and weeping bitterly.

The account speaks of the people of Israel. They had punished the tribe of Benjamin severely for a terrible crime, and they had also sworn not to give them their daughters as wives. Now a tribe was about to disappear, and the people cry out to God in pain, asking why this happened. Some scholars see here genuine repentance; others note that they are weeping over the consequences of their own hasty decisions.

For today: when our hasty decisions cause pain, the best thing is to bring everything to God honestly, without excuses, and ask him for wisdom to repair what we can.
exp.5:31:
That day Gideon was given a new name: Jerubbaal. The name is understood to mean "let Baal contend with him," that is, "let Baal defend himself" or "let Baal bring his case." The phrase is a challenge: the god is invited to answer for himself.

The speaker is the biblical narrative, which repeats the words of Joash, Gideon's father. The people of the town wanted to kill Gideon because he tore down the altar of Baal, a false god. Joash challenged them: if Baal is truly a god, let him defend himself. The new name recalls that challenge. Scholars agree on the basics, though some debate the exact meaning of the name.

For today: you do not need to defend God with violence or fear. You can stand firm in your faith with calm and confidence, and let the truth speak for itself, while you obey with courage and humility.
exp.3:13:
Deborah urged Barak to get up and act, because the LORD had already given Sisera into his hand. In the Berean Standard Bible, the phrase "Has not the LORD gone before you?" makes the same point the explanation makes about God going ahead of them, opening the way.

So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him.

Deborah was a prophetess and judge of Israel. Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army, had nine hundred chariots of iron, a force that terrified Israel. Barak had hesitated before, and Deborah reminded him that the victory came from God, not from weapons. God acted, as the following verses show.

For today: when you know that God is calling you to do something, do not wait until you feel fearless. Take the step with confidence, remembering that God goes before you, even when the challenge seems enormous.
exp.18:27:
"Get up," he tells her. "Let us go." But she does not answer. He puts her on his donkey and sets out for home. The text does not make clear whether she was already dead or died afterward. Many think she was already dead, but this is not stated with certainty.

The one speaking is the Levite, her husband. The night before, some men of Gibeah abused her while he was inside the house. His cold words to her show that he did not care about her pain. The book presents a dark time, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them.

Today, let us not be indifferent to those who suffer. If we see mistreatment or injustice, let us not look away. Let us defend the vulnerable, listen to their pain, and act with compassion, as Jesus did with the wounded.
exp.19:24:
This verse tells how, on the same day of battle, the men of Benjamin came out of the city of Gibeah and cut down another eighteen thousand Israelites. All of them were armed with swords. The reader should note that the Benjamites were striking down the Israelites as they fought, and the phrase "armed with swords" shows that these were men ready for battle.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin, their own brothers, over a terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The Israelites had wept and sought God's counsel, and he told them to go up. Even so, they lost. The text does not explain why, and it can be understood in several ways.

For today: obeying God does not always bring immediate or easy results. Even so, we can keep weeping, praying, and seeking him sincerely, without ceasing to trust him when we do not understand what is happening.
exp.8:25:
It says that a man named Gaal, son of Ebed, arrived at Shechem together with his brothers and crossed into the city. The leaders of Shechem began to put their confidence in him. "Shechem" is the city of Shechem, and "crossed into" means that they moved over into the city.

The narrator is describing how God allowed the sin of Abimelech and the men of Shechem, who killed the seventy sons of Jerubbaal (Gideon), to come back upon them as a consequence. The leaders of Shechem were already dissatisfied with Abimelech, and Gaal appears as a new leader. The Bible does not explain where he came from or who he exactly was; we only see that he took advantage of the tension.

For today: before trusting someone who promises solutions, let us observe their character and their motives. Someone who trusts whatever is convenient at the moment may end up in new troubles. Let us seek God's guidance and wise counsel.
exp.20:4:
The explanation says that the Israelites asked who among all the tribes of Israel had not come to the assembly before the LORD. They had taken a solemn oath: anyone who failed to come up before the LORD at Mizpah would surely be put to death. The phrase "come up" is used because they were gathering toward a higher place. The "assembly" is the gathering of the people.

The Israelites are speaking after the terrible war against Benjamin because of a horrible crime in Gibeah. Now they grieve because one tribe has nearly disappeared. They look for who was absent from the gathering, because the oath has left them trapped. This leads to the plan to seek out Jabesh-gilead. The book shows a time of great confusion, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them.

For today: let us think before promising something lightly. Hasty oaths can cause pain and leave us in dead ends. Before speaking with firmness, let us ask God for wisdom, and when we fail, let us seek to make things right with humility and not with more mistakes.
exp.15:28:
Samson reaches out for the two central pillars that are holding up the temple. He braces himself against them, pressing with all his strength, with his right hand on one pillar and his left hand on the other.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Judges. Samson, captured and blinded, was in the Philistine temple, where he was being mocked during a festival. Shortly before this, he had prayed to God, asking for strength one last time. He was a man full of flaws, but in the end he returned to depending on God. His death is presented as part of his work of delivering Israel, although some readers debate how to judge his motives of revenge.

For today: even after failing, we can return to God with humility and sincerity. He can use our weakness, and an honest prayer is always a good place to begin again.
exp.18:15:
This verse presents an elderly man who comes home in the evening from his work in the field. He was from the hill country of Ephraim, but he was living in Gibeah, a town whose men were Benjamites. Here, "living" means staying in a place that is not his own, so he was a stranger there. "That evening" means as the day was coming to an end.

The narrator tells this while a Levite and his group wait in the square, and no one takes them in. Among so many neighbors, the only one who notices them is a foreigner like them. The text does not explain his motives, but the contrast is clear: the hospitality came from someone from outside, not from the people of the place.

For today: let us think about who is alone or without a place around us, such as someone new in the church, at work, or in the neighborhood, and let us offer a simple welcome, even when no one else does.
exp.17:18:
The men of the tribe of Dan tell the priest to be quiet, to put his hand over his mouth, and to come with them. They want him to be their father, meaning their spiritual guide and counselor, and their priest. They ask him whether it is not better for him to serve a whole tribe and family in Israel than the household of one person.

The five spies and the six hundred armed men of Dan are the ones speaking. They are looking for a place to settle, and they take Micah's religious objects with them. The priest protests only weakly, and then he is pleased. Judges shows a time of disorder, when each person did what seemed right to him.

For today: let us make sure our decisions are not moved only by convenience or advancement. Let us first ask what pleases God, not only what benefits us.
exp.2:23:
The verse says that after Ehud had left, Eglon's servants came and found the doors of the upper room locked. So they assumed the king was relieving himself in the cool room. The upper room was a cool, private room in the palace.

The king's servants speak. Ehud had killed Eglon, king of Moab, who oppressed Israel, and he had locked the doors when he left. The servants suspected nothing and, out of respect, they waited. That time allowed Ehud to escape. Some understand this as part of the deliverance God gave his people through Ehud.

For today: we sometimes draw quick conclusions without having all the information, and we get it wrong. Before assuming the worst or the best about a situation, it is wise to stop, ask questions, and pray for wisdom.
exp.12:0:
The verse says that the Israelites again did what the LORD regarded as evil. As a result, he handed them over to the Philistines for forty years. The verse uses the word "again," and "handed them over" means that he left them under the power of others.

This verse opens a new stage in the book of Judges. The one who narrates is the author of the book, who is not named. It repeats a pattern: Israel turns away from God, suffers oppression, and then cries out for help. This time the text does not mention the people asking for help. Even so, God begins to prepare a deliverer, Samson, as seen in what follows.

For today: when you notice that you have turned away from God and feel the consequences, do not wait until you are desperate. Return to him soon and with humility, trusting that his grace continues to work even when we have not asked for it.
exp.15:29:
Samson says, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he pushes with all his strength against the pillars, and the temple falls on the lords and all the people in it. In his death he kills more enemies than he had killed in his whole life. The word "pushes" means he presses his weight against the pillars and shoves hard.

Samson speaks, blind and a prisoner, in the temple of Dagon, where the Philistines had mocked him. Earlier he had prayed to God, asking for strength one last time. His life was full of mistakes, but God heard him. Some see here a personal revenge, and others a final act of self-giving for his people. The text shows both.

For today: even if we have failed often, we can return to God with humility and ask for his help. He can use even our last steps for something good.
exp.20:6:
What it says: The Israelites ask what they should do about wives for the surviving men of Benjamin. The problem is that they had sworn by the LORD not to give them their daughters in marriage.

Context: The leaders of Israel are speaking, gathered at Mizpah. After a civil war, nearly the whole tribe of Benjamin had been destroyed, and now they feel grief because a tribe could disappear. Their own hasty vows have left them trapped. The book shows a time of great disorder, and it does not approve of everything the people do.

For today: Think before you promise or swear something in the heat of the moment, because words carry weight. And if you have already made a mistake, seek repentance and God's wisdom, not solutions that cause more harm.
exp.9:17:
The verse says that the rulers of Gilead asked one another who would be willing to launch the attack against the Ammonites. They promised that whoever did it would become the head of all who live in Gilead.

The Israelites of Gilead were gathered at Mizpah, and the Ammonites had assembled to attack them. Earlier, the people had put away their foreign gods and returned to serve the LORD. But they still had no one to lead them in battle. This verse sets the scene for Jephthah to appear in Judges 11, although his name is not mentioned here.

For today: God asks us to return to Him with sincerity, but also to act responsibly in the face of problems. If there is a need around you, do not wait for someone else to take the first step. Pray and ask yourself what you can do with humility and courage.
exp.14:18:
God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived. That is why he named the spring En-hakkore, which means something like "the spring of the one who called out." The word "hollow" here most likely refers to a hollow or cavity in the rock, though some understand it as a crack in the ground.

Samson had just defeated a thousand Philistines using the jawbone of a donkey. Exhausted and very thirsty, he recognized that God had given him the victory, and he feared dying at the hands of his enemies. So he called out to the LORD.

When you are worn out after a great battle, do not lean on your own strength. Speak to God honestly, as Samson did, and trust that he can give you what you need.
exp.19:29:
This verse tells how the Israelites attacked the tribe of Benjamin for the third time. They lined up for battle against Gibeah, as they had done before in the two earlier attempts. The phrase "arrayed themselves" means they arranged their troops in order to fight.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel was at war with Benjamin because this tribe had protected the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah. Israel had already suffered two painful defeats. This time they sought God's guidance, and He told them to go up, promising them the victory. So they used an ambush, and the Benjamites, confident, fell into the trap.

For today: sometimes we fail more than once. Before trying again, let us seek God's direction with humility, and not simply repeat the same thing in our own strength.
exp.8:30:
Zebul, the official in charge of the city, secretly sent messengers to Abimelech with a warning. He told him that Gaal, son of Ebed, and his brothers had come to Shechem and were stirring up the city against him. In this verse, the word translated "covertly" describes acting in secret, with hidden purpose. The phrase "against you" shows that Gaal was turning the people of the city against Abimelech.

Zebul had heard Gaal speak with contempt of Abimelech, and he was angry. As the authority in Shechem, he acted quietly to alert his lord. Then he proposes a plan: to attack at dawn. The account shows a time of violence, betrayal, and rivalry for power.

For today: the Bible tells this story without approving everything its characters do. It reminds us that pride, intrigue, and ambition hurt many people. Let us seek to resolve conflicts with truth, humility, and justice, trusting in God.
exp.19:4:
The Levite tells how the men of Gibeah rose up against him during the night and surrounded the house, intending to kill him. He says they abused his concubine (a secondary wife) so badly that she died. Here "abused" describes brutal, violent mistreatment.

The Levite is speaking before the tribes gathered at Mizpah. He wants Israel to judge the crime of Gibeah. But his account is partial: according to chapter 19, he himself handed the woman over to the mob, and here he leaves that out. His version seeks to win the people's support.

For today: before judging or acting on what someone tells us, let us hear the whole story and seek the truth honestly. Also, let us care for and defend the vulnerable, rather than protecting ourselves.
exp.5:26:
This verse tells how Gideon took ten of his servants and did what the Lord had told him to do. But he was too afraid of his father's household and the men of the town, so he carried it out at night instead of in the daytime. The wooden pole used in false worship is the object this verse is about here.

God had told him to tear down the altar to Baal that belonged to his father and to offer a bull to the Lord. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had turned away from God. Gideon was still unsure of himself, but God was preparing him to free his people.

Obeying God does not always feel easy, and fear can stay with us. Gideon did not wait until he was completely brave; he obeyed while afraid. Take the step God shows you, even if your knees are shaking.
exp.20:19:
This verse tells us that the leaders of Israel gave an order to the men of Benjamin: "Go, hide in the vineyards." The instruction means to conceal yourselves and wait in ambush, that is, to lie in hiding so that you can surprise someone. It was the start of a plan that would let them obtain wives.

The elders of Israel are the ones speaking. After a civil war the tribe of Benjamin had nearly been wiped out, and the other tribes had sworn not to give them their daughters in marriage. To keep that oath without letting Benjamin disappear, they came up with a way out: to seize women during the festival at Shiloh. The book shows a time of great disorder, and it does not present this plan as an example to imitate.

For today: when we make mistakes, we should not fix them with another deception or injustice. Let us seek honest solutions, with humility, that respect both people and God.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel turned away from the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of Egypt. Instead of following him, they chased after the various gods of the peoples around them and bowed down to those gods. This provoked the LORD to anger.

The book of Judges is narrated by an author who is not named in the text. It explains why Israel suffered so many problems. The generation that had seen God's works had already died, and the new one did not know what he had done. And so a cycle of forgetting, punishment, and rescue began.

For today: let us not assume that faith passes on by itself from parents to children. It is wise to tell at home what God has done, to read his Word together, and to thank him often, so that his work is not forgotten.
exp.8:1:
Abimelech asks the leaders of Shechem to hear him out, and then he poses a question: is it better for them to be ruled by seventy men, all sons of Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon), or by just one man? Then he reminds them, "Remember that I am your own flesh and blood," meaning that they are family.

Abimelech is speaking to the family of his mother, who came from Shechem. Gideon had died, and Abimelech wanted to be king. His question is a trap, because no one had said that the seventy brothers wanted to rule. He uses the family tie to win support for his ambition.

Today, let us be wary of anyone who uses closeness or blood ties to gain power. Before backing someone, let us look at his character and his motives, not just at how close he seems to us.
exp.16:8:
Here Micah asks a young man who has arrived at his house, "Where are you from?" The young man answers that he is a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and that he is on his way to settle wherever he can find a place to live.

Micah had in his house a shrine with idols, made according to his own way. This Levite was wandering without a fixed place to serve God. Micah sees the opportunity to hire him as his personal priest. The book of Judges repeats that in those days there was no king in Israel and each person did what seemed right in his own eyes, so the scene shows a time of spiritual disorder.

For today: when we lack direction, let us not accept just any offer merely for comfort or out of need. Let us seek God's guidance and his Word before deciding where and with whom to serve.
exp.0:18:
The verse says that the LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country. But they could not drive out the people who lived on the plains, because those people had chariots of iron. The plains were the flat lowlands, and the chariots were war chariots, which gave those people a strong military advantage.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells how the tribes of Israel kept fighting to take the land of Canaan after the death of Joshua. The text does not fully explain why Judah could not overcome the people of the plains. Some think it was a lack of faith, others that it was a military limitation. What it does show is that the conquest was left incomplete.

For today: God is with us, but we should not let the fear of the "chariots of iron" in life hold us back. When something seems too big for us, let us trust in God and keep moving forward in faith.
exp.1:17:
It says that whenever the LORD raised up a judge for the Israelites, he was with that judge and saved them from the hands of their enemies for as long as the judge was still alive. The LORD was moved to pity by the groaning of the people who were suffering under those who oppressed and afflicted them, and he changed his course to help them.

The one telling the story is the author of the Book of Judges, who summarizes a pattern that repeats. Israel abandoned the LORD, suffered at the hands of its neighbors, cried out, and the LORD sent a deliverer. The following verses show that when the judge died, the people returned to their evil ways.

For today: God hears the cry of those who suffer and is moved to pity, even when our own mistakes have caused the problem. But his help should lead us to a lasting change, not just temporary relief. We can pray with confidence and, once we have been delivered, remain faithful to God.
exp.19:7:
The explanation says that all the people of Israel, united "as one man," stood up and promised not to return to their tents or to their houses until a decision was made about the crime committed. The words "tent" and "house" here simply refer to the places where each family lived.

The Levite, whose concubine was mistreated and killed in Gibeah, had just told what happened before the assembly of the tribes. They answered with one voice. What follows is their plan to act against Gibeah of Benjamin. It should be noted that we hear the account from only one side, and that this book describes a time of great violence and disorder.

For today: when there is a serious injustice, unity and seriousness help, but it is wise to seek the truth and act with calm and justice, not only with anger. Let us ask God for wisdom before we react.
exp.10:17:
This verse tells how Israel, after being refused passage, did not fight against Edom or Moab but traveled around them through the wilderness. They went along the east side of Moab and camped on the far side of the Arnon River. The Arnon was the border of Moab, so Israel did not enter their territory.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, speaks here and sends a message to the king of the Ammonites. This king was claiming lands, and Jephthah reminds him of the history: Israel bypassed the lands of Edom and Moab and did not take what was not theirs.

For today: when someone shuts a door in our face, we do not always have to force it open. Sometimes wisdom means respecting limits, taking the longer road, and waiting with patience, trusting that God is still guiding.
exp.18:17:
He tells the old man where he is coming from and where he is going. He says he is traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote hill country of Ephraim, where he is from. He says he went to Bethlehem, but now he is going to the house of the LORD. Some scholars think the original text said "to my house." What is clear is that no one has taken him into their home to spend the night.

A Levite traveler is speaking, answering the old man who asked him who he was and where he was going. They were in the square of Gibeah, a town of Benjamin. It was normal to take in travelers, but no one had done so. That shows how cold that place was.

Today we can open our doors to someone who is alone or in need, without waiting for someone else to do it first. A meal, a phone call, or a place to rest can be a real way of showing love.
exp.14:6:
Samson speaks to the Philistines after they burned his wife and her father. In the Berean Standard Bible, he tells them, "Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you." That is, he is saying that what they did has provoked him, and he will not stop until he has paid them back.

Samson had been in conflict with the Philistines since they took his wife and gave her to another man. He burned their fields, and they answered by killing the woman and her father. Now Samson responds with even more violence. The Bible shows here a cycle of revenge, not an example that we should imitate.

For today: when someone hurts us, revenge promises to end the pain, but it almost always prolongs it. Let us ask God for help to forgive, to seek justice in a healthy way, and not to let anger make our decisions for us.
exp.19:19:
The explanation says the Israelites went out to fight against the tribe of Benjamin and took up their battle positions in front of Gibeah. "Took up their battle positions" means they took their places in formation, ready to fight. "Men" here means the fighting men, the soldiers.

This is part of the account in the book of Judges, when Israel had no king and disorder reigned. A terrible wrong had been done in Gibeah, and the Benjamites protected the guilty instead of handing them over. So the tribes came together to punish the evil. They had consulted God, and He told them that Judah should go first. Even so, the next verse shows that they lost that day. This reminds us that being right in a cause does not guarantee an easy path.

For today: when you seek to do what is right and things go wrong, do not give up or doubt everything at once. Keep seeking God with humility, examine your heart, and move forward with patience.
exp.19:15:
Among the men of Benjamin there were seven hundred select soldiers, highly skilled with the sling. The Berean text describes them as left-handers, and this detail is what their skill rests on. Each one could sling a stone at a hair's breadth without missing.

The narrator of the book tells how Benjamin prepared for war against the other tribes of Israel. Benjamin refused to hand over the men of Gibeah who had committed a terrible crime. Although they were few compared with Israel, they had very well-trained soldiers.

For today: talent or skill is a gift, but it does not make our cause just. Let us ask God for humility to use what we know how to do in the service of good and truth, and not to defend what is wrong.
exp.5:8:
God reminds the Israelites that he rescued them from slavery in Egypt and from all the oppressors who had hurt them. He also drove those enemies out before them and gave them their land. The phrase "I drove them out before you" means that he cleared those enemies away so that Israel could enter and settle the land.

A prophet, whose name is not mentioned, speaks on behalf of the LORD. Israel was suffering under the Midianites and cried out to God. Before sending a deliverer, God reminds them of his past faithfulness. He then points out that they had not obeyed him, since they were following the ways of the gods of the Amorites.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, remember how God helped you before. That strengthens your trust and encourages you to obey him, giving him the place that belongs to him in your life.
exp.12:21:
Manoah tells his wife that they are going to die, for they have seen God. The words that need explaining are "á" (a) and "moriremos" (we are going to die). Manoah understands that the visitor was the angel of the LORD, and he feels a very great fear.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a child, and the angel had announced that the boy would be Samson. When the angel went up in the flame of the altar, Manoah was terrified. At that time it was believed that seeing God meant death (Exodus 33:20). His wife, calmly, reasons that God would not have accepted their offering or given them this promise if he wanted to kill them.

When we feel fear before something of God that we do not understand, we can remember what he has already done for us. His past goodness helps us to trust, as this woman did.
exp.13:7:
What it says: Samson returns some time later to take the Philistine woman as his wife. He leaves the road to look at the lion's carcass, which he had killed earlier. Inside it he finds a swarm of bees with honey.

Context: It is the narrator of the book of Judges who tells this. Samson was going to marry a Philistine woman, and God used that situation to act against the Philistines, who ruled over Israel. The text does not explain every detail, but the honey found in a dead animal becomes the basis of the riddle Samson will later propose. Also, touching a dead body made a Nazirite unclean, and this shows that Samson was not a perfect example.

For today: God can bring something good from unexpected places, but that does not excuse neglecting what He asks. Let us seek to obey Him sincerely and give thanks for His blessings.
exp.15:24:
The explanation says that the Philistines, already in good spirits from the feast, asked for Samson to be brought out of the prison to entertain them. The phrase "to entertain us" in the verse is put here in plain terms: they wanted him brought out to amuse them, and they treated him as a thing to be mocked. They stationed him between the pillars of the house.

The speakers are the Philistine rulers and people, gathered to honor their god Dagon. They believed their god had given them victory over Samson. He was blind and a prisoner, for earlier he had failed in his calling. They did not know that God would still work in him, and that this mockery was setting the stage for the final moment.

For today: when someone mocks us, or it seems that all is lost, let us not forget that God can work even in our weakness. And let us not celebrate with pride, because the victory we boast of may be fleeting.
exp.20:13:
This verse tells how the men of Benjamin came back, and they were given as wives the young women of Jabesh-gilead who had been spared. The women were given to them. But there were not enough women for all the Benjamites who remained.

The narrator describes the end of a civil war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, which had nearly been wiped out. The Israelites had sworn not to give their daughters to Benjamin, and now they were looking for a way out. Their solution included the killing of the people of Jabesh-gilead. The book notes that in those days there was no king and everyone did what seemed right to them. For that reason, the story is not presented as a model to imitate.

For today: when we make mistakes, let us not fix them with other mistakes. Before deciding, let us seek God's guidance and his Word, and not only our own reasoning.
exp.11:6:
This verse closes the story of Jephthah in a few words. It says he led Israel for six years, that when he died he was buried in one of the cities of Gilead, his homeland. The phrase "the Gileadite" means he came from the region of Gilead, and "judged" here means that he governed and led the people, not only that he handed down verdicts.

The narrator tells this right after the conflict between Jephthah and the men of Ephraim, which ended in great tragedy. It is a sober summary, without praise. The Bible shows Jephthah with both light and shadow: a brave leader, but also rash, as seen in his earlier vow.

For today: our life will be brief, and in the end what matters is how we have treated others. Let us ask God for wisdom to resolve conflicts with peace and not with pride or violence.
exp.18:5:
It says that the Levite and his father-in-law sat down together and ate and drank. Then the young woman's father asked the Levite to agree to stay overnight and let his heart be merry. "Damsel" means young woman, and "man" refers to the Levite, her husband.

The one speaking is the father-in-law, the father of the Levite's concubine. The Levite had come to bring his wife back home. The father-in-law welcomed him warmly and showed him great hospitality, pressing him to stay. Later, that insistence delays the journey until it grows late, and this brings serious consequences in the account.

Today we can learn to be hospitable and generous toward others. But we also need to take care that our good intentions do not pressure others or make them lose the time they need. Good hospitality also respects the decisions and plans of the other person.
exp.8:6:
This verse tells how Jotham, on hearing that the people of Shechem had made Abimelech king, went up to the top of Mount Gerizim. From there he raised his voice and cried out, asking them to listen to him. He said, "Listen to me, O leaders of Shechem, and may God listen to you," meaning: just as you listen to me, may God listen to you. The words "Listen to me" are a request to hear what he has to say, and "O leaders of Shechem" refers to the men who held authority in the city.

Jotham speaks. He is Gideon's youngest son, the only one who survived when Abimelech killed his seventy brothers. From a high place, where his voice could carry far, he wants to denounce the injustice of crowning a murderer. He will do it through a fable about the trees.

For today: when we see someone in power acting wrongly, and others applaud, we can speak with courage and truth, without violence, trusting that God hears and judges with justice.
exp.0:7:
It says that the men of Judah attacked Jerusalem and captured it. "Put the city to the sword" means they killed its inhabitants with the sword, and "set it on fire" means they burned the city.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how the tribes of Israel, after the death of Joshua, tried to take the promised land. Judah goes first. This is a war account from that era, not an instruction for today. Later on, Jerusalem appears again in the hands of the Jebusites (Judges 1:21), so the victory may have been partial or temporary. Scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: this book shows that many victories are left half-finished. Ask God for perseverance to faithfully complete what He has entrusted to you, without settling for a good start that is left unfinished.
exp.8:7:
The trees wanted a king, so they first went to the olive tree and asked it to reign over them. The phrase "set out to anoint a king for themselves" shows that the trees were choosing one of their own. The wording "for themselves" makes clear that the king was meant to rule them. It is a fable: the trees stand for people, and the olive was a very valuable tree because of its oil.

The speaker is Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, who survived when Abimelech killed his brothers. From Mount Gerizim, Jotham tells this story to the people of Shechem, who had just made Abimelech king. Through the fable he shows them, with irony, what they had done wrong. Many understand that he is criticizing an unjust choice filled with violence.

For today: before following a leader or accepting a position of power, it is wise to ask ourselves whether that person or that path is worthy and whether it honors God. Not everyone who wants to rule serves well.
exp.17:30:
They set up for themselves the carved image that Micah had made, and it was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh. The explanation says that the people of Dan set up and kept the carved image Micah had made. That image remained in place for as long as the house of God, meaning the tabernacle, stood at Shiloh. "Set up" means that they put it in place and established it. A "carved image" is a carved idol.

The speaker is the narrator of Judges, who closes the story of the tribe of Dan. They took the idol and Micah's priest, and settled in Laish, which they renamed Dan. The book shows a time of religious disorder, when each person did what seemed right to them. The contrast is strong: true worship was at Shiloh, yet Dan preferred a made-up worship.

For today: we should not settle for a faith that suits only ourselves. It is worth asking whether we worship God as He has revealed Himself in His Word, or as is more comfortable for us.
exp.8:40:
Abimelech stayed in Arumah, a place near Shechem. Meanwhile, Zebul, the ruler of the city, drove Gaal and his brothers out so that they would no longer live there. "Drove out" means that he forced them to leave. Their being driven out of Shechem means that they could no longer live there.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how Gaal had just lost a battle against Abimelech. Zebul was loyal to Abimelech and had been in conflict with Gaal. Seeing him weakened, he took the chance to force him out of the city. The story shows a time of violence and betrayal, where the ambition for power brings division and pain.

Today we can remember that whoever relies on force or pride ends up falling. Let us seek to serve with humility, without fighting for power, and trust that God is the one who truly sustains.
exp.3:21:
What the passage says: Barak was chasing Sisera, the commander of the enemy army. Jael came out to meet him and told him she would show him the man he was looking for. Barak went into the tent with her and found Sisera dead, with a tent peg through his temple. The "tent peg" is a large stake used to hold the tent in place, and "lay" means that he was lying stretched out.

Context: The narrator tells how the battle between Israel and King Jabin of Canaan ended. The prophetess Deborah had announced that the honor of defeating Sisera would go to a woman (Judges 4:9). The verses that follow say that it was God who brought down Jabin. The text reports the event without approving or condemning Jael's methods, and some readers debate that point.

For today: God can keep his promises in ways we do not expect, and through people whom almost no one takes into account. Trust that he is at work, and ask him for courage and wisdom to act justly and faithfully wherever you are.
exp.15:17:
This verse tells that Delilah realized Samson had finally told her everything he had been hiding. Then she sent a message to the rulers of the Philistines and asked them to come once more, because she now had the secret. They came to her, bringing the money in their hands. The phrase "lords of the Philistines" refers to the rulers or chiefs of the Philistines, and "he has revealed to me all that is in his heart" means he had opened up completely what was most inward.

The narrator describes here the moment of betrayal. Delilah had pressed Samson day after day, and the Philistines had promised her money in exchange for discovering the source of his strength. She had called them before, but now she trusts that Samson spoke the truth.

For today: let us guard the deepest part of our hearts. We should open it with wisdom, and not give in to the constant pressure of someone who seeks their own gain. God is the safest refuge in whom to entrust everything.
exp.3:10:
This verse tells us that a man named Heber, from the family of the Kenites, had moved away from his people and pitched his tent by the great tree of Zaanannim, near Kedesh. The Kenites were descendants of Hobab, who was Moses' father-in-law. Moving away from the Kenites means that Heber had left the group and settled apart from them.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. While Barak and Deborah gather Israel's army, the account introduces Heber, who seems like an isolated detail. But it sets up what comes next, since his wife Jael will play a key role in the story. Scholars are not certain why Heber moved away from his people.

For today: God can use people and details that seem small or unimportant. Trust that your life, even in its ordinary parts, can be part of what He is doing, and be faithful where you are.
exp.0:12:
Here it is told that Othniel, son of Kenaz, captured the city of Debir. In the Berean Standard Bible, the verse says that Othniel captured the city, and that Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage, as Caleb had promised.

The book's narrator tells this at the beginning of Judges, when Israel was taking possession of the promised land. Caleb had offered his daughter to whoever conquered the city. The verse calls Kenaz Caleb's younger brother, and the Hebrew text allows that phrase to be read as a younger brother or as a younger relative. Later on, Othniel will become the first judge of Israel.

For today: Othniel acted with courage and carried out his task. Let us ask God for the courage to do what is ours to do, and trust that He keeps His promises in His own time.
exp.8:9:
In this verse, after the olive tree refuses to be their king, the trees ask the fig tree to rule over them. The words "Come and reign over us" are an invitation: the trees are asking the fig tree to take the throne. "Reign" here means "rule as king."

The verse is part of a fable that Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, tells from Mount Gerizim. The men of Shechem had just made Abimelech king, even though he had killed his brothers. Jotham uses the trees to show that the best ones do not want to dominate, and that in the end the one who reigns is the one who serves. The interpretation of each detail of the fable is debated, but its general message is clear.

Today we can notice that those who bear fruit and bless others tend to be humble. Before choosing leaders, it is wise to look at their character and not only at their ambition.
exp.11:3:
Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against the tribe of Ephraim, and the men of Gilead struck them down. Ephraim had mocked them, saying that the Gileadites were fugitives living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh, as if they were people without land of their own, living on the borders of others' lands.

The narrator tells of the moment when Ephraim, upset at not having been called to fight against Ammon, attacks Jephthah. Ephraim was a proud and powerful tribe. Its contempt wounded Gilead, and the quarrel ended in a war between Israelite brothers, a very sad thing.

For today: pride and words of disdain can ignite enormous conflicts. Before responding with anger or mockery, it is wise to listen, to speak with humility, and to seek peace, as Proverbs 15:1 teaches.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that the LORD became angry with Israel and handed them over to their enemies, the Philistines and the Ammonites, who came to dominate them. The phrase "burned against" describes a strong anger, one rooted in the righteousness of God. The word "sold" here means "handed over," like someone placing something into the hands of another. The Philistines and the Ammonites were neighboring peoples who became their oppressors.

The narrator tells this after saying that Israel had abandoned the LORD and served the gods of the surrounding nations. This was not a whimsical anger. God had warned that idolatry would bring consequences. The text goes on to show that this oppression lasted eighteen years and was very painful.

For today: when we give first place to other things instead of God, sooner or later we feel the emptiness and the weight of that decision. But this account moves forward and shows that God listens when his people turn back and cry out to him. Today you can return to God with sincerity, without delay.
exp.10:11:
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites to ask why he was coming to fight against Israel. The question in the verse, "What do you have against me?", means "What is your problem with me?" or "What is your reason?" Jephthah does not answer with a sword but with a question. Messengers are official representatives who speak on behalf of someone else.

Jephthah had just been chosen as leader of Gilead, after the elders called him to defend them. The Ammonites were already threatening them. Before fighting, Jephthah seeks to know the reason for the conflict and tries to talk it through. The king's answer, in the verses that follow, shows that he was claiming land.

Before reacting with anger or fighting, it is wise to ask and to listen. Speaking clearly about a conflict can clear up misunderstandings, and sometimes it prevents greater harm. Even when the other side does not want to listen, we will have acted with good sense and peace.
exp.15:19:
Delilah wakes Samson with a cry: "Samson, the Philistines are here!" He gets up confident, thinking he will escape and shake himself free as he has before. But he did not know something very serious: the LORD had already departed from him.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. Samson was a Nazirite, set apart for God from his birth. He had revealed the secret of his hair to Delilah, and she betrayed him for money. The text does not present his strength as a kind of magic tied to his hair; the hair was the sign of his consecration, and that vow had already been broken.

For today: let us not confuse past blessings with the presence of God. If we have played with what God has entrusted to us, we can become so used to sin that we fail to notice the danger. It is wise to guard our relationship with Him every day, and to remember that God still receives those who return to Him with humility.
exp.1:3:
When the angel of the LORD finished speaking to all the Israelites, the people lifted up their voices and wept. The weeping shows that his words reached their hearts.

Context: the angel of the LORD speaks on God's behalf and reminds Israel that they did not obey. God had told them not to make alliances with the peoples of Canaan and to tear down their altars, but they did not do it. Because of this, those peoples would remain a threat to them. The place was called Bochim, which means "those who weep." The explanation does not say here whether their repentance was deep or temporary; the book later shows that they failed again.

For today: weeping over sin is a good beginning, but God also seeks a real change. If He shows you something you must leave behind, respond with humility and with concrete steps of obedience.
exp.9:15:
This verse tells how the Israelites put away the foreign gods they had been worshiping and returned to serving the LORD. It also says that he "could no longer bear the misery of Israel," meaning that God could not stand to watch his people suffer any longer and was moved with compassion. Here "misery" means suffering or hardship.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes this moment. Israel had fallen into idolatry and was suffering oppression from the Ammonites. God had told them to cry out to the gods they had chosen, and the people answered by acknowledging their sin. Their actions showed that their repentance was sincere. Some interpreters understand that God was moved by their distress; others see a human expression used to describe his compassion.

For today: true repentance is not only saying "I was wrong," but also removing whatever has taken the place of God. Ask yourself what you have been giving first place, and hand it over to him with confidence in his compassion.
exp.5:28:
Here we see that the people of the town wake up and find the altar of Baal destroyed. They ask one another, "Who did this?" After searching and questioning, they are told that Gideon, son of Joash, did it. The text says they investigated thoroughly, meaning they searched and asked carefully until they got an answer. The wooden pole beside the altar probably refers to an object used in worship of a goddess called Asherah.

The men of Ophrah speak. Gideon had obeyed God, but he did it at night out of fear. Now his act comes to light, and the town, which worshiped Baal, becomes enraged and prepares to go against Gideon's family.

Obeying God can bring rejection, even from those close to us. Gideon was afraid and yet obeyed. God does not expect us to feel no fear, but to take the step of faith. Ask Him for courage to do what is right today.
exp.19:47:
The explanation says that the men of Israel turned back against the other Benjamites and put them to the sword. They did not only kill the people in the cities, but also the animals and everything else they found there. In addition, they burned down all the cities in their path. The word "turned" in the verse means "came back," and the phrase about putting people to the sword simply means they were killed with the sword.

The narrator of the book describes the end of a civil war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. It all began with a terrible crime in Gibeah, and Benjamin defended the guilty instead of handing them over. The book repeats that in those days there was no king in Israel and everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. The text tells what happened, but it does not present it as an example to imitate.

For today: when we do not correct wrong in time and allow pride to grow, the consequences can be far more painful than we imagine. Let us seek justice with humility, and not with revenge.
exp.2:9:
The explanation says that the Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel, and because of that he became Israel's judge and went out to war. The Lord gave the enemy king, Cushan-rishathaim, into Othniel's hand, and Othniel prevailed against him. "Judge" here means that he governed and defended the people. "Came upon" describes the Spirit coming over him, and "prevailed against him" means that he won. The verse calls the enemy's land "Aram," the same region the earlier text calls Mesopotamia.

The narrator of the book explains a cycle: Israel turns away from God, suffers oppression, cries out, and God sends a deliverer. Othniel is the first judge. After his victory there was peace for forty years, until the people again turned to disobedience.

For today: Othniel's victory did not come only from his own strength, but from God. When you face something bigger than yourself, pray and ask for His help. And when He gives you peace, do not forget Him.
exp.19:3:
Here the Levite answers the question of Israel and begins to tell what happened. He says that he and his concubine (a wife of secondary rank) came to Gibeah, a town in Benjamin, to spend the night. The phrase "to spend the night" means to stay as a guest and sleep there.

The one speaking is the Levite, husband of the woman who was murdered. The tribes gathered at Mizpah and asked for an account of that wickedness. He is the main witness, though his account is partial: later he tells the events in a way that makes him look better and leaves out details. This story takes place in a time of great moral chaos in Israel.

For today: before judging or acting in the face of injustice, it is wise to listen calmly and seek the whole truth. And as the Bible teaches, our response to wickedness should pursue justice without adding more violence.
exp.12:17:
Here the angel answers with a question of his own: "Why do you ask my name, since it is beyond comprehension?" His name is beyond comprehension, meaning it lies past what Manoah can grasp.

Manoah and his wife had been promised a son, Samson. Manoah, not knowing that he was speaking with an angel, wanted to know his name so that he could honor him when the promise was fulfilled. The angel redirects the attention toward the Lord, to whom the sacrifice was to be offered. Then he ascends in the flame of the altar, and only then does Manoah understand who he was.

Today, God does not always answer all our questions or reveal all his plans. We can trust that he is wonderful and faithful, and direct our gratitude and honor to God, not to the messengers or to the blessings.
exp.5:35:
Gideon speaks to God and begins a request: "If you are truly going to save Israel by my hand, as you have said..." The sentence is left unfinished here and is completed in the following verse. "By my hand" means "through me" or "using my own effort."

Gideon had already received God's call and the promise of victory over Midian. Now the Spirit of the LORD clothes him, he blows the trumpet, and several tribes join him. With an army gathered and a great deal of responsibility, he asks for a sign with a fleece of wool. Some see in this a lack of faith; others see a desire to be sure. The Bible does not explain it, and God responds with patience.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them honestly before God, but do not stop trusting what he has already told you in his Word.
exp.5:16:
Gideon says to the Lord, "If I have found favor in your sight, give me a sign that it is you who is speaking with me." To find favor means to be accepted and looked on kindly. A sign is a clear, visible proof.

Gideon is a humble young man from the tribe of Manasseh. God, through his angel, has just called him to rescue Israel from the Midianites. Gideon feels small and unsure. Although God promises to be with him, he asks for confirmation. Some see here a lack of faith, while others see a sincere desire to be certain that it is God who is speaking.

For today: when you doubt what God asks of you, bring your fears to him honestly. Seek him in his Word and in prayer, and do not act on impulse alone. He patiently deals with those who want to obey him.
exp.6:1:
God tells Gideon that his army is too large. If Israel won with so many soldiers, the people would take the credit and say, "My own hand has saved me." That is, they would boast that they did it all themselves.

The one speaking is the LORD, the God of Israel. The Midianites were oppressing the people, and Gideon had gathered troops to fight them. God wants it to be clear that the victory comes from Him, not from the number of soldiers. So He begins to reduce the army, first by sending home those who were afraid, and then through a test at the water.

For today: when God helps us through difficulties, let us give Him the credit. Recognizing His help keeps us humble and teaches us to trust Him, not only our own resources or abilities.
exp.18:7:
On the fifth day, the Levite got up early to leave for home, but the young woman's father said, "Please refresh your heart." So they waited until late afternoon, and the two of them ate. The young woman is the father's daughter, and "waited" means that they delayed their departure.

The speaker is the young woman's father, who wants to keep his son-in-law with hospitality. The Levite had gone to bring back his concubine, and the father looks after him with food and rest. But each day he manages to prolong the departure, and that delay leads to a journey by night, with serious consequences that the story tells later.

For today: hospitality is good, but we also need wisdom to decide well about our timing. A kindness without prudence can lead us to postpone what matters. Let us ask God for discernment to know when to stay and when to leave.
exp.19:17:
The Israelites set out and went up to Bethel, and they asked God: "Who of us shall go up first to fight against the Benjamites?" Inquiring of God here means seeking his answer. The LORD replied: "Judah will be first."

The Israelites are gathered to punish a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, a town of Benjamin. The Benjamites refused to hand over the guilty men. Before fighting, Israel asks God. He only tells them who goes first; he does not promise victory. In fact, in the verses that follow, Israel suffers defeats first.

For today: before making hard decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer. But do not confuse his direction with a guarantee that everything will be easy; sometimes he leads us by a path that requires patience and humility.
exp.1:13:
God was deeply angered by Israel, and for that reason he allowed plunderers to raid them and their neighboring enemies to overpower them. The explanation of the words is this: "burned against" means that God's anger was strong and fierce; "those who plundered them" are the raiders who stole from them; "sold them" means that he let them fall under the control of others; and "no longer able to resist" means that they could no longer stand up against their enemies.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after the death of Joshua. The new generation abandoned the God who had brought them out of Egypt and worshiped Baal and Ashtaroth. God had warned that this would bring consequences, and here it comes true. But the following context shows that God did not abandon them completely: he raised up judges to rescue them.

For today: when we turn away from God, we lose the strength to face difficulties. Yet his discipline seeks to bring us back to himself, and his mercy remains open. Today you can return to him with sincerity.
exp.6:17:
Gideon gives an order to his three hundred men. He and the hundred men with him will blow their horns first, and then the other groups must blow theirs too, from all around the enemy camp. Then they are to shout, "For the LORD and for Gideon!" The word "camp" refers to the Midianite encampment.

Gideon speaks as a leader before the night attack against Midian. God had already reduced the army to three hundred so that it would be clear that the victory came from Him. That is why the plan uses no swords, only horns, jars, and torches. Gideon asks that everyone follow his signal and do exactly as he does.

For today: God often works when we obey in faith, even when the plan seems weak or strange. Unity also matters, since each person has a place and fulfills it, trusting that the victory belongs to God.
exp.10:16:
This verse tells how Israel asked the king of Edom for permission to pass through his land, and he refused. Israel did the same with the king of Moab, and he would not agree either. So the people stayed at Kadesh.

The verse says Israel sent messengers, and that is what they were: people sent to speak for Israel and deliver its request.

Here Jephthah, a judge of Israel, speaks. He sends a message to the king of the Ammonites, who was claiming lands. Jephthah reviews the history to show that Israel acted with respect: it asked for passage peacefully and did not take land from Edom or Moab. With this he argues that the Ammonite claim has no basis.

For today: when there is a conflict, look first for dialogue and peace, and respect the limits of others. Even when you are told no, you can accept it with patience, without answering with violence or resentment.
exp.6:16:
Gideon tells his three hundred men: "Watch me and do as I do." When he reaches the edge of the enemy camp, they must copy each of his movements exactly. The phrase "watch me" means simply "look at me," and "do as I do" means do what he does.

Gideon speaks here as judge of Israel. God had already encouraged him through the dream of a Midianite soldier, and now he arranges everything for an attack at night. With so few men, the victory depended on their acting together and paying close attention to their leader, trusting that God would fight for them.

For today: sometimes God calls us to follow with careful attention and obedience, without rushing ahead or hesitating. We can ask ourselves: am I watching God and following his direction, or acting on my own? Taking small, obedient steps alongside others may be part of what God uses to accomplish his purposes.
exp.4:20:
The River Kishon swept them away, the ancient river, the River Kishon. The verse calls it the "ancient river," perhaps because it was a waterway known for a long time, though some think the word carries a different shade of meaning. The words "swept them away" and "march on, O my soul, in strength" appear in the verse above, and Deborah is speaking to herself here, urging herself forward with strength in the face of the enemy.

This is the song of Deborah and Barak after their defeat of Sisera's army. The account in Judges 4 and 5 suggests that flooding from the river helped Israel, since the iron chariots were rendered useless. Deborah sees in this the hand of God, who fought for his people.

For today: God can use circumstances we do not control to help us. When you face something that seems greater than you, do your part with courage and trust that God is also at work where you cannot reach. Then, thank him.
exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Judges. It says that after Joshua died, the people of Israel asked the Lord who should be the first to go up and fight for them against the Canaanites. The phrase "inquired of the Lord" means they sought God's direction. The words "go up" are used because the land was hilly. The Canaanites were the peoples who lived in that land.

The speakers are the people, who no longer had their leader Joshua. They had received the promise of inheriting the land, but some territories still had to be taken. The text does not say exactly how they inquired of God; some think it was through the priest, but the passage does not make this clear. God answers that Judah will go first.

For today: when one stage ends or an important leader is missing, the first step is to ask God before acting. And as Judah did with Simeon, it is good to ask for help and to walk together with others.
exp.5:37:
That is what happened. God did what Gideon had asked. When Gideon got up early the next morning, he squeezed the fleece and wrung out the dew, enough to fill a bowl with water.

Gideon was called to deliver Israel from their oppressors, the Midianites. Although God had already spoken to him, he still hesitated and asked for a sign with the fleece. The Bible tells this without presenting it as a model to follow. Some see it as a weakness of faith, others as humility. Even so, God answered with patience.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them honestly to God. But do not depend only on signs; also seek his Word, prayer, and the wise counsel of other believers.
exp.6:3:
God tells Gideon that there are still too many men in his army, even after twenty-two thousand have gone home. He orders him to take them down to the water, and there God will sift them. God will say who goes and who does not. "Sift" here means to sort out and separate, much like testing and refining.

The LORD is speaking to Gideon, judge of Israel, before the battle against Midian. God wants Israel not to boast, saying, "I saved myself by my own strength." That is why he reduces the army, so that the victory is seen as his work.

For today: God does not depend on our strength, our numbers, or our resources. When you feel small or have little, trust that God can act precisely there. And when something turns out well, give him the glory.
exp.15:26:
This verse describes the place where Samson was: a temple full of people, with all the Philistine lords present. On the roof there were about three thousand men and women watching him entertain them. "Entertain" here means to amuse or put on a show for others. The "lords" are the rulers or leaders of the Philistines.

Here it is not a character speaking but the narrator. The Philistines were holding a feast in honor of their god Dagon, because they believed they had defeated Samson. He was blind and a prisoner, and they used him as their entertainment. The text prepares for his prayer to God and his final act.

For today: even in moments of humiliation, when everything seems lost, we can turn back to God with humility and sincerity. Samson failed greatly, but in the end he called out to God. He still listens to those who come to Him.
exp.8:49:
Judges 9:50 tells us that Abimelech, after destroying the tower of Shechem, went to a city called Thebez. There he surrounded it with his army, attacked it, and captured it. "Encamped against" means surrounding a city so that no one can go in or out, and so forcing it to surrender. "Captured it" means he took control of the city.

This is the account from the book of Judges. Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. He had already burned the stronghold of Shechem with a thousand people inside. Now, with the same violence, he attacks Thebez. The narrator does not approve of this; he shows how power gained through wickedness keeps bringing destruction. The exact details of why he attacked Thebez are not explained.

For today: unlimited ambition is never satisfied, and it ends up harming many people. Let us ask God for a humble heart that serves and does not seek to dominate.
exp.3:11:
When Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up Mount Tabor, he knew Israel was preparing to fight. Sisera was the commander of the Canaanite army that had oppressed Israel.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Barak had gathered ten thousand men from Zebulun and Naphtali, encouraged by the prophetess Deborah. Tabor was a high mountain, a safe place to gather. The account shows that Sisera reacted quickly, for he gathered his nine hundred chariots of iron. Humanly speaking, Israel was at a disadvantage.

For today: God sometimes asks us to take a step of faith even when the enemy's resources seem greater. Barak went up the mountain without yet seeing the victory, and he trusted in God's word. Obey what God places on your heart, even when you feel small.
exp.17:25:
Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, so he turned around and went back home. The word "stronger" here refers to the fact that they were more numerous and armed.

This is part of the story in Judges 17 and 18. The Danites were looking for land to settle in. They passed by Micah's house, took his idols, and persuaded the priest to go with them. Micah followed them, demanding them back, but they threatened him. The narrator shows a time of disorder, when religion was used for convenience and force ruled.

For today: trusting in things we make ourselves, such as money, image, or control, leaves us empty when someone takes them away. Micah called "my gods" what he had made with his own hands, and he could not defend them. It is wise to place our security in God, who cannot be stolen or overcome.
exp.19:27:
This verse tells how Israel again asked God whether they should fight against Benjamin. Phinehas, the son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, was serving before the ark. The Israelites ask directly, "Should we again go out to battle against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop?" They want to know whether they should keep fighting or hold back. God answers, "Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand."

The Israelites had suffered two heavy defeats at the hands of Benjamin, their own brother tribe, who was protecting the men guilty of a terrible crime in Gibeah. Now they weep, fast, offer sacrifices, and seek God through the priest. The Israelites speak, and the Lord answers. Earlier they had gone to battle without waiting for so long.

For today: before making hard decisions, it is wise to stop, pray with humility, and seek God's guidance, not simply trust in our own strength or in our anger.
exp.13:9:
This verse tells that Samson's father went to visit the Philistine woman whom Samson was going to marry, and that Samson held a wedding feast there. A "feast" is a meal with food and drink. The verse says this was customary for the bridegroom, meaning it was the expected practice at that time.

This is the account of the narrator of the book of Judges. Samson had already killed a lion and had eaten honey from its body without telling his parents. Now he celebrates his wedding in Philistine territory, following local customs. Scholars do not fully agree on whether this was an Israelite or a Philistine custom. The text only says it was usual. Later, this feast will lead to a riddle and to serious troubles.

For today: following a social custom does not always mean it is wise. Before we let ourselves be carried along by "what everyone does," it is good to ask God whether that path honors him and takes care of us.
exp.6:0:
This verse tells us that Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, got up early in the morning with all the men who were with him and camped beside the spring of Harod. The Midianite camp was to the north of them, in the valley near the hill of Moreh. The phrase "camped beside the spring of Harod" describes the same act of setting up camp.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Israel was oppressed by Midian, and God had called Gideon to deliver it. The name Jerubbaal was given to him when he destroyed his father's altar to Baal. The verse sets the scene: two armies facing each other, and soon God will say that Israel has too many people.

For today: Gideon rose early and acted in obedience, but God would teach him that victory does not depend on our own strength. We can take our steps with diligence and, at the same time, trust that God is the one who sustains the outcome.
exp.15:5:
Delilah asks Samson to tell her the source of his great strength and how he could be tied up and subdued. The phrase "Please tell me" is her request for him to explain the secret or reveal it. Her wording here is a direct question about how he can be bound and overpowered.

It is Delilah who speaks, a woman with whom Samson had fallen in love. The Philistine rulers, enemies of Israel, offered her a great deal of money to discover that secret. She pretends affection, but her real purpose is to betray him. Samson responds with deceptions, yet he keeps toying with danger.

For today: let us guard our hearts and the relationships where we place our trust. If someone insists on knowing the most vulnerable parts of us and we notice signs of deceit, it is wise to set boundaries. Let us ask God for discernment so that we do not play with what can harm us.
exp.13:19:
The Spirit of the Lord came upon Samson with power. He went down to Ashkelon, struck down thirty men from that city, and took their belongings. The clothing he took was made up of sets of fine garments. He gave these to the men who had solved his riddle. Then, burning with anger, he went back to his father's house. Meanwhile, his wife was given to one of the men who had been with him, that is, a companion who had come along to the wedding.

Samson had wagered thirty sets of clothing with the Philistines that they could not solve his riddle. They pressured his wife, she got the answer out of him and revealed it to them. Samson had to pay the wager. The text shows that God used this situation against the Philistines, but it does not approve of Samson's violence or his anger. The Bible here simply tells what happened.

For today: anger handled badly damages relationships and causes harm that cannot be undone. Before reacting, stop, pray, and seek to calm yourself.
exp.8:42:
Abimelech, it says, took his men and divided them into three groups. He lay in wait in the fields, that is, he hid soldiers so they could attack by surprise. When he saw the people of Shechem coming out of the city, he rose up against them and attacked them. The verse says he took his men and divided them into three companies, and that he attacked the people; in the wording the reader sees, "divided" and "attacked" are the words to notice.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king by violence, killing his brothers. Now Shechem had rebelled against him. The passage shows how the curse that Jotham had announced comes to pass: the violence and betrayal turned back on them.

For today: God sees the evil that is done through deceit and ambition. Whoever seeks power by trampling on others ends up reaping destruction. It is wise to seek what is just and to trust God, not force or cunning.
exp.8:14:
The bramble, a thorny shrub, answers the trees that want it as their king. It says: "If you really are anointing me as king over you, come and find refuge in my shade." But it also warns: if not, fire will come out of the thornbush and consume even the cedars of Lebanon, the largest and strongest trees. To find refuge means to seek safety.

The one speaking is Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). He tells this fable from Mount Gerizim to criticize the people of Shechem, who had made Abimelech king after he killed his brothers. The good trees, like the vine, refused to reign; the thornbush, which gives almost no shade, represents Abimelech, who threatens to destroy.

For today: let us be wary of anyone who promises protection but governs with threats. Let us seek leaders who are humble and of good character, and let us be that way ourselves.
exp.17:11:
The explanation says that the 600 men of the tribe of Dan, while on their way, camped near Kiriath-jearim, in the territory of Judah. For this reason the place west of Kiriath-jearim kept the name "camp of Dan" (in Hebrew, Mahaneh-dan), and it was still called that when the book was written. "Camped" means they set up their camp.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. He explains where a place name that his readers already knew came from. The Danites did not yet have a secure land of their own, and they were looking for a place to settle. They travel armed toward Laish, and on the way they will pass by the house of Micah, where it is seen that their decisions do not consult God, but are guided by convenience.

For today: our decisions leave marks, sometimes for years. Before moving toward what seems safe and plentiful, it is wise to stop and ask God whether the path we are taking is also the one He approves.
exp.2:21:
This verse describes with brutal frankness how Ehud drove the sword into Eglon, king of Moab. The "handle" is the grip, and the "blade" is the sharp part. The king was so fat that the handle sank in after the blade, and Ehud could not pull the sword back out. The phrase about the bowels means that the king's body emptied itself.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel had been oppressed by Moab for eighteen years, and God raised up Ehud as a deliverer. The book recounts the event without embellishment, to show how that oppression came to an end. It does not say that everything Ehud did is a model to imitate.

For today: God can work even in dark times and through imperfect people. When you feel oppressed, trust that He has not forgotten you, and seek His guidance before you act.
exp.10:10:
Then Jephthah went back with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their leader and commander. Next, Jephthah repeated all his terms in the presence of the Lord at Mizpah, that is, he restated his agreement and his cause before God, as one who lays the matter before Him.

The narrator tells us that Gilead was threatened by the Ammonites. The elders had rejected Jephthah earlier, but now they sought him because they needed him. He asked that his leadership be real, and they agreed to keep it. Mizpah was a place where the people gathered. The text does not say in detail what Jephthah prayed or said there.

For today: before taking on an important responsibility or resolving a conflict, bring it before God with sincerity. Present your commitments and your plans in prayer, and ask Him for guidance to act with humility and truth.
exp.17:20:
This verse says that the men of the tribe of Dan turned around and left. They put their small children, their livestock and their possessions in front of them. "Possessions" means belongings or the things they carried. "Turned" means they came back around, that is, they changed direction.
