The Danites were looking for a territory to settle, and they took with them the priest and the sacred objects of Micah. They placed the weakest and the most valuable at the front, away from Micah's house. Some think they did this to protect them from a possible attack from behind. The Bible does not explain this with certainty. It was a time of disorder, when each person did whatever seemed right to them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking God or merely using religious things for our own plans. Caring for the weak is good, but doing so while taking what belongs to others reminds us that good actions do not justify unjust means.
exp.5:7:
It says that God sent a prophet, a man who spoke on God's behalf, to speak to the people of Israel. The message begins by reminding them of something very basic: the LORD, the God of Israel, brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

The people were greatly impoverished by the Midianites, who oppressed them, and they cried out to God asking for help. Before sending a deliverer, God speaks to them through this prophet, whose name is not mentioned. He reminds them of what he had already done for them and, in the verses that follow, points out that they had not obeyed him.

For today: when you are in trouble, before asking for help, remember how God has cared for you before. That strengthens trust, and it also invites us to examine whether we are obeying him.
exp.18:10:
The verse says the group was near Jebus, and the day was almost gone. The servant suggests to his master that they stop at that Jebusite city and spend the night there.

The servant speaks for a Levite who was returning home with his concubine. They had lingered in Bethlehem, at the father-in-law's house, and left late. The servant thinks practically: find shelter before dark. Jebus is the old name of Jerusalem. His master rejects the idea because the city belonged to foreigners, and he prefers to reach Gibeah, where Israelites lived. That leads to a very painful story.

For today: when a decision seems sensible, stop to pray and seek counsel. Choosing out of pride, prejudice, or haste, without seeking God, can bring serious consequences.
exp.6:4:
God brings the people down to the water to test them. He tells Gideon to set apart those who lap up the water with their tongues like a dog, and also those who kneel down to drink. The LORD is the name of God, and to proclaim means to announce aloud. The text that follows makes clear that those who lapped did so by bringing water to their mouths with their hand.

God speaks to Gideon, who is about to fight against the Midianites. Twenty-two thousand men had already gone home out of fear, and ten thousand remained. God says that these are still too many, so that Israel will not boast that it won by its own strength. It is not known for certain why this test distinguishes the soldiers; it has been interpreted in several ways.

Today: when you face something that is bigger than you, remember that God does not need your abundance of resources. Do what you can faithfully, and trust that the victory comes from Him.
exp.13:3:
This verse explains that Samson's parents did not realize that all of this came from the LORD. The phrase "who was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines" means that God was looking for an opportunity to confront the Philistines. The verse also reminds us that at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Samson has just asked to marry a Philistine woman, and his parents opposed it, because the Philistines were not part of God's people. The text does not approve Samson's decision; it shows that God can use even confusing situations to advance his purposes. Some scholars understand it this way, while others place more emphasis on Samson's responsibility.

For today: even when we do not understand everything that is happening, God continues to work. Even so, do not use this as an excuse to decide badly; seek his guidance and trust that he can bring something good out of it.
exp.1:1:
God tells them not to make agreements or friendly dealings with the peoples who lived in Canaan, and to tear down their altars, where they worshiped other gods. The question "What is this you have done?" expresses grief and rebuke, not just anger.

The one speaking is the angel of the LORD, who carries a direct message from God. He says it to Israel at Bochim, after the death of Joshua. He reminds them that God was faithful in bringing them out of Egypt and giving them the land, but they did not keep their part. Some understand this "angel" to be an ordinary messenger, and others to be a special appearance of God himself; the text does not fully settle the question.

Today, ask yourself which things God asked you to leave behind and which you have put off until later. Obeying only in part often brings bigger problems. Ask him for help to obey with a sincere heart.
exp.8:31:
It says that Abimelech should set out at night, together with the people who are with him, and hide his men in the field. "Lie in wait" means to prepare a surprise attack, staying hidden in order to fall upon the enemy. "Now then" means "so, right away."

The one speaking is Zebul, the officer in charge of the city of Shechem. He is speaking to Abimelech, who ruled there. Gaal had stirred up the men of Shechem against Abimelech, and Zebul, angry, warned him in secret. The text says he did it with cunning, so that Gaal would not notice.

For today: this passage shows a story of violence and deceit, and the Bible tells it without approving it. It invites us to distrust cunning and anger as ways of resolving conflicts, and to seek peace and truth.
exp.2:8:
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel, son of Kenaz and the younger brother of Caleb, to deliver them. The verse names Othniel's father as Kenaz and describes him as Caleb's younger brother. Some read this as a brother in the closest sense, while others take it as a younger relative more broadly; the wording allows both understandings.

Context: the book of Judges shows that Israel had turned away from the LORD and served the Baals, false gods. As a result, they lived for eight years under a foreign king, Cushan-rishathaim. The book follows a repeated pattern: sin, oppression, crying out, and rescue. Othniel is the first of the judges.

For today: when you feel trapped by your mistakes or their consequences, return to God with a sincere heart. He hears the cry of anyone who turns back to Him, and He can raise up help, sometimes through ordinary people.
exp.18:9:
The explanation says that the Levite was unwilling to spend another night at his father-in-law's house. He got up and left with his concubine and his two saddled donkeys. He arrived opposite Jebus, the old name for Jerusalem. A concubine was a woman joined to a man, with a lower standing than a wife.

It is part of a very dark story, from a time when everyone did what seemed right to him. The narrator tells how the father-in-law urged them to stay for several days, but the man decided to leave late, with the day already fading. That hasty decision left them travelling by night and led them into what happened next.

For today: decisions made in a hurry, without thinking about the risks, can bring painful consequences. Before you act, stop to pray, listen to counsel, and think things through calmly.
exp.2:19:
Ehud approaches King Eglon, who was alone in the cool upper room of his palace. Ehud tells him he has a word from God for him. Eglon rises from his seat. The phrase that means "approached him" simply means "drew near to him."

Israel was under the control of Moab, and Eglon was its oppressive king. Ehud, a deliverer whom God raised up, had already delivered the tribute and managed to be alone with the king under the pretense of a secret message. The phrase "a word from God" can be understood in more than one way: as a deception to gain access to the king, or as a declaration of God's judgment that would really come. The text does not make this clear.

For today: this passage reminds us that God works in the middle of situations of oppression and uses ordinary people. It also invites us to be careful with the name of God: to speak of it honestly, without manipulating others with it.
exp.14:7:
He attacked the Philistines ruthlessly and killed a great many of them. The phrase "struck them ruthlessly" describes a savage, complete blow, and the reader should note how forceful this language is. He then went down and stayed in the cave at the rock of Etam, in the territory of Judah.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. The Philistines had burned Samson's wife and her father, and Samson answered with personal revenge. God used Samson against Philistine domination, although his motives were very human and mixed.

For today: revenge rarely ends a conflict; it almost always makes it grow, as what follows shows. When faced with an offense, first seek calm, prayer and wise counsel, and let God do justice.
exp.5:13:
This verse says that the Lord turns to Gideon and tells him to go in the strength he has and save Israel from Midian. Then he asks: "Am I not sending you?"

Israel was suffering under the oppression of Midian. Gideon had complained, asking where the wonders of God were. Here the Lord himself answers. The text speaks of the angel of the Lord and then of the Lord, and many see in this God speaking through his messenger. God does not argue with him; he sends him. Gideon felt small, but the sending did not depend on his size, but on the presence of God.

For today: when God gives you a task that feels too big for you, do not look only at your limits. Take the step, trusting that the one who sends you goes with you.
exp.19:12:
The explanation says that the tribes of Israel asked Benjamin to hand over the wicked men of Gibeah so they could be put to death and the evil purged from Israel. The verse calls these men "wicked," and the explanation notes that the wording points to people who were morally corrupt and who had no regard for what is right. The tribes wanted to remove this evil from among the people. But the Benjamites refused to heed the voice of their fellow Israelites.

Here the tribes of Israel speak together after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah against the concubine of a Levite. First they asked what had happened, and now they demand justice. Benjamin, instead of correcting the guilty, defended them, and that led to a war between brothers.

For today: when someone in our group, family, or church does something wrong, defending them out of loyalty only makes the harm worse. Truly loving someone includes acknowledging the wrong, seeking justice, and accepting correction with humility.
exp.3:19:
Here Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite army, asks Jael to stand at the entrance to the tent and, if anyone comes asking whether there is a man here, to say no. The word "tent" refers to the tent where the family lived.

Sisera speaks as one who has fled in exhaustion after his army was defeated by Israel. He felt safe and wanted to hide. He trusted Jael, but she used that trust to kill him, as the following verses tell. Interpreters debate how to evaluate her act; the text presents it as part of how God gave Israel the victory.

Today, this verse invites us not to place our security in human shelters that seem firm. Only in God is there a true refuge. It also reminds us to ask for wisdom to know whom we should trust.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that God left some peoples in the land so that the younger generations of Israel would learn to fight. The phrase "if only to teach warfare" means that the later generations, the children and grandchildren, would gain that experience. The words "especially to those who had not known it formerly" in the verse refer to those who had not lived through the earlier wars in Canaan.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, explaining why enemy nations remained in the land. The generation that conquered Canaan with Joshua had already died. The younger people did not have that experience. The text says this also served to test whether Israel would obey the commandments of the Lord.

For today: difficulties can be a school of faith. God does not always remove right away what He asks of us, but in those challenges we can learn to trust Him and obey Him with greater firmness.
exp.0:9:
This verse tells how the tribe of Judah marched against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron, a city that was formerly known as Kiriath-arba. There they struck down three men: Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. After the death of Joshua, Israel was still working to take hold of the promised land. Judah goes first, and the account draws on what Joshua 15:14 says about Caleb, who also drove these three out of Hebron. Some think these are the same events told again; others think it was a new campaign. The Bible does not make this completely clear.

For today: God often gives us victories step by step, not all at once. Trust Him and take the next step in front of you, even if the problem seems as large as a giant.
exp.18:29:
The explanation says that those who saw the pieces of the woman's body were horrified. They said that nothing like this had been seen or done since the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt. Then they make an appeal: "Think it over" means think it through carefully; "take counsel" means get advice and decide what to do; "speak up" means say plainly what you think.

It is the narrator who records the people's reaction. The Levite sent the pieces throughout Israel to denounce the horrible crime committed in Gibeah. This account shows the moral disorder of a time when, as the book says, "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." The text describes these events with grief, but it does not approve of them.

For today: we should not become accustomed to injustice or violence. When something is wrong, we should stop, think calmly, seek wise counsel, and speak up for those who suffer, especially the most vulnerable.
exp.18:1:
She was unfaithful to him and left him, the explanation says. She went back to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah and stayed there four months.

The text describes her departure as unfaithfulness, though what exactly that means is not spelled out here. Some understand it to refer to sexual unfaithfulness, and others understand it to mean that she abandoned her husband or became angry with him; scholars do not agree. The word for her, as a secondary wife, indicates a wife of lower standing than a first wife.

Context: the narrator of Judges speaks, and begins a sad story from a time when there was no king in Israel. The book shows how the people went astray when each one did what seemed right to him. This account prepares the way for very painful events that come later.

For today: when a relationship breaks down, let us not allow time to pass in silence and pride. Let us seek God, ask for wisdom, and try to speak with humility and honesty, seeking reconciliation where it is possible and healthy.
exp.9:2:
After Tola, God allowed another leader to rise up in Israel, named Jair. He was a Gileadite, that is, from the region of Gilead, east of the Jordan River. Judging here does not mean only settling disputes, but also governing and guiding the people. He did this for twenty-two years. The word "followed" means that he came after Tola in time, taking up leadership of Israel.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, who is recounting the periods of leadership in Israel. Jair appears between two judges who led during times of great instability. The text gives no details of his deeds; it only says there was peace and order under his guidance, and that his family had standing. Soon after, the people would turn away from God again.

Even though the Bible says little about someone, their steady faithfulness counts for a great deal. God uses people who serve with constancy, without fame or great accomplishments. Today you can serve with that same spirit in your home, your work, or your church.
exp.4:22:
The explanation says that the angel of the LORD commands that Meroz and its people be cursed with a strong curse. The reason is that they did not come to help the LORD, that is, his people, in the battle against the mighty enemies. "Curse Meroz" means calling for punishment to fall on the place; "her inhabitants" are the people who lived there.

This comes from the Song of Deborah and Barak, sung after the victory over the army of Sisera. The song speaks of how the river Kishon helped bring about the victory. Meroz is a place whose location is not known for certain, and the Bible does not explain in detail what they failed to do. Their fault was staying out and not taking part when Israel was in danger. Then the song contrasts this with Jael, whom it blesses.

For today: do not confuse neutrality with prudence when God gives you a clear opportunity to help. Ask him today where you can serve, and take one concrete step, even a small one.
exp.15:27:
Samson prays to God urgently. He asks God to remember him and to strengthen him just once more, so that with one blow he can pay back the Philistines for his two eyes. The request for strength means "make me strong," and the verse's own words "remember me" and "strengthen me" carry the plea clearly.

Samson speaks while blind and a prisoner. The Philistines have brought him into their temple to mock him while they celebrate their god Dagon. He had failed badly before, and yet here he again calls out to the Lord. His prayer mixes faith with a desire for personal vengeance. The text does not say that everything in his attitude was exemplary, but it shows that God heard him.

For today: even if you have failed and feel weak or humbled, you can return to God with sincerity. Ask him for strength, but also ask him to purify your motives, so that you do not act out of resentment alone.
exp.7:18:
Gideon explains why he is going to kill the two Midianite kings. He says that the men they killed at Tabor were his brothers, the sons of his own mother. He swears, "As surely as the LORD lives," which is a way of saying that he is certain of what he is about to say. If the kings had let those men live, he would not kill them.

Gideon, judge of Israel, speaks after pursuing and capturing Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. His earlier answer confirms that the victims were men of high rank. Gideon acts as an avenger of his family, following the custom of his time. The account does not say that God commanded him here, and some readers see in this more personal revenge than justice.

For today: grief for our own people is real, but revenge can cloud judgment. When we are wounded, it is wise to bring our pain to God and seek justice with humility, without letting resentment rule us.
exp.8:0:
This verse tells that Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon), went to Shechem. There he went to his mother's brothers and spoke with them and with all the clan of his mother. "Spoke with them" means that he began to persuade them of something.

The one acting here is Abimelech, son of Gideon and of a concubine from Shechem (Judges 8:31). Gideon had died, and Abimelech was seeking power. He relied on his relatives in Shechem to gain influence. What follows shows that his plan was ambitious and violent. The Bible does not say that God sent him.

For today: be careful about using family ties to gain power or advantages. Before seeking a position or a goal, it is wise to ask ourselves whether our motive is to serve or simply to be above others. Let us ask God for humility and uprightness.
exp.7:28:
Jerubbaal, another name for Gideon, returned home and settled down there. The verse says he "returned home" and "settled down," which means he went back to his own household and stayed there. It reads like a quiet ending after the war.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking. Gideon had freed Israel from Midian and had refused to become king. However, the ephod he made from the gold of the spoils became a snare for the people, and the sons and later history of his household show that his withdrawal did not close the matter. Some see here a well-earned rest; others, a warning that something had been left crooked.

For today: stepping back from a season does not erase the effect of your decisions. Take care with what you leave to your family and to others, so that your example draws them near to God and not to things that take his place.
exp.19:34:
It says that the LORD defeated the tribe of Benjamin in front of Israel's army. That day the Israelites killed 25,100 Benjamites, all of them armed with swords, that is, men ready for battle. The word "defeated" means that God brought them down and gave Israel the victory.

The narrator of the book tells this after a horrible crime in Gibeah. Benjamin did not hand over the guilty men and chose war against their own brothers. Israel had already lost two battles, and this time it used an ambush. The text credits the victory to the LORD, though it also shows human strategy. It is a dark time, when everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.

Today it reminds us that covering up evil and refusing to correct it brings painful consequences. If we know that something is wrong, it is good to acknowledge it with humility, ask for God's guidance, and not defend what is wrong merely out of loyalty to our own people.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that Israel again did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD. They served the Baals and the Ashtoreths, along with the gods of Aram, Sidon, and Moab, and the gods of the Ammonites and the Philistines. In the end the verse says they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him.

Context: the narrator of the book of Judges tells the story of Israel after the death of the judge Jair. It is a pattern that repeats: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, and then cry out for help. Here the idolatry reaches wider than before, since they serve the gods of many neighboring peoples. The next verse shows that God allowed them to be oppressed for eighteen years.

For today: it is not easy to serve God with a divided heart. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our lives, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.19:45:
This verse gives the total number of Benjamite soldiers who died in the battle that day: 25,000 swordsmen. The description "men of valor" means they were brave, trained warriors. The total is the sum of the 18,000, 5,000, and 2,000 mentioned in the verses before, although that sum does not quite match (it gives 25,000), and some scholars explain these as approximate figures.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah and Benjamin's refusal to hand over the guilty men. It is a time of great disorder, and the book ends by saying that everyone did what seemed right to them.

For today: when wrong is not confronted in time and with humility, pride and stubbornness can destroy whole families and communities. Let us seek to correct the error soon.
exp.16:11:
Micah ordained the Levite, which means he formally appointed him to be his priest. That young man then stayed on living in Micah's house and served him in the family's religious matters.

The book of Judges describes a disorderly time, and the text sums it up by saying that everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes. Micah had his own shrine with idols, and now he hired a Levite out of convenience. According to the law of Moses, priests were to be descendants of Aaron, and God was not to be worshiped with images. Micah believes that this way God will bless him, but he does it his own way and not according to what God had commanded.

For today: having religious things is not enough to please God. It is worth asking ourselves whether we worship Him as He says in His Word or as is comfortable for us.
exp.4:21:
The verse says the thundering hooves of the horses were heard, the wild galloping of the stallions. It means the horses were running so hard and so fast that the sound of their hooves rolled like thunder. "Thundered" describes the pounding of the hooves, and "mad galloping" describes the frantic, leaping run of the horses. "His stallions" refers to Sisera's horses, which were fleeing in great haste.

This verse is part of the Song of Deborah and Barak, a victory song. Israel defeated the army of Sisera, which had chariots and horses. Earlier the text says the river Kishon swept the enemies away. Some understand that a storm flooded the plain; the text gives no further detail. Here the desperate flight of the army is described.

For today: human strength, however great it may seem, cannot stand against what God decides. When you face something that intimidates you, trust God and obey Him, without depending only on your own resources.
exp.8:44:
This verse tells us that Abimelech fought against the city of Shechem all day long. In the end he captured it, killed its people, and tore the city down. Then he scattered salt over the ruins. Many understand this as a symbolic act meant to curse the city and leave it barren, although the Bible does not fully explain its meaning.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Abimelech, son of Gideon, had made himself king by killing his brothers with the help of the men of Shechem. Afterward they rebelled against him. His revenge was brutal, just as Jotham had warned in his parable.

For today: power used with violence and pride always ends up destroying, even the one who wields it. Let us ask God for humility to resolve conflicts with justice and mercy, not with revenge.
exp.10:4:
This verse tells us that the Ammonites made war with Israel, and so the elders of Gilead went to get Jephthah from the land of Tob. The phrase "went to get Jephthah" means they went to bring him back. The "elders" were the older men who led the community.

This is part of the story of Jephthah. His brothers had driven him out of the family home, and he went to live in Tob, where men with no fixed trade gathered around him. Now the elders who had earlier rejected him need him, because he was a brave warrior. The narrator only reports the events; the reasons behind each person's actions become clearer in what follows.

Today, this text invites us not to close our hearts because of past pain. If someone who hurt us comes back, we can ask God for wisdom to speak with truth, set healthy boundaries, and remain open to reconciliation.
exp.13:2:
Samson's parents push back on him: can't you find a woman among your own relatives or among our people? Why must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to find a wife? Samson's answer is blunt: "Get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes." In plain terms, he liked her.

His parents were speaking out of concern for their son's faith and identity, since God's people were not to marry into neighboring nations that worshiped other gods. The verse that follows says that God was working through this situation to act against the Philistines, who were oppressing Israel. That does not mean everything about Samson's conduct was good.

For today: before making an important decision, such as marriage, do not rely only on what attracts you. Listen to the counsel of wise people, and ask God what He wants for your life.
exp.0:35:
This verse says that the territory of the Amorites extended from the "Ascent of Akrabbim," a mountain pass, to Sela and beyond. "Border" means frontier or boundary. Sela is generally identified with a rocky site, but its exact location is not known for certain.

The author of the book, who is not named, summarizes how the conquest of the promised land was going. Several tribes had not finished driving out the peoples who lived there. The Amorites even pressed the tribe of Dan so that it could not go down into the valleys. This verse marks how far Amorite control reached.

For today: what we leave unfinished can grow and limit us. If there is something God has asked you to face, such as a bad habit or a pending decision, do not postpone it. Ask Him for strength and take one concrete step today.
exp.7:8:
Gideon tells the people of Penuel that when he returns in triumph, he will tear down their tower. The word "return" appears in the verse you are reading, so the phrase is rendered as "When I return in triumph," and the meaning is that he is coming back from battle having won. "Tear down" means to pull down or destroy, as the verse says.

Gideon is chasing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian. He is tired, and he asked the men of Penuel for bread for his soldiers, but they refused, just as the men of Succoth did. They probably feared reprisals if the Midianites remained alive. The tower was surely their place of defense and their pride. Gideon answers with a harsh threat. The text tells us what he said, and later he carries it out.

For today: helping someone who works for a good cause is an act of courage and generosity. Refusing out of fear or comfort can bring consequences. Let us ask God for the courage to support others when they need it most.
exp.0:10:
The explanation says that the tribe of Judah, after taking Hebron, continued its campaign and marched against the people of Debir. This city was formerly known as Kiriath-sepher, a name that is understood to mean "city of the book" or "city of letters," though the exact meaning is uncertain. The verse's "From there they marched" points back to the tribe's earlier movement, and "the inhabitants" are the Canaanite residents of the city.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He tells how Judah, after the death of Joshua, continued the conquest of the promised land. It is an account similar to the one in Joshua 15:15-17. This advance shows a tribe acting together and taking the initiative, with Caleb encouraging others to join the task.

For today: God often gives us victories step by step. After an achievement, do not stop; take the next step in faith, without waiting to feel completely ready, and walk alongside others who can help you.
exp.16:0:
This verse introduces a new character: a man named Micah from the hill country of Ephraim. "The hill country of Ephraim" refers to the highlands of the tribe of Ephraim. It is a simple introduction, but it opens an important story.

The narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. This story begins a dark section of the book, where it shows how the people were turning away from God. Later, Micah confesses that he took money from his mother, and she uses it to make an image, something God's law forbade.

Today we can learn that what is religious and what is right are not always the same. We can talk about God and still do things our own way. Let us ask God that his Word guide our faith.
exp.7:3:
This verse tells us that Gideon came to the Jordan River and crossed it, together with his three hundred men. They were exhausted because they had been chasing the enemy. The word "pursuit" here refers to the chase of the fleeing Midianites.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. Gideon had just calmed the men of Ephraim, who were upset, with a humble answer. Now he keeps going after the kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna. Although his group was small and worn out, he did not stop. Soon he will ask for bread in Succoth, but there he will not receive it.

For today: sometimes we keep going with our strength nearly spent. We can finish what God has placed in our hands, but it is also wise to ask for help in time and to rest in Him, without being ashamed of our weariness.
exp.7:26:
It says that Gideon took the gold the people gave him and made from it an ephod, a sacred garment similar to the one the priest used. He placed it in Ophrah, his hometown. The phrase "prostituted themselves" here means that Israel was unfaithful to God, worshiping that object as if it were a god.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. Gideon had just defeated Midian, and the people gave him the spoils as a thank-you. We do not know for certain what Gideon meant to do with the ephod. Some think he wanted to remember the victory, others that he sought a way to consult God. Whatever his intent, it ended up becoming a snare to him and his household.

For today: even good things, such as a memory, a success, or a tradition, can take the place of God. Let us ask Him to keep us from making into the center of our lives what should only help us remember Him.
exp.19:42:
This verse describes how the army of Israel surrounded the men of Benjamin, pursued them, and easily overtook them, so that they were completely defeated. The pursuit went toward the area of Gibeah, on its eastern side. "Pursued" means to chase after with determination, and "overtook" means to catch up with them.

It is part of the account of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. No one speaks here; the narrator reports the events. Benjamin had defended the men of Gibeah, who were guilty of a terrible crime against a Levite's concubine. The text shows a time of great moral disorder, and the book repeats that there was no king in Israel. Some details of the place, such as Menuhah, are not entirely certain.

For today: when we do not correct wrong in time, and out of pride we defend it, the consequences can grow and harm many people. Let us ask God for humility to acknowledge our faults early.
exp.1:21:
God says he left some nations in the land to test Israel. He wanted to see whether his people would walk in the way of the LORD, that is, live by his ways and obey him, as their fathers had done, or whether they would not. The word "test" here simply means to find out what is true, and "keep" means to follow and practice.

God himself speaks, according to the account in the book of Judges. Israel had broken the covenant and disobeyed, so God decided not to drive out the nations that remained after the death of Joshua. The text presents these nations as a test to see the faithfulness of the people.

Today we can remember that trials and difficulties reveal what is in our hearts. Instead of blaming circumstances, we can ask God for help to follow him faithfully each day, even when it is not easy.
exp.10:23:
Jephthah, the judge of Israel, is the one speaking. He sends a message to the king of the Ammonites, who claimed lands east of the Jordan. Jephthah argues that Israel received that land legitimately and held it for a long time without dispute. His argument uses the Ammonites' own reasoning: each people keeps what it believes its god has granted it. Scholars note that Chemosh was the god of Moab; the Bible itself does not make clear why it attributes him to Ammon.

The verse asks: "Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us." In the sense used here, "possess" means to hold something as one's own.

For today: before claiming something, it is wise to recognize what God has already given us and to give thanks for it, rather than living always fighting over what belongs to others.
exp.13:18:
Samson answered the men of the city with a comparison: if they had not plowed with his heifer, they would never have solved his riddle. The word "plowed" refers to working the ground with a team of animals, and the "heifer" is a young cow. With this image, Samson refers to his wife indirectly, and accuses the men of having used her to get the answer out of him.

Samson speaks at his wedding feast with a Philistine woman. He had proposed a riddle with a wager. She wept and pressed him for seven days until he explained it, and she told it to her people. Samson feels betrayed and mocked. Many understand the phrase as an insult, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: constant pressure can wear down trust. Let us guard secrets and promises, and not manipulate others with tears or insistence. Let us seek wisdom and honesty in our relationships.
exp.5:9:
He reminds them who he is: "I am the LORD your God." He tells them not to fear the gods of the Amorites, a people who lived in the land they were living in. God spoke to them, but they did not obey him.

A prophet speaks here, whose name is not mentioned, sent by God. Israel was suffering oppression from Midian because they had followed other gods. Before sending Gideon as their deliverer, God shows them that their suffering is not because he has abandoned them, but because they had turned away from him.

For today: God reminds us of his faithfulness so that we return to trusting him. Today you can ask yourself: what is it that frightens me, or that has taken God's place in my life? Hand it over to him in prayer, and obey the one thing he has already shown you.
exp.10:3:
Some time after Jephthah had been pushed out by his brothers and was living far away in Tob, the Ammonites attacked Israel. The verse does not say how long that was. Here the narrator of Judges tells us that the people who had rejected Jephthah now face a serious threat, and they will need the man they once turned away. This moment sets up the turn in the story: the crisis drives them to seek out the one they had despised.

For today: do not write anyone off because of their past or because of how others treated them. God often uses people who were rejected. And if someone has rejected you, ask God for wisdom to respond with humility when circumstances change.
exp.10:38:
After the two months had passed, Jephthah's daughter returned to her father, and he carried out the vow he had made. The verse says she had never had relations with a man. The text does not clearly say what Jephthah did: some understand that he offered her as a sacrifice, and others that he dedicated her to serving God her whole life, without marriage.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had promised God that he would offer whatever came out of his house first if he won the battle. His daughter came out. She accepted her father's vow, but asked for two months to weep with her friends because she would have no marriage or children. The account says that Israel remembered her every year.

Before promising anything, think carefully about what you say. Hasty words can wound those we love most. Ask God for wisdom, and remember with respect those who suffer because of other people's decisions.
exp.11:12:
After Elon, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, led Israel. Here, to "judge" means that he guided the people, settled disputes and made decisions with authority. The phrase "from Pirathon" tells us where he was from.

This is not a speech by a character; it is the narrator of the book of Judges, who names Israel's leaders one after another. Abdon is one of the minor judges: the Bible tells us little about him. The verses that follow say that he had many sons and grandsons, that he led for eight years, and that he was buried in Pirathon. We know no more details about his leadership.

For today: God also uses people who are little known. Perhaps no one applauds your service, but God sees it. Be faithful in your place, in your family or in your work, without seeking fame.
exp.10:21:
This verse says that Israel took control of all the land of the Amorites. That land ran from the Arnon river in the south to the Jabbok river in the north, and from the wilderness in the east to the Jordan river in the west. The word "seizing" in this verse means taking control of territory by force, and the land described is the territory between these rivers and the wilderness.

The speaker is Jephthah, a judge of Israel. He sends a message to the king of the Ammonites, who claimed those lands. Jephthah explains that Israel did not start the war: they asked peacefully for passage, Sihon refused, and attacked. Jephthah insists that God gave them that victory, so the Ammonite claim had no basis.

For today: when you face a conflict, try to act with honesty and remember what God has already done for you. Recognizing his work in your own story gives you firmness to defend what is right without unnecessary violence and without pride.
exp.18:22:
The owner of the house goes out to speak with the violent men surrounding his home. He begs them not to do this wicked thing, because the traveler is a guest under his roof. The men who threaten the guest are described as people with no respect for God. "Wicked" here means a very serious and unjust act.

The one speaking is an older man who had taken in a Levite and his concubine in Gibeah. In those times, protecting a guest was a sacred duty. Yet the account shows a corrupted society: shortly afterward he offers his daughter and the concubine, something terrible. The Bible records this as a sign of Israel's moral decline, without approving it.

For today: defending the vulnerable is good, but we must never do so by sacrificing other innocent people. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to protect people with justice and compassion.
exp.1:18:
When the judge whom God had raised up died, the people turned back to their old ways. They behaved worse than their ancestors: they went after other gods, served them, and bowed down to them. Those gods belonged to the surrounding nations. They would not give up their evil practices or their stubborn ways.

The book's narrator describes a cycle that kept repeating in Israel: the people drifted away from God, suffered oppression, cried out, God sent a judge who delivered them, and when that judge died they went right back to the same thing. That is why God grows angry in the next verse: they had broken his covenant.

For today: it is not enough to depend on a good leader or on a strong spiritual moment. Our faith needs its own roots in God. Today you can set aside a fixed time to pray and read the Bible, so that your obedience does not depend on other people or on circumstances.
exp.19:23:
This verse tells us that the Israelites advanced against the tribe of Benjamin the next day, to fight once more. "Advanced" means they moved forward to engage in battle. "Benjamites" refers to the people of the tribe of Benjamin, brothers of Israel.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel is at war against one of its own tribes, because Benjamin protected men from Gibeah who had committed a terrible crime. On the first day Israel lost the battle, wept, and asked God whether they should fight again. God told them to go up, yet they still suffered another defeat. The Bible does not fully explain that outcome.

For today: sometimes we obey with good intentions and still face difficulties we do not understand. In those moments, we can do as Israel did: come to God with tears and prayer, and not trust only in our own strength.
exp.18:23:
Here the elderly owner of the house wants to protect his guest, a Levite who was traveling. To do this, he offers to hand over his own virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine to the violent mob. "Use them" and "do with them as you wish" mean to abuse them, and "such a vile thing" refers to the sexual assault of the guest.

An elderly man from Gibeah, in the land of Benjamin, is speaking. The men of the city, called "sons of Belial" (wicked people), demand to abuse the visitor. The book presents this as part of the moral decline of Israel, when "every man did what was right in his own eyes." The Bible records this event but does not approve of it.

For today: protecting the vulnerable never justifies sacrificing another innocent person. Today we can courageously defend women and the weak, and reject any wickedness that tries to disguise itself as duty.
exp.7:29:
It says that Gideon had seventy sons of his own. The phrase "of his own" simply means they were his children by blood. It also explains that he had many wives, which means he practiced polygamy.

The book of Judges tells this as a narrator, with no one speaking. It comes right after Gideon defeated Midian and after he refused to become king. Yet he later made an ephod that the people worshiped (v. 27). This verse shows his household growing with the customs of his time, and the text immediately mentions Abimelech, whose story will end in violence. The Bible does not approve of polygamy here; it only reports it, and its consequences appear later.

For today: a life of victories can have neglected areas. Examine your decisions at home and in your relationships with humility, because what seems normal today may bring pain to your children tomorrow.
exp.18:2:
The verse tells that the Levite got up and went after his concubine, who had gone back to her father's house. He wanted to speak to her kindly, to win her back with gentle words, and to bring her home again. He took with him a servant and a pair of donkeys. She brought him into her father's house, and when her father saw him, he gladly welcomed him.

The narrator tells this in a dark time, when there was no king in Israel and everyone did what seemed right to them. This story opens one of the saddest accounts in Judges. Scholars debate why she left, but the text shows the man seeking reconciliation.

For today: when a relationship breaks, reaching out to the other person with soft and humble words, instead of pride or silence, is a first step toward healing.
exp.17:4:
The five men from the tribe of Dan ask the young Levite to seek God's guidance. They want to know whether the journey they are planning will go well. "Prosperous" here means going well, succeeding. The request is to seek divine guidance before going forward.

The Danites were looking for a territory where they could settle. When they arrived at the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the Levite, who worked as Micah's priest. They asked him for a word from God, and he told them to go in peace. However, the whole atmosphere is one of religious disorder: there were idols in that house and a hired priest. For this reason, that answer does not guarantee that the plan truly came from God.

It is good to seek God's guidance before deciding. But we must consult him with sincerity, in the light of his Word, and not simply look for someone who will tell us what we want to hear.
exp.10:1:
This verse tells us that Gilead, Jephthah's father, also had a wife who was his lawful wife, and she bore him other sons. When those sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out of the house and told him he would have no inheritance in their father's house because he was the son of another woman.

The ones speaking are Jephthah's half-brothers. According to the law and custom of the time, the inheritance belonged to the sons of the main wife. That is why they rejected him, and that rejection led him to flee to the land of Tob, where he gathered around himself men without direction.

For today: our origin or the rejection we suffer does not define our worth or our future. God can use the person others set aside. And we can look with respect on those whom people leave out.
exp.17:13:
Here the five men who had gone ahead to spy out the land of Laish speak to their brothers of the tribe of Dan. They point out that one of the houses in Laish, the house of Micah, holds an ephod (a sacred garment used in worship), household gods, a carved image, and a molten idol. They then urge their brothers: "Now think about what you should do."

The Danite spies now speak, and they are about to go with six hundred armed men. They were looking for land where they could settle. The text does not clearly state what their intentions are, but what follows shows that these objects interest them, and in the end they take them away. It is a disorderly time, in which each person did what seemed right to him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are really seeking God or only religious things that give us security. Before deciding anything, it is wise to pause and ask: does this please God, or does it only suit me?
exp.8:46:
When Abimelech was told that all the leaders in the tower of Shechem had gathered there, the report came to him from someone else. "Was told" means that people brought him the news. "Gathered there" means they had come together in that place, the stronghold of the temple of Baal-berith, as we saw earlier.

Here no particular character speaks; only a fact is reported. Abimelech, who had come to power through violence, had already destroyed the city. Now he learns where his enemies have taken refuge. That information allows him to attack them all at once. The account shows the consequences of ambition and violence, and it fulfills the curse that Jotham had announced earlier.

For today: taking refuge in places or things that cannot save us, such as a false temple, is useless. Let us seek our security in God, not in power or in religion without true faith.
exp.8:36:
Gaal speaks up again and says that he sees people coming down from the center of the land, and that one group is coming by way of the Diviners' Oak. "Again" simply means "once more." A "company" is an armed group, a band of soldiers. The place name is uncertain; it is connected with the Diviners' Oak, but its exact meaning and location are not known for certain.

Gaal speaks with Zebul, the ruler of the city of Shechem, who was secretly supporting Abimelech. Gaal had challenged Abimelech with bold words. Now, seeing that real danger was approaching, Zebul deceived him with his words, and Gaal could no longer deny what he saw: the army was coming toward him.

For today: be careful about speaking with great confidence and pride. When trials come, our words are exposed. It is better to live with humility and to choose well whom we trust.
exp.6:24:
This verse tells how the men of Ephraim captured Oreb and Zeeb, two leaders of Midian. Oreb was killed at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb was killed at the winepress of Zeeb, the place where grapes were trodden. Then they kept pursuing the Midianites and brought the heads of both men to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Gideon had won with only three hundred men, and now he asked Ephraim for help to cut off the enemy's escape at the fords of the Jordan. The places took the names of these leaders, according to the account.

For today: God uses many people in one work. Gideon began it, but Ephraim also did its part. Respond promptly when someone asks you for help, without waiting to be first.
exp.19:5:
Here the Levite tells the tribes of Israel what he did: he took the body of his concubine, cut it into pieces, and sent them throughout the land of Israel's inheritance. A concubine was a wife of secondary rank. The verse says the men had committed a "lewd and disgraceful act," and the explanation here describes that offense as a serious wrong.

The Levite speaks before the assembly of Israel. He seeks justice for what happened in Gibeah, where violent men abused his concubine and she died. His account is not entirely complete, since it leaves out that he himself handed her over to them. The Bible records this brutal act; it does not approve of it.

Today, when we learn of an injustice, we should seek the complete truth and act with justice and compassion, without being carried away by anger or by partial accounts. God calls us to defend the vulnerable.
exp.9:16:
Two armies are getting ready for war in this verse. The Ammonites were called to arms and set up camp in Gilead, and the Israelites gathered and set up camp at Mizpah. The word "camped" here means they set up a military camp.

The narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just confessed its sin, had gotten rid of its foreign gods, and had returned to serving the LORD. Now it faces the threat of Ammon, but it still has no leader. The next verse shows that the leaders of Gilead were looking for someone to lead the battle. The text does not say here how everything would end.

For today: true repentance includes turning away from whatever pulls us away from God. But problems do not disappear right away. When you face a difficulty, keep trusting God even when you do not yet see the solution.
exp.15:0:
The explanation says that Samson went to Gaza, a city of the Philistines, and there he saw a prostitute and spent the night with her.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells this without softening it. Samson was a judge of Israel and had been set apart for God from his birth, yet here he acts according to his desires. The verses that follow show that the people of Gaza surrounded him to kill him, and that God, even so, gave him strength to escape. The text does not approve of his conduct; it shows his weakness and God's patience.

For today: God can use imperfect people, but that does not justify sin. It is wise to watch our steps and not toy with temptation, because it always brings consequences.
exp.2:3:
God left those nations in the land to test Israel. He wanted to find out whether his people would keep the commandments the LORD had given their ancestors through Moses.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges explains why neighboring peoples remained in Canaan. Israel had not finished obeying God in the conquest. The verses that follow show that they failed: they mixed with those peoples, married them, and worshiped their gods.

For us today, difficulties can reveal how much we trust God and how much we obey him. Rather than blaming our circumstances, we can ask him for help to follow his word, especially when it is easier to go along with what everyone else is doing.
exp.7:34:
This verse says that the people of Israel did not show kindness to the family of Gideon. The phrase "did not show kindness" means they showed no loyalty or thanks. Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, had done many good things for Israel, but after his death no one repaid his family for them.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is summing up the situation. Gideon had rescued Israel from the Midianites. But when he died, the people turned away from God and followed Baal, a false god. They forgot God, and they also forgot the good they had received through Gideon. The next chapter tells how his family was treated.

For today: let us cultivate gratitude. Remembering what God has done for us, and what others have done for our good, helps us to be loyal and to respond with kindness.
exp.3:12:
Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army, called together all his military strength: nine hundred iron chariots and all the men with him. He led them from Harosheth-hagoyim, his base, to the River Kishon.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Sisera had learned that Barak had gone up to Mount Tabor, and he responded by preparing for battle. Israel had been oppressed for twenty years, and the chariots were a symbol of human strength. The text does not say that God was taken by surprise; Deborah soon announces that the LORD had already given Sisera into Barak's hands.

For today: sometimes our problems look enormous, with iron chariots standing before us. This passage invites us not to measure everything by visible strength, but to trust that God works even when human resources seem superior.
exp.19:25:
After the second defeat, all the Israelites, all the people, went up to Bethel. There they sat weeping before the LORD. They fasted that day until evening and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD. The burnt offerings were offerings burned up completely, and the peace offerings were offerings of fellowship with God.

The narrator of Judges tells this in a time of great moral disorder. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin because of a terrible crime committed in Gibeah. They had already lost many men in two battles. Now, in sorrow, they seek God at Bethel.

For today: when you face a failure, do not rely only on your own plans. Come to God with sincerity, humility, and sorrow, and ask Him for direction before you move forward.
exp.10:9:
The elders of Gilead answer Jephthah with a solemn oath. They say, "The LORD is our witness," meaning that God is witness and judge of what they agree to. They add, "if we do not do as you say," which in plain terms means "if we fail to keep what we have promised." It is like saying, "May God hold us accountable if we do not do it."

The leaders of Gilead speak here. Years earlier they had rejected Jephthah, but now the Ammonites were attacking them and they needed a leader to defend them. Jephthah distrusted them and asked for a clear promise: if he fought and won, they would make him their head. They seal the agreement by calling God as witness.

For today: when you make a promise, remember that God hears it. Keep your word, especially when the favor you asked for is no longer urgent, and work to make amends humbly for past offenses.
exp.12:13:
The angel repeats the rules the wife of Manoah was to follow while she waited to bear a child. She must not eat anything that comes from the vine: no grapes and no wine. "Strong drink" was a strong, fermented beverage, unlike the apple juice of today. She also must not eat anything unclean, that is, what the law of Moses declared impure. She must do everything the angel had commanded her.

The angel of the LORD is speaking. Manoah had asked how to raise the promised child, who would be Samson, set apart for God from his birth as a Nazirite. These rules prepared the mother for that calling. The angel answers with firmness, and then Manoah still does not understand who is speaking to him.

For today: when God entrusts us with something, it is worth caring for the small details of obedience. We can ask ourselves what habit we should let go of in order to live with more devotion and trust in Him.
exp.19:36:
The men in ambush rushed suddenly against Gibeah and spread through the city, putting every inhabitant to the sword. The word "suddenly" in the verse means quickly and without warning, and "put to the sword" means killed with the blade.

This passage is part of the account in Judges 20, told as a narrative rather than as a speech. The tribes of Israel were fighting against Benjamin because that tribe protected the guilty parties in a terrible crime in Gibeah. Israel pretended to retreat to draw Benjamin away from the city, while the ambush took Gibeah. The text shows a harsh war in a time of great moral and spiritual disorder in Israel.

For today: when wrongdoing is tolerated out of loyalty to "our own people," the consequences can grow until they destroy everything. We must seek justice with humility and not protect what is wrong.
exp.19:41:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin fled before Israel and ran toward the wilderness, but they could not escape. The battle caught up with them, and the men coming out of the cities struck them down there. So they were trapped in the middle, with no way out. The phrase "the battle overtook them" describes the fighting that caught up with them, and "fled before the men of Israel" means that they turned and ran away from Israel's army.

The narrator tells the end of a civil war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. Benjamin had defended the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah (chapter 19). Israel set up an ambush, set the city on fire, and the smoke was the signal. When they saw it, Benjamin understood that their defeat was certain.

For today: sin that is protected or justified ends up closing in around us. It is better to recognize evil in time and correct our course, instead of hardening ourselves and defending what is wrong out of pride or misplaced loyalty.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, which led them to deal deceitfully with him. "Spirit of animosity" here means a mood of hostility and mistrust, and "deceitfully" means that they turned against him through dishonest dealings. There are different ways to understand whether this was a spiritual being or an attitude of hostility; in either case, the text says that God sent it or allowed it.

The narrator of the book tells this after Abimelech had ruled for three years. He had killed his seventy brothers to become king, and Shechem had supported him. Now the story shows that this violence would bring consequences, as the following verses say.

For today: do not build your life on injustice or associate with those who practice it. Sooner or later, what is sown with wickedness produces division. Seek honest paths, even if they are slower.
exp.15:30:
After Samson died in the Philistine temple, his brothers and his father's whole family went down to get him. They carried his body back and buried it between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of his father Manoah. The text also says that Samson had led Israel for twenty years. Here "led" means leading and delivering the people, not only settling disputes.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. He closes the story of Samson, who was an imperfect deliverer, full of flaws, yet used by God against the Philistines. His family was able to recover the body and give him a proper burial, something important in that culture. Some understand the twenty years as a single period, and others see some uncertainty about how they fit with 15:20.

For today: God can work even through people with serious flaws. We must not trust in our own strength, but we can return to God with humility and serve him to the end.
exp.15:20:
The explanation says that the Philistines seized Samson, gouged out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza. There he was bound with bronze shackles and made to grind grain in the prison. Grinding was hard and humiliating work, normally done by slaves or animals. The word "seized" in this verse means that they grabbed hold of him by force.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, not a character. He recounts the consequences of Samson departing from his commitment to God and revealing his secret to Delilah. His strength left him, and he did not realize that God had departed from him. The Philistines took the opportunity to take revenge on their enemy.

For today: let us not toy with what God has entrusted to us. Small compromises can lead us to lose a great deal without our noticing. But the story goes on, and God can still restore whoever returns to him with humility.
exp.18:19:
The explanation says that the old man welcomed the traveler with a greeting of peace and offered to supply everything he needed. His only request was that he not spend the night in the square, that is, outdoors in the town square.

The one speaking is an old man who lived in Gibeah, although he was from the region of Ephraim. The Levite was traveling with his concubine and his servant, and no one had invited them to spend the night. The old man sees the danger of sleeping in the street and takes them in. What follows shows that the danger was real: the town was full of wickedness.

Today, this scene encourages us to practice hospitality and to care for the one who is helpless. Perhaps we can offer concrete help to a traveler, a migrant, or a needy neighbor. But it also reminds us to be prudent, because good can face wickedness.
exp.20:17:
The elders of Israel explain a problem: they cannot give their daughters as wives to the surviving men of Benjamin, because all Israel made a vow and placed a curse on anyone who gives a wife to a Benjamite. The word "But" at the start simply signals a contrast with what came before, and "Cursed is he" means that anyone who breaks the oath falls under a curse.

After the terrible war against Benjamin, nearly the whole tribe died, and the women as well. The elders want the tribe not to disappear, but they are trapped by their own hasty promise. That is why they look for a way out, which in the verses that follow turns out to be very questionable.

For today: let us think before we speak and promise. Words spoken in anger or haste can bring painful consequences. And when we fail, let us seek God with humility instead of inventing solutions that cause even more harm.
exp.7:11:
Zebah and Zalmunna, the two kings of Midian, fled, but Gideon pursued them and captured them. "Routing their entire army" here means that he threw the whole enemy force into panic and disorder. "Captured" means that the two kings were seized as prisoners.

This is part of the account in the book of Judges. The narrator tells how Gideon, with his three hundred men, followed the Midianites to Karkor, where the army was confident and unguarded. Gideon surprised them and captured their kings. No one speaks directly; the author only relates the events. Then Gideon returns and deals with the men of Succoth, who had not helped him.

For today: Gideon did not stop halfway, even though he was tired. When God gives us a task, it is good to finish it with perseverance and to trust that He sustains our strength.
exp.19:22:
The Israelites went up to Bethel, the place where the ark of God was, and wept before the LORD until evening. Then they asked Him, "Should we again draw near for battle against our brothers the Benjamites?" The LORD answered, "Go up against them."

The narrator tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. Benjamin protected the guilty men of a terrible crime in Gibeah, and the other tribes went out to punish them. They had already lost twenty-two thousand men on the first day. That is why they weep and ask again. Although the LORD says to go up, the following text shows that they will suffer another defeat, and the Bible does not fully explain why. Some think God was correcting them as well.

For today: when something goes wrong for us, it is good to weep and to seek God with sincerity. But we must also be willing to listen and to examine our own hearts, not only to ask Him to go along with what we have already decided.
exp.0:34:
The verse says the Amorites were determined to keep living in Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim. But when the house of Joseph grew in strength, they forced the Amorites into labor. Here "determined" shows that the Amorites were set on staying where they were. The phrase "grew in strength" describes the house of Joseph becoming powerful enough to take control of them.

This is the narrator of the book of Judges, who sums up how the tribes did not fully drive out the peoples of Canaan. The Amorites had pressed hard on the tribe of Dan, and now the house of Joseph gains the upper hand over them in that region. Even so, the overall picture is of an incomplete conquest: instead of driving the Amorites out, they put them to work, and that would cause trouble later on.

For today: partial victories can tempt us to settle for less. It is worth asking ourselves what things we have kept under our own control instead of truly handing over to God, and asking him for strength to obey him completely.
exp.14:9:
The men of Judah ask the Philistines why they have attacked them. The Philistines reply plainly: they have come to arrest Samson and to pay him back for what he has done to them. The word used for "arrest" here means to seize or take him into custody, and the reference to coming up reflects that they were moving toward the higher ground of Judah.

The Philistines were ruling over Israel at that time. Samson had struck them hard in revenge for earlier wrongs, and then he took refuge in a cave in Judah. The Philistines camped there and pressed on Judah. Then, as the next passage shows, three thousand men of Judah went to hand him over, instead of standing by him.

For today: revenge produces more revenge, and often innocent people end up paying the cost. Before responding in anger, it is wise to pause, ask God for wisdom, and look for ways of peace.
exp.0:14:
Axsah answers her father Caleb with respect and asks him for a blessing, meaning a favorable gift. She points out that the land he has already given her is dry, with no water, and asks him to add springs of water as well. Caleb grants her both the upper springs and the lower springs.

She speaks as Caleb's daughter, newly married to Othniel. Caleb had given her land in the Negev, a dry region where water was essential for living and for planting. She asks boldly and with good reason, and her father responds with generosity. The springs "upper and lower" show that she received plenty. The text does not say exactly where they were.

For today: we can approach God with confidence and ask Him for what we truly need, without shame. If a gift is good but incomplete, like a land without water, He invites us to ask with simplicity and humility.
exp.3:5:
Deborah sends for Barak, a man from Kedesh in the territory of Naphtali. She reminds him that the LORD, the God of Israel, had already given him a command: to march to Mount Tabor and take ten thousand men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun.

Deborah speaks as a prophetess and judge of Israel, the one to whom the people came to have their disputes settled. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, a Canaanite king, and she passes on to Barak a message from God. Her words are not a question of doubt: she reminds him of something he already knew. The text does not explain why Barak had not yet acted.

For today: when we know what God is asking of us, it is best to obey without delay. Ask yourself what concrete step you have been putting off, and take a first step today, trusting that God goes ahead of you.
exp.7:5:
The leaders of Succoth answer Gideon with mockery. They ask whether Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, are already in his possession, as if that were the only reason they might give bread to his army. The leaders are the chiefs or rulers of the city. The army is Gideon's company of men.

Gideon and his three hundred men were exhausted, pursuing the enemy kings across the Jordan. They asked only for some food. The leaders of Succoth did not want to help, perhaps out of fear of reprisals from Midian if Gideon failed, though the text does not explain this. Their answer shows contempt and a lack of solidarity with those who were fighting for Israel.

Today we can learn not to deny help to someone who works with sacrifice for the good of others. Sometimes fear or calculation holds us back, but a simple, timely help is also obedience to God.
exp.16:1:
Here Micah confesses to his mother that he was the one who took the eleven hundred shekels of silver. Because she had spoken a curse about the thief, he becomes afraid and gives the silver back. Instead of rebuking him, she blesses him in the name of the LORD. The silver had been taken from her, and a shekel was a unit of weight used for silver.

The book of Judges describes a time of spiritual disorder, when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." Micah confesses perhaps out of fear of the curse, and it is not clear that there was any deep repentance. The mother's blessing sounds pious, but what follows is the making of an image, something God had forbidden.

For today: confessing a wrong is good, but our faith needs to obey the Word of God, not merely use religious words. Let us examine whether what we do "for God" truly pleases Him.
exp.6:6:
God tells Gideon that with only the three hundred men who lapped the water he will save Israel and hand the Midianites over to them. The rest of the soldiers are to go home. The verse uses plain language here, and "deliver" means that God will give the victory into Israel's hands.

The Lord is speaking. Gideon had a large army, but God reduced it little by little so that Israel would not boast that it had won by its own strength. The text does not fully explain why the men who lapped the water were the ones chosen; some think they showed more alertness, but this is not certain. What is clear is that God chose a few to show his power.

For today: when you feel small or short on resources, remember that God does not depend on your strength. Listen to him, take the step he asks of you, and trust that he sustains the result.
exp.9:8:
The explanation says that the Ammonites, who were already oppressing the Israelites east of the Jordan, crossed the river to attack the tribes on the other side as well: Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim. With this, Israel's suffering grew greatly. The phrase "Israel was in deep distress" means that they were deeply troubled and oppressed.

The narrator of the book of Judges explains that God allowed this oppression because the people had turned away from Him to serve the Baals, false gods of the neighboring peoples. They had already endured eighteen years of suffering. Now the trouble reached the heartland of the land, and this moved them to cry out to God, as seen in the next verse.

For today: sometimes we ignore small warnings, and the problem grows until we can no longer avoid it. When something in your life pulls you away from God, do not wait until you are desperate. Return to Him soon, with sincerity, and He will receive you.
exp.0:11:
Caleb makes a public promise: whoever attacks the city of Kiriath-sepher and captures it will receive his daughter Acsah in marriage. The city is also called Debir, which was its earlier name.

Caleb, a faithful man of the tribe of Judah, speaks here, and he was already elderly. Judah was taking possession of its territory, and Caleb offers a reward to encourage someone to conquer Debir. According to the following verse, Othniel, a nephew or close relative of Caleb, took the city. Marriages were then arranged between families, and this promise was a way of honoring courage.

For today: Caleb trusted that God would give the victory and sought out people willing to act. Ask yourself what difficult task God is inviting you to undertake, and take a concrete step in faith, without waiting for others to do it for you.
exp.8:18:
This verse says: "If you have acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal and his household today, then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and may he rejoice in you." It is a sentence with irony. "Jerubbaal" is another name for Gideon. "Faithfully" and "honestly" mean dealing with others in a trustworthy and sincere way. "Rejoice" means to be glad or to take pleasure in something.

Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, who escaped the massacre, is the speaker. From the top of Mount Gerizim he shouts to the people of Shechem after telling them a parable. They had killed seventy sons of Gideon and had made Abimelech king. Jotham tells them that if they truly acted justly, they should enjoy their decision; if not, punishment will come.

For today: before supporting a leader or making a decision, let us ask whether it is just and honest, not only convenient. God sees the intentions of the heart.
exp.4:17:
Zebulun was a people who risked their lives, and Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield. The verse means that these tribes did not hold back to protect themselves. They threw themselves into danger, ready even to face death, in the high ground where the fighting took place.

This verse belongs to the song of Deborah and Barak, sung after the victory over Sisera. Deborah honors the tribes that came out to fight and calls out those that stayed behind, naming Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher. Zebulun and Naphtali stand as an example of commitment, since they were the tribes Barak had gathered, as Judges 4 describes.

For today: God often works through those who respond with courage and commitment. Ask yourself what good task you have been waiting to do from the comfort of your position, and take one concrete step of service this week.
exp.2:20:
Ehud, who was left-handed, reached with his left hand, pulled the sword from his right thigh, and plunged it into Eglon's belly. A short blade like this was strapped to his right thigh. Normally a guard searches for weapons on the left side, which is where a right-handed man would carry one, and that is why no one suspected him.

We are in the time of the judges. Israel was oppressed by Eglon, king of Moab, because of their disobedience to God. Ehud, of the tribe of Benjamin, was raised up as a deliverer and carried the tribute to the king. Then he asked to be alone with him, saying that he had a message from God. The passage presents this as part of Israel's deliverance, though it is a raw and violent account.

For today: God can use people with traits that others overlook, as Ehud was used with his left hand. Do not look down on yourself, and trust that God works even in difficult times.
exp.3:14:
It was God himself who routed Sisera, his chariots and his whole army. "Routed" means that he scattered them and threw them into confusion. "With the sword" means that they were defeated in battle. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled on foot.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Deborah, a prophetess of Israel, had just encouraged Barak to attack, assuring him that God was going before him. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, and Sisera was his military commander with nine hundred iron chariots. The text credits the victory to God, not to Israel's strength.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, move forward with obedience and trust. God can work in ways you do not expect, and the glory belongs to him.
exp.20:5:
The people of Israel felt deep grief over what had happened to the tribe of Benjamin, whom they call "their brothers." Their sorrow was real. The phrase "cut off" means that the tribe was close to vanishing altogether.

The Israelites are speaking at Bethel after a terrible civil war against Benjamin, which left very few survivors. They had made a vow not to give their daughters to them as wives. Now they see that their own decision puts an entire tribe at risk. Their response, as will be seen later, was complicated and painful.

For today: when anger leads us to say or promise things without thinking, those words can hurt later. It is wise to pause, acknowledge the harm, seek reconciliation, and ask God for direction before we act.
exp.8:26:
They went out into the fields, gathered grapes from their vineyards, and trod them to make wine, and then they held a festival. Afterward they went into the house of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech. Here "cursed" means that they spoke against him with contempt and wished him harm.

The narrator tells us that the people of Shechem had already turned against Abimelech, the man they had earlier backed as king, even though he had killed his own brothers to take power. With the arrival of Gaal, they gained confidence and dared to rebel. Their feast was religious, but it did not make them better; it only fed their anger.

For today: a celebration or outward religious activity does not change a heart full of resentment or injustice. Before complaining about others, it is wise to examine our own decisions and ask God to give us a humble heart.
exp.4:2:
Deborah calls on the kings and the princes to listen closely. Her words are "Listen, O kings!" and "Give ear, O princes!", so the explanation simply says that she asks them to listen and to pay attention. She declares that she will sing and offer praise to the Lord, the God of Israel. The song is not centered on her, but on God.

Deborah speaks together with Barak, after a victory over the Canaanites. This song celebrates what God did for Israel and also that the people offered themselves willingly. The "kings" and "princes" may be rulers of other nations or leaders in general; interpreters do not fully agree. What is clear is that the praise is proclaimed in public.

Today we can thank God openly, without shame, for what he has done in our lives. A simple testimony, a song, or a shared prayer can encourage others and place the glory where it belongs: in the Lord.
exp.20:7:
