This verse tells how the Israelites asked who had failed to come up to gather before the LORD at Mizpah. On checking, they found that no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the assembly. Coming up to the LORD means showing up for the gathering called before the LORD.

The speaker is the congregation of Israel, at the end of the book of Judges, a time of great disorder. After the war they had nearly wiped out the tribe of Benjamin, and now they were looking for wives for the survivors without breaking their oath. They found an excuse to attack Jabesh-gilead. The account describes what happened but does not approve of it; the book itself shows a people who did what was right in their own eyes.

For today: be careful about using religion to justify hasty decisions. Before you act, ask yourself whether you are seeking God's will or simply fixing your own mistakes in your own way.
exp.10:14:
This verse begins Jephthah's reply to the king of Ammon. Jephthah says that Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.

The phrase "This is what Jephthah says" introduces his message word for word, and the name "Jephthah" is the judge of Israel who sends this reply.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, speaks through messengers. The Ammonite king claimed the land between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers and demanded that it be returned. Jephthah answers with the history: when Israel came out of Egypt, it respected the borders of Moab and Ammon. He tries to settle the conflict with words before fighting.

For today: before reacting in a conflict, seek the facts and speak with truth and calm. Pursuing peace through honest dialogue honors God, even when the other side does not want to listen.
exp.8:29:
This verse says that Zebul, the governor of the city of Shechem, became very angry when he heard what Gaal, the son of Ebed, said. The phrase "he burned with anger" means that his anger flared up strongly. Zebul was the official placed over the city to govern it.

Gaal had just spoken badly of Abimelech and of Zebul, and he encouraged the people of Shechem to rebel. Zebul served Abimelech, so he felt that he and his lord were under attack. The Bible does not explain all his motives, but his anger led him to send a secret message to Abimelech so that he would prepare an ambush.

For today: anger can push us to act with cunning and violence. Before responding to an offense, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek a fair and calm answer, as James 1:19-20 teaches.
exp.19:43:
This verse says that in that battle eighteen thousand Benjamites fell, all of them men of valor, meaning capable and courageous fighters. The Hebrew sense here is of a heavy loss among the most skilled warriors of the tribe.

The book of Judges is a narrative, and here it is not God speaking but the narrator. It tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin, whose people protected the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah instead of handing them over to justice. The text does not celebrate the slaughter. Rather, it shows a people broken, who did what was right in their own eyes. When the fear of God is lost, uncorrected sin drags everyone into tragedy.

For today: do not excuse or hide wrongdoing in order to protect your own. Correcting it in time, with humility and truth, keeps a small fault from ending in much greater harm.
exp.17:28:
The verse tells how the tribe of Dan renamed the city they had just taken. Before, it was called Laish, but now they called it Dan, in honor of their forefather, a son of Jacob, who was also called Israel. The phrase "after their forefather" means the city took its new name from him.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. It is a disorderly time, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The Danites had not managed to take the land that belonged to them, and they attacked a peaceful people who had no one to defend them. They also carried off Micah's idols and his priest. The account does not approve of what they did; rather, it shows how far they were from God.

For today: a good name or an achievement does not make a decision good. Before we celebrate what we have accomplished, let us ask whether we achieved it in a way that pleases God.
exp.17:9:
The spies from the tribe of Dan report what they saw in the north. They say that they will come to an unsuspecting people and a spacious land (the word "spacious" here means wide, with plenty of room). They assure the others that God has delivered it into their hand and that nothing on earth is lacking there.

The ones speaking are five men whom Dan sent to explore, and now they encourage their brothers in Zorah and Eshtaol to go and take the land. Dan had not yet received the inheritance that had been assigned to it. Although they say "God has delivered it," the text does not show that God commanded this; it was their own interpretation, and the account soon shows violence against a peaceful people.

Today we can learn not to confuse a good opportunity with the will of God. Before acting, it is wise to pray, seek wise counsel, and ask ourselves whether what we desire is right and honors God.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that Ehud, after handing over the tribute to King Eglon, ushered out the people who had carried that gift. The word "tribute" means the payment, and "ushered out" means he led them away to go back. The people refers to the men who had carried the payment.

The account tells that Israel was under the rule of Moab and paid tribute to Eglon. Ehud, a man whom God raised up as a deliverer, had a dagger hidden on him. By sending his companions away, he was free to ask for a private audience with the king. The Bible presents this as part of Israel's deliverance; it does not say that every act in the account is an example to imitate.

For today: when God calls us to a difficult task, it is wise to act with wisdom and preparation, not in a rush. Before taking an important step, pray, think carefully, and try to do it with prudence and trust in God.
exp.16:5:
The explanation says that in those days Israel had no king to rule, and that everyone acted as they saw fit. "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" means acting on one's own view, without asking what God thought.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking, and no one knows for certain who he was. He wants to explain why the people were so disordered after the judges. Micah makes an image, an ephod (a priestly garment) and household idols, and he appoints his son as priest. All of this went against God's law, yet he did it as if it were a good thing.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I follow only what I feel or what suits me? It is wise to measure our decisions by God's Word and to seek counsel from other mature believers, rather than trusting only our own opinion.
exp.10:27:
This verse tells us that the king of the Ammonites paid no heed to the message Jephthah sent him. "Paid no heed" means that he did not pay attention to it and did not consider what was said. The "message" was the arguments and explanations Jephthah gave him.

The narrator of the book explains what happened after Jephthah, a judge of Israel, sent messengers to the king of Ammon. The Ammonites wanted to fight against Israel over some lands. Jephthah defended Israel's claim with arguments, saying that Israel had lived in those lands for three hundred years, and he left the final judgment in God's hands. Even so, the king refused to hear him, and that opened the way to war.

For today: working for peace by speaking clearly and with respect is worth the effort, even when the other person will not listen. When we have done what we can, we can leave the outcome in God's hands, for he judges with justice.
exp.8:2:
This verse tells that Abimelech's mother's brothers went to speak to the leaders of Shechem and repeated everything he had asked them to say. The leaders of Shechem were won over and sided with Abimelech, because they thought: "He is one of ours, he is our relative." The words "their hearts were inclined to follow him" mean that they were drawn toward him and decided to back him.

Abimelech was the son of Gideon and of a woman from Shechem. He wanted to be king, and he used family ties to win the city's support. What follows shows that his plan was unjust: he paid violent men and killed almost all of his brothers.

For today: let us not follow someone only because he is "one of ours," whether by family, friendship or group. Before supporting a person, let us look at his character, his intentions and his fruits, and ask God for wisdom to choose well.
exp.13:6:
Judges 14:7 says that Samson went down to Timnah and spoke with the woman, because she was pleasing to his eyes. Being pleasing to his eyes means that he was attracted to her and drawn to her. It is a simple step, but he had already decided that he wanted to marry her.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He tells how Samson pressed on with his desire, even though his parents did not agree that he should marry a woman from a people who were enemies of Israel. Earlier, the Spirit of the LORD had come upon him and helped him against the lion. The text says that God was seeking an occasion against the Philistines, but that does not mean everything Samson did was an example to follow.

For today: before following a desire of the heart, stop to pray and ask for wise counsel. Feeling drawn to something does not prove that it is the best choice or what God wants.
exp.0:20:
The explanation says that the tribe of Benjamin failed to drive out the Jebusites, a people who lived in Jerusalem. Because of this, the Jebusites continued to live in the city alongside the Benjamites. The verse's statement that the Jebusites live there "to this day" means that this situation was still going on when the book was written.

The book of Judges begins by telling how each tribe tried to take possession of the promised land. The narrator, whose name we do not know for certain, shows some successes, such as that of Judah, but also some failures. Here Benjamin does not finish the task that God had given it. A pattern can be seen: partial obedience that, little by little, brings problems later on.

For today: sometimes we leave something unfinished that we know we must resolve, like a bad habit or a damaged relationship. What we tolerate today can grow tomorrow. Ask God for strength to finish what He asks of you, step by step.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that the leaders of all the tribes of Israel came to the assembly of God's people. With them were four hundred thousand men on foot, armed with swords. The phrase "presented themselves" in this explanation means that they showed up and gathered there together.

The book of Judges tells this without naming its narrator. Israel comes together at Mizpah because of a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, in the territory of Benjamin, against the concubine of a Levite. The tribes gather to learn what happened and to decide how to respond. The figure of four hundred thousand can be understood literally, though some scholars debate how numbers were used in these accounts.

For today: when there is a serious injustice, it is wise to come together, hear the facts, and seek God before acting. Unity is valuable, but it needs truth, calm, and justice, not just anger.
exp.5:15:
God answers Gideon with a promise: "Surely I will be with you." Because of that presence, Gideon would strike down the Midianites as one man, meaning all of them would fall in one decisive blow, with no resistance left behind.

The Lord, who had appeared to Gideon, speaks. Israel was oppressed by Midian, and Gideon felt small: his family was poor, and he was the youngest in his house. God does not correct his weakness with praise, but with a promise. Afterward Gideon asks for a sign, and God patiently waits.

When God calls you to something that seems bigger than you, do not look first at your limits, but at his company. Take the step you can, trusting that his presence sustains you, and speak with him honestly about your fears.
exp.5:21:
Gideon realizes that the one who spoke to him was the angel of the LORD, and he is frightened. He cries out, "Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!" The words express fear and surprise. "Face to face" means that he saw him directly, from the front.

Gideon is an Israelite chosen to deliver his people from the Midianites. Earlier he asked for a sign, and the fire that came out of the rock confirmed to him that God was speaking. In that time it was believed that seeing God or his messenger could cost a person their life. That is why God calms him right away with a word of peace and assurance that he will not die.

When God draws near, it is natural to feel fear or smallness. But He does not call us to crush us, but to give us peace and confidence. If today you feel afraid of what God asks of you, bring it to him honestly, as Gideon did, and listen for his word of calm.
exp.4:26:
It says that Sisera, the commander of the enemy army, collapsed and fell and then lay still at Jael's feet. The repetition of "collapsed" and "fell" makes the reader see the scene slowly, almost moment by moment. The verse describes him falling right where he had collapsed, and it never reaches the point of a clear, separate ending. The "temples" are the sides of the head.

The one speaking is Deborah, together with Barak, in a song of victory after the battle against the Canaanite army. They celebrate that God delivered Israel through an unexpected woman. The poem uses repetition to stress that the powerful oppressor was completely defeated. Interpreters discuss how to judge Jael's method, since the text narrates it and celebrates it, but does not present it as an example to imitate.

For today: God can work through people no one expected. We can trust that no human power is greater than He is, and be willing to serve with courage wherever we are placed.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that the tribe of Judah captured three Philistine cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, each along with the territory around it. The phrase "each with its territory" refers to the land surrounding each city.

The book of Judges begins by describing how each tribe tried to take its share of the promised land after the death of Joshua. Here the narrator highlights the successes of Judah, the strongest tribe. But notice that the next verse says they could not drive out those who lived in the plains, and some scholars believe these cities were lost later, although this is debated.

Today we can learn that a victory is not permanent if we stop taking care of it. God gives us progress in life, but we must keep trusting him steadily, never taking anything for granted forever.
exp.17:5:
Here the priest of Micah tells the five men from the tribe of Dan: "Go in peace. The Lord is watching over your journey." That is, he assures them that God approves their journey. "The Lord is watching over your journey" means that God sees it and directs it.

The Danites were looking for a place to settle. They stopped at the house of Micah, where this young Levite served as a paid priest, with an idol and an ephod. They asked him to seek God's answer. He gave them a reassuring reply, but the text does not say that God spoke. This happens in a time of religious disorder, so his answer may be more convenient than faithful.

Today, not every religious voice that encourages us speaks on God's behalf. Before deciding, let us compare what we hear with the Bible and seek wise counsel.
exp.19:13:
The explanation says that the people of Benjamin, instead of handing over the guilty men, came together from their cities at Gibeah to go out and fight against the rest of Israel. "Instead" is the meaning here. "Go out and fight" means to set out to war.

The narrator tells what happened after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The other tribes asked Benjamin to hand over those men, called "sons of Belial," that is, wicked people, so that justice could be done. Benjamin refused to listen to his brothers and chose to protect his own and fight. Thus a grave sin turned into a war between brothers.

For today: when someone from our own side does something wrong, defending them out of loyalty only makes the harm greater. Let us ask God for humility to recognize the wrong, correct it, and seek justice, even when it hurts.
exp.20:22:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin did as they were instructed: each one took a wife from among the women who were dancing at Shiloh, seizing them by force. Then they went back to their own inheritance, rebuilt their towns, and settled in them.

The people of Israel had nearly wiped out the tribe of Benjamin in a civil war, and they had sworn not to give their daughters to them in marriage. So that a tribe would not disappear, the elders looked for this way out. The book does not approve of it: it ends by saying there was no king and everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. Many read this as a criticism of that era.

For today: a rash promise can lead us into unjust arrangements. When we get things wrong, we should not cover one wrong with another, but seek God and act with justice and humility.
exp.15:23:
This verse tells how the Philistines, seeing Samson held captive, praised their god Dagon. They said that their god had handed them victory over the man who had destroyed their land and killed many of their people.

The speakers are the Philistine people, gathered at a great religious feast. Samson was blind and imprisoned because he had revealed the secret of his strength. The Philistines credited their triumph to Dagon, but the account shows that Samson had fallen through his own disobedience. His hair was already beginning to grow back, which hints that something would change.

For today: it is easy to celebrate too soon and to believe that everything is settled when someone falls. God continues to work even in moments of apparent defeat. It is wise to live with humility, without boasting of victories or giving up in our failures.
exp.0:21:
These verses say that the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, called "the house of Joseph" because they descended from his two sons, attacked the city of Bethel. The word "attacked" fits the setting, since the region was hilly and the tribes had to climb to reach the city. Most importantly, "the LORD was with them": God was with them in the fight.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. After the death of Joshua, each tribe was to take the portion of land allotted to it. Just before this, the tribe of Benjamin is recorded as having failed to drive out the Jebusites. This verse contrasts with that: the house of Joseph acts, and the LORD is with them. The account that follows, however, shows that they also used spies and careful planning.

For today: when you face a difficult task, plan wisely and take concrete steps, but first seek the presence of God. His companionship gives you more security than your own strength.
exp.20:8:
The explanation says that the people of Israel were counted, meaning a tally was taken of who was present at the assembly, and it was found that none of the residents of Jabesh-gilead were there. "Were counted" means they took attendance, and the word "residents" in this verse refers to the people who lived in that town.

This happens after the nearly fatal war against the tribe of Benjamin. Israel had sworn not to give their daughters to the Benjamites, who were left without wives, and they were looking for a way out. They noticed that Jabesh-gilead had not come to the gathering at Mizpah. The account is told by the narrator, and what follows is violent. The Bible records it but does not approve of it; the book shows a time of moral chaos.

For today: be careful with hasty promises and with "fixes" that correct one wrong by committing a greater one. Before acting, let us ask God for wisdom and humility to correct things with justice and mercy.
exp.1:14:
Whenever Israel marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them to bring calamity, just as He had sworn to them. This means that every time the Israelites set out to fight or to undertake any venture, God opposed them and things went badly. It fulfilled what God had warned them of and had promised them with an oath. "Marched out" refers to their military campaigns or undertakings; "the hand of the LORD" speaks of his power at work; "greatly distressed" means that he brought them great suffering.

The narrator of the book, whose author is not known with certainty, explains why Israel was defeated after the death of Joshua. The people had abandoned God to worship Baal and Ashtaroth. God had already warned them in the law (for example, Deuteronomy 28) that disobedience would bring consequences. Here we see his faithfulness to what he said.

For today: God is serious, but he is also patient. If you notice that you have drifted away from him, do not wait to suffer more; return to him soon and sincerely, for he remains ready to rescue.
exp.10:33:
Jephthah returns victorious to his home in Mizpah, and his daughter comes out to greet him with tambourines and dancing, as was done to celebrate a victory. The text emphasizes that she was his only child, and that he had no other son or daughter. The word "tambourines" refers to the hand drums played at such celebrations, and "his only child" means that she was everything he had.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had made a vow to God before the battle: he would offer whatever came out of his house to meet him first (Judges 11:30-31). Perhaps he did not think about the consequences. Interpreters debate what happened to her afterward: some believe she was sacrificed, others that she was dedicated to serving God her whole life, without marrying. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: before we promise something to God or to others, let us think calmly and sincerely about what we are really promising. Words spoken lightly can bring deep sorrow, and God values wisdom and obedience more than hasty promises.
exp.14:16:
It says that Samson, when he had finished his song of victory, threw down the jawbone he had been holding. Then he named the place Ramath-lehi. In Hebrew that name can sound like "the height of the jaw," though some also understand it as "he threw away the jaw." Perhaps the name holds both meanings.

Here the narrator is speaking, telling what Samson did. The Philistines had bound him to hand him over, but he broke the ropes and defeated a thousand men. After shouting his triumphant poem, he laid down the weapon and marked the spot to remember what happened there.

For today: after a victory, it is easy to keep the jawbone and boast. Samson spoke about himself, but soon he was thirsty and cried out to God. When something goes well for you, remember that you depend on God, and thank him before you move on.
exp.17:2:
The five men from the tribe of Dan, who were traveling through the land to explore it, passed near the house of Micah. They recognized the voice of the young Levite who was there and went over to him. They asked him three questions in a row: who brought him there, what he was doing, and why he was there. "They recognized his voice" may mean that they already knew him, or that they noticed his Levite accent; the text does not make this clear.

The speakers are the Danite scouts. Dan had not yet taken possession of its inheritance and was looking for a place to settle. It was a time of disorder, when there was no king in Israel. They are surprised to find a Levite, who was supposed to serve in the worship of the Lord, working as a private priest in a private home.

For today: when we find ourselves in a strange place, it is worth asking ourselves those same questions with sincerity: what am I doing here, and why? We should ask God for direction, instead of following only comfort or convenience.
exp.7:27:
This verse says that the Midianites were defeated and left unable to fight back against Israel. The phrase "did not raise its head again" means they lost their strength and never regained power or dared to attack again. After that victory, the land had rest for forty years while Gideon lived.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is summing up the result of Gideon's victory. But the surrounding context shows a sad contrast: Gideon made an ephod from the gold that was gathered, and the people turned aside after it. An ephod was a sacred garment; the Bible does not explain in detail its purpose here, but it calls it a snare.

For today: God can give us victories and rest, but afterward we must guard the heart. Let what we receive from God not become a stumbling block or take the place of God Himself.
exp.5:19:
What it says: God's angel tells Gideon to take the meat and the unleavened bread, place them on a rock, and pour out the broth. A "rock" here is a large stone, and the "broth" is the liquid from the cooked meat. Gideon does exactly what he is told.

Context: Gideon was an Israelite who felt small and afraid, and he asked for a sign to confirm that God was speaking to him. He had prepared a young goat and bread as an offering of hospitality. The angel changes the purpose of that meal: he turns it into an offering on the rock, and then a fire rises up and consumes it. Some believe this angel is a special appearance of God himself, and others see him as a messenger; the text calls him "the angel of God."

For today: When God asks you to do something, even if you don't fully understand it, you can take a simple step of obedience. He often affirms the faith of those who trust and obey.
exp.6:21:
The three hundred men of Gideon kept sounding their horns, which were rams' horns. The LORD made the enemy soldiers, confused in the darkness, turn their swords against one another, even throughout the whole camp. Then the army fled toward places such as Beth-shittah, Zererah, and the border of Abel-meholah, near Tabbath.

This is told by the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel was oppressed by Midian, and the LORD had reduced Gideon's army to three hundred men so that it would be clear the victory came from Him. The men did not fight with swords, but with pitchers, torches, and horns.

The LORD can work with little when we obey Him with simplicity. We do not always have to be strong or many; it is enough to be faithful in what He asks of us, and to trust Him with the result.
exp.7:6:
Gideon promises that, when the LORD gives him victory over Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, he will punish the leaders of Succoth. Here "tear" means to beat or tear apart, the way grain was threshed. The "thorns and briers" are plants with hard, sharp spines. "Delivered into my hand" means that the LORD would give him the win over them.

Gideon and his 300 men were exhausted, pursuing the enemy kings. He asked the people of Succoth for bread, but they refused with mockery, because they doubted he would win. Gideon answers with anger and a harsh threat. The text tells us what he said and then what he did, but it does not say that God ordered that revenge.

Today we can learn to help those who are tired from serving, without waiting to see results. We should also take care with our reactions: anger, even when justified, can lead us to excess.
exp.1:4:
This verse says the people gave that place the name Bochim, which means "the weepers." There they offered sacrifices to the LORD.

The angel of the LORD had just rebuked Israel for not obeying: they had made agreements with the peoples of the land and had not torn down their altars. As a result, those peoples would remain a pressure and a snare for them. Hearing this, the people wept. The sacrifices show that they wanted to draw near to God. The text does not say whether their repentance was deep, and the book later shows that it did not last.

For today: weeping over sin is a good beginning, but God also expects real change. If something pulls you away from Him, do not tolerate it; ask Him for help to leave it behind and to obey Him with steadiness.
exp.11:0:
The men of the tribe of Ephraim gathered together and crossed the Jordan to Zaphon. They confronted Jephthah, asking why he went to fight the Ammonites without calling them to go with him. They threatened to burn his house down with him inside it. The phrase "crossed the Jordan to Zaphon" in the verse describes the direction the men moved as they came to confront him.

The Ephraimites speak to Jephthah in anger. They came from a strong and proud tribe, and they felt ignored when God gave the victory to someone else. Jephthah answers that he did call them, and they did not help. Some scholars see wounded pride and jealousy here, though the text itself says nothing more about their motives.

When someone else receives recognition, we can feel pushed aside. Before we make claims or pick a fight, it is wise to examine our hearts and ask whether our anger comes from pride. Rejoicing in the success of others prevents conflicts that harm many people.
exp.4:29:
These women near Sisera's mother try to calm her. They assure her that her son is delayed because he is finding and dividing up the spoil of war. The word for "young woman" in the older text is rendered here as "girl," and what is taken from a defeated enemy is called "spoil." They imagine dyed garments and embroidered cloth for Sisera and for the warriors who fought with him.

This passage is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, sung after Israel's victory. The speaker is a wise lady of the court, and Sisera's mother also convinces herself. The song shows with irony how she dreams of gains, not knowing that her son has been defeated. Some understand that the text also reflects the harshness of ancient warfare, without approving of it.

For today: beware of illusions that comfort us but are not true. Let us rather place our trust in God and seek the truth with humility.
exp.20:12:
This verse tells that all the people of Israel sent a message of peace to the men of the tribe of Benjamin, who were at the rock of Rimmon, a high, rocky place. They offered them peace, that is, they invited them to return without fighting. The phrase "the whole congregation" refers to the gathered community of Israel, and the message was sent to bring the Benjamites back.

Israel and Benjamin had come out of a terrible civil war. Almost the whole tribe of Benjamin had been killed, and only about six hundred men remained. The other Israelites had sworn not to give them their daughters as wives. Now they grieved that a tribe would disappear, and they looked for a way out, though by very violent and questionable means, as the story shows.

For today: offering peace and reconciliation is good, but it must be done with justice and without causing new harm. Let us seek to heal broken relationships with humility and truth.
exp.10:25:
It says that Israel had been living in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, along with all the cities along the banks of the Arnon, for three hundred years. Jephthah asks the Ammonite king why, during all that time, he did not try to take those lands back. "Villages" here means the smaller towns nearby, and the Arnon is the river that marks the border.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, speaks in a message to the king of Ammon. The Ammonites claimed that Israel had taken that land from them. Jephthah tries to avoid war with a historical argument: no one made any claim for centuries. Some scholars debate how to calculate those three hundred years, but the point is that a long time had passed.

For today: before fighting over a conflict, it is wise to speak calmly and review the facts. Seeking the truth and dialogue can prevent harm, even when the other person does not want to listen, as happened here.
exp.10:5:
The elders of Gilead ask Jephthah to come back and be their commander, so that they can fight against the Ammonites. The name "Ammonites" is the people, and the wording shows they want him to lead them into battle.

The leaders of Gilead are speaking. Israel was facing a threat of war. Earlier they had rejected Jephthah and driven him away from his family, and he was living far off, in the land of Tob. Now, in their trouble, they seek him out because they need his courage and experience. Jephthah will point this out to them right away.

For today: when we need to ask forgiveness or seek help from someone we have hurt, let us do it with humility and sincerity, and not merely out of convenience. And if someone wronged us and later comes looking for us, let us ask God for wisdom to respond with truth and grace.
exp.4:12:
The explanation says that the few survivors of the people of Israel came down and prevailed over the nobles and the powerful. The phrase the verse uses here means to go down against, or to press forward into battle against, the enemy. The "nobles" are the great and powerful men, and "the mighty" are the enemy warriors. The speaker says it was the LORD's people who came down against them, and that the LORD gave them this victory.

This verse is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, sung after the victory over the army of Sisera, which had many iron chariots. Deborah, a prophetess and judge, sings that Israel, though it had become small and weakened, won thanks to God. Some understand the "me" in the verse to refer to Deborah and others to the whole people; the text allows both readings.

For today: when you feel small or without strength in the face of a large problem, remember that victory does not depend on your size but on God's help. Trust in Him and thank Him when He helps you.
exp.17:29:
The Danites set up idols for themselves, and Jonathan, son of Gershom, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the day the land went into captivity.

The narrator of Judges tells how the tribe of Dan conquered Laish and took the idol of Micah along with his priest. It is a disordered time, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The account shows how worship became corrupted.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we worship God as He has revealed Himself or as it suits us. A comfortable faith, made to our own measure, ends up pulling us away from Him.
exp.0:26:
This verse tells us that the tribe of Manasseh did not manage to drive out the inhabitants of several Canaanite cities: Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, and Megiddo, along with their villages (the smaller towns around them). The verse says Manasseh "failed to drive out" these people. The Canaanites were determined to stay in that land.

The narrator of the book of Judges reviews how each tribe only partly carried out the task of taking the promised land. Earlier, God had commanded Israel not to live alongside those peoples. The book shows that this incomplete obedience set the stage for spiritual problems that would come later, when Israel mixed with their customs.

For today: when we leave halfway what God asks us to change, the things we tolerate tend to grow. Ask God for honesty to recognize which habit or attitude you have allowed to live in your heart, and for courage to face it with his help.
exp.12:8:
God listened to Manoah's prayer and sent the angel again. What stands out is that the angel did not appear to Manoah this time, but once more to his wife, who was alone in the field.

The phrase "returned" means that he came back a second time. The Berean Standard Bible reads "returned," so the explanation uses that word.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel had already told her that she would have a son who would be a Nazirite, that is, set apart for God. Manoah, worried, asked for help in knowing how to raise him. God answered, though not in the way he had expected. Some believe the woman had a special sensitivity for receiving the message, but the text does not explain this.

Today we can pray with confidence when we need direction. God listens, even when his answer comes in a way different from what we imagined. Let us learn to be attentive and to value those whom God uses to guide us.
exp.8:33:
Abimelech rose up by night, along with all his troops, and set out to lie in wait against the city of Shechem. He split his men into four groups to surround the city. To lie in wait means to stay hidden in order to attack by surprise, and a company here means a group of soldiers.

The plan came from Zebul, an official of Shechem who was loyal to Abimelech, and he sent word to him in secret. The city had turned against Abimelech and was backing Gaal. Zebul advised him to attack at dawn, when Gaal went out. The account shows violence and revenge in a time of disorder in Israel.

For today: this passage reminds us that ambition and violence bring more violence. We can ask God to help us resolve conflicts with humility, without deceit or revenge, seeking peace with others.
exp.20:3:
The next day the people got up early, built an altar there, and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings. These were two kinds of offerings: burnt offerings, which were burned whole in honor of God, and peace offerings, which expressed fellowship and thankfulness, and from which a portion was shared. The words "built" and "early" are the ones that matter here. "Built" means constructed, and "early" means very early in the morning.

The narrator recounts what happened after the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. The Israelites wept before God because one tribe was almost gone. They had made a severe oath and now regretted it. The text does not say that God commanded this, so we do not know whether their way of acting was the right one. We see a people who seek God, but with hasty decisions.

Today we can learn that seeking God with grief and repentance is good, but it is wise to think before making promises or decisions of great weight. It is better to pray first and ask for wisdom.
exp.5:33:
The Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon with power, as if he were putting on a garment. The verse says the Spirit came upon him, and it means that God's power covered him completely. Then Gideon blew the ram's horn, which was used to call people to war, and the Abiezrites, his clan, gathered and followed him.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Judges. Midianites, Amalekites and peoples from the east had crossed the Jordan and camped in the valley of Jezreel to attack Israel. Gideon, who had already torn down the altar of Baal, now receives strength from God to lead the people. He goes from being a fearful man to being a leader.

For today: when God calls you to something difficult, it does not depend on your own strength, but on his Spirit. Take the step of obedience that lies before you, even if you feel small, and trust that God is with you and will give you what you need.
exp.3:9:
This verse tells that Barak summoned the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. From there he set out with ten thousand men following him, and Deborah went along with him. The verse's words "went up" mean they set out and marched forward, and "ten thousand men followed him" means they came behind him, going where he led.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel was oppressed by King Jabin of Canaan and his military commander, Sisera. God had called Barak through the prophetess Deborah. Barak hesitated and asked that she go with him, and she agreed. Now he obeys and sets out with the people.

For today: obedience to God does not require that everything be perfect or that we have no fear. Barak moved forward with his doubts, and God worked. Take the step God shows you, and seek the support of people of faith who encourage you to keep going.
exp.14:8:
The Philistines, enemies of Israel, went up into the territory of Judah and camped there. They deployed their forces near the town of Lehi. The word "camped" means they settled in with their army, and "deployed" means they positioned their troops across the area.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The Philistines were dominating Israel, and Samson had struck them hard in revenge for what they had done to his wife and her father. Now they respond with force, but they do not attack Samson directly. Instead they pressure the whole tribe of Judah to hand him over. This shows how violence breeds more violence.

For today: when someone wounds us, revenge seems just, but it almost always brings consequences that reach other people. Before responding in anger, it is wise to think about who else will be affected and to seek, calmly, the path of forgiveness.
exp.4:4:
The explanation says the mountains "quaked", that is, they trembled before the LORD's presence. It mentions Sinai, the mountain where God revealed himself to Israel. The name "the One of Sinai" in the verse points to this same sense of God's presence. The language is poetic: it shows that even the firmest parts of creation tremble before the LORD.

The speaker is Deborah, together with Barak, in a song of victory over the Canaanites. She remembers how God showed his power and majesty in the past. Some think it also alludes to rain or a storm that helped in the battle, but the text does not make this clear. With this she means that the same God of Sinai is the one who gave victory to his people.

For today: when you face something that seems immense and impossible, remember that God is greater than any mountain. Trust in him and praise him with gratitude.
exp.5:12:
Gideon answers the angel honestly and with pain. If the Lord is with us, he asks, why has all this come upon us? He asks where the wonders are that our fathers told us about, such as the time the Lord brought them up out of Egypt. He feels that the Lord has forsaken them and handed them over into the hand of Midian. "Come upon" means that something has fallen on them; "forsaken" means abandoned.

Gideon speaks in a time of oppression. The Midianites were raiding Israel's harvests, and for that reason he was threshing wheat in secret in a winepress. The angel greeted him by saying that the Lord was with him, and Gideon responds out of his hard experience. Some see here a lack of faith; others see an honest complaint. The text does not condemn him.

When pain makes you doubt God, do not hide it. Tell him honestly, as Gideon did. God hears your questions and can answer you, even when you do not yet understand what is happening.
exp.17:7:
Verse 8 tells us that the five men who had gone to scout the land returned to their people at Zorah and Eshtaol. There their brothers from the tribe of Dan asked them, "What did you find?", meaning, "How did it go, and what news do you bring?" And the scouts began to answer.

The background is that the tribe of Dan was looking for a place to settle. The five spies had seen Laish, a quiet city with no nearby allies. Earlier, a priest had told them to go in peace, and they took this as God's approval. Now they return with an enthusiastic report. The Bible does not say that this priest spoke on God's behalf, and this account contains a great deal of disobedience.

For today: when we make an important decision, it is not enough that something sounds good or that someone tells us to go ahead. Let us ask God for wisdom, compare what we hear with his Word, and seek sound counsel.
exp.10:22:
Here Jephthah tells the king of the Ammonites that the LORD, the God of Israel, is the one who drove the Amorites out of that land so that it would belong to His people Israel. Then he asks them firmly, "Should you now possess it?" The word "driven out" means that the Amorites were forced to leave, and "possess" means to take something as one's own.

Jephthah speaks as the leader of Israel, and he sends this message to the king of the Ammonites, who was claiming those lands. Jephthah argues that Israel received the territory from the Amorites, not from Ammon, and that Israel has lived there for a long time. He tries to settle the conflict with words before going to war. Some scholars point out that Jephthah mentions Chemosh, the god of Moab, alongside the god of Ammon, and the Bible does not fully clarify that detail.

For today: before fighting for something, it is wise to think with clarity and calm. Recognizing what God has given us gives us firmness and humility to engage in dialogue.
exp.12:19:
This verse tells how, as the flame of the sacrifice rose from the altar into the sky, the angel of the LORD also went up in the flame, and Manoah and his wife saw it. They fell facedown to the ground. The phrase "fell facedown" means lowering oneself to the ground as a sign of respect and worship.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a child, who would be Samson. The angel had given them instructions, and Manoah wanted to offer a sacrifice. When he asked the angel's name, the angel answered that it was secret, a name beyond understanding. Seeing him rise in the flame, they understood that he was a messenger of God. Then Manoah became afraid, because it was believed that seeing God was dangerous.

For today: when God reveals himself to us in unexpected ways, the best response is humility and worship. We can draw near to him with reverence and gratitude, trusting that his plans are greater than our own.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that, even while Israel was suffering because of its disobedience, God did not completely abandon them. Then the LORD raised up judges, which means he set up leaders and placed them in position. These judges saved the people from those who plundered them, that is, from those who robbed them and took what belonged to them.

The book of Judges tells the story of Israel after the death of Joshua. The narrator explains that the people turned away from God and worshiped other gods, and for that reason they suffered oppression. But when they cried out, God responded with compassion. The judges were not kings; they were deliverers and leaders chosen by God for each situation.

For today: although our mistakes bring consequences, God remains merciful. If you are in a difficult situation because of your own decisions, you can return to Him sincerely, trusting that He is still willing to help you.
exp.12:23:
This verse says that the woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him. The phrase "gave birth" and the naming of the child are the plain sense of the text. About the meaning of "Samson," some connect it with the Hebrew word for "sun," but this is not entirely certain.

The narrator tells this after an angel announced to Manoah and his wife the birth of a son. Manoah was afraid he would die for having seen God, but his wife calmed him with good judgment: God would not have accepted their offering or given them that promise if he wanted to destroy them. Here we see the promise fulfilled.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when we feel fear or doubt. Let us trust his character, and when we raise or guide others, let us ask for his blessing on their growth.
exp.6:19:
The explanation says that Gideon's three hundred men, divided into three companies, blew their horns and smashed the jars that hid the torches. In their left hands they held the torches, and in their right hands the horns, which they blew. Then they shouted: "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"

Gideon had given these instructions to his men. God had reduced the army to three hundred so that Israel would know that the victory came from Him. It was night, and the camp of Midian was surrounded. The confusion that followed was the work of God, not of human strength.

For today: God can use our simple obedience, even when it seems small or illogical. We do not have to be the strongest or the most numerous. It is enough to do with faith what He asks of us and to leave the result to Him.
exp.10:35:
Here the daughter of Jephthah answers her father. She tells him that if he has given his word to the LORD, he must keep it, because the LORD has already given him victory over the Ammonites. The phrase "you have given your word" means that he made a solemn promise to God.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had promised God that he would offer whatever came out of his house first to meet him if he won the battle. The one who came out was his only daughter. The text does not clearly explain what happened afterward: some understand that she was offered as a sacrifice, others that she was dedicated to live unmarried in the service of God. Interpreters debate this.

For today: let us think carefully before we speak, especially when we make promises to God or to others. And let us value the humble faith of this young woman, who trusted God even in the midst of her grief.
exp.7:15:
Gideon took the elders of the city, and he used the thorns and briers of the wilderness to discipline the men of Succoth. The word "briers" refers to plants with very sharp thorns. "Discipline" can also be understood as "teaching them a lesson" or "making them pay for what they did." Some scholars think he struck them with these plants, though the text gives no further details.

Gideon was pursuing the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna. When he asked the men of Succoth for bread for his exhausted soldiers, the city's leaders mocked him and refused to help. Now, after capturing the kings, Gideon returns and carries out the warning he had given them. His reaction mixes a sense of justice with personal anger, and the Bible here simply tells what happened without fully approving of it.

Today we can learn to help those who are worn out from serving others. Refusing support when we are able to give it has consequences. And as we seek justice, we must be careful that revenge does not take control of us.
exp.6:2:
Gideon is told to announce to the people that anyone who is afraid and trembling may turn back and leave Mount Gilead. Twenty-two thousand went home, and ten thousand remained.

God speaks to Gideon before he faces the Midianites. The army was too large, and God wanted Israel not to boast that its own strength had won the victory. So he reduces the number, so that everyone would recognize that salvation comes from him.

God does not need our abundance of resources, talents, or support in order to act. Sometimes he makes us depend on him by taking away the things we trusted in. If today you feel you have little strength, remember that his power can shine in your weakness, and that the credit always belongs to him.
exp.8:37:
Zebul turns Gaal's own boast against him. Gaal had said, "Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?" Now Zebul asks him where that gloating has gone. The people Gaal ridiculed, "Are these not the people you ridiculed?", are the very ones now coming to attack. So Zebul sends him out with a challenge: "Go out now and fight them!"

Zebul is the ruler of the city of Shechem and serves Abimelech. Meanwhile he pretends to be on Gaal's side. Earlier he told Gaal that what they were seeing were only shadows of the mountains, in order to buy time. When Abimelech is already close, Zebul stops pretending and turns Gaal's own words against him. The text does not say that Zebul was sincere with Gaal, and the account shows everyone acting with violence and deceit.

For today: let us be careful about what we say when we are full of pride, because sooner or later our words can come back to us. It is better to speak with humility and not to promise what we cannot fulfill.
exp.19:33:
It says that ten thousand select men from all Israel made a frontal assault against Gibeah, and that the fighting became fierce. The Benjamites did not realize that disaster was upon them. The wording "disaster was upon them" speaks of their ruin being close at hand.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel was at war against the tribe of Benjamin, because that tribe had protected criminal men from Gibeah. Israel pretended to flee in order to draw the Benjamites out of the city, while an ambush waited. The Benjamites trusted in their earlier victories and did not see the trap.

For today: past success can make us careless. When a person feels secure because of what they have already achieved, and does not examine their path with humility, they may fail to see the danger. Let us ask God for wisdom and honestly review our decisions.
exp.5:22:
God speaks to Gideon and says: "Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die." The word "peace" here is a greeting and also a promise of calm. "The LORD" is the name of God.

Gideon had just realized that his visitor was the angel of the Lord, and that the fire had consumed his offering. He was very frightened, because at that time it was believed that seeing God face to face could cost a person his life. The Lord himself calms him. Afterward, Gideon builds an altar and calls it "The LORD is peace," and later he receives the task of tearing down the altar of Baal.

When we feel fear before God or before what he asks of us, we can remember that he draws near to give us peace. Before asking us something difficult, he gives us assurance. We can come to him with confidence and honesty.
exp.12:3:
The explanation says that the woman of Manoah, while she waits for her son, must not drink wine or strong drink (a fermented drink, such as apple or fruit cider), and must not eat anything unclean, that is, anything the law of Moses declared impure for God's people. The phrase "Now please be careful" is like saying: "So be careful from now on."

The angel of the LORD speaks to this woman who could not have children. He announces that she will have a son who will be a Nazirite, set apart for God from before birth, and who will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Since the boy will be set apart, she also takes care of her own life from the time of her pregnancy. How this connects with the care of the child in the womb is understood in several ways, but the text shows that God's calling begins very early.

For today: when God entrusts us with something important, such as a family or a job, it is worth looking after our habits from the beginning, with obedience and gratitude.
exp.4:18:
The explanation says that several Canaanite kings came together to fight against Israel at Taanach, near the waters of Megiddo. The phrase "they took no plunder of silver" refers to the spoils, or wealth, they hoped to carry off after winning. But they left with nothing: they lost the battle and gained no riches.

This verse is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, which celebrates the victory over Sisera and the army of Jabin. Deborah praises the tribes that answered the call and rebukes those that did not. The kings came with confidence and ambition, but God intervened. The following verse shows that the victory came from heaven, and the torrent of Kishon swept the enemy away.

For today: plans based only on ambition or power can fail, even when they seem strong. We can trust that God cares for his people, and we are called to obey him with courage, without depending on silver or human strength.
exp.13:0:
The verse tells us that one day Samson went down to Timnah, a town near his own land, and there he saw a young Philistine woman. The phrase "went down" reflects the fact that Timnah sat at a lower elevation. The word "saw" here shows that she caught his attention, and calling her a young Philistine woman makes clear that she belonged to that people.

It is the narrator who tells this story. The Philistines held power over Israel at that time, and God had forbidden marrying neighboring peoples who would turn the Israelites away from Him. Samson's parents are worried, but he is guided by what he sees. Judges also says, in verse 4, that God would use this against the Philistines, and interpreters explain that in different ways.

For today: do not make important decisions only because something attracts you. Listen to the advice of wise people, and ask God whether that decision fits with His will.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that Gideon's three hundred men did not advance or fight. They stayed still, each one in his position, surrounding the enemy camp. Meanwhile, the entire Midianite army was thrown into confusion, and they fled in a panic, crying out as they ran.

The account tells what happened at night, when Gideon and his men surrounded the Midianites with trumpets, pitchers, and torches. God had reduced Israel's army so that it would be clear the victory came from Him. The text says that the enemies turned their swords against one another, so the confusion was not only human fear.

For today: sometimes God asks us for faithfulness in the place He has given us, not for us to be the ones in the spotlight. Stand firm in your place, obey what He shows you, and trust that He can act beyond your strength.
exp.19:6:
Here the speaker says to all the Israelites: "Behold, all you Israelites, give your advice and verdict here and now." The phrase "give your advice and verdict here and now" means "give your opinion and decide what should be done." It is an invitation to decide together.

The one speaking is the Levite whose concubine was abused and killed in Gibeah, a city of Benjamin. He tells his version of what happened before the assembly of Israel. Notice that his account has its own emphases, and it does not mention that he himself handed the woman over to her attackers. The story takes place in a time of great violence and moral disorder.

For today: before reacting to an injustice, it is wise to seek advice and listen calmly. But we should also ask for wisdom to weigh all the facts, and not let ourselves be carried away by only one version or by anger.
exp.20:9:
The explanation says that the people of Israel sent twelve thousand of their most valiant men against Jabesh-gilead. They were commanded to put to the sword everyone living there, including women and children. The phrase "put to the sword" means killing with the sword. The congregation is the gathering of the whole nation of Israel.

It is the assembly of the tribes that speaks. They had sworn at Mizpah that anyone who did not come up to them would be put to death. Since no one from Jabesh-gilead came, they acted in this way. They wanted to get wives for the survivors of Benjamin, a tribe that had been nearly destroyed. The book ends by saying that at that time there was no king and each person did whatever seemed right to them. The text tells what happened, but it does not present it as an example to follow.

For today: before we promise something with force, let us ask God for wisdom. A hasty vow can lead us to commit injustice.
exp.5:23:
This verse says that Gideon built an altar to the LORD in that place and named it "The LORD Is Peace." It adds that the altar was still standing "to this day," meaning at the time the account was written, in Ophrah, a town of the Abiezrites.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Gideon had just seen the angel of the LORD and feared he would die, because people believed that seeing God face to face meant death. God said to him, "Peace be with you; do not fear." The altar was his grateful response to that word of peace.

For today: when God gives you calm in the middle of fear, do not let it pass. Thank Him with a concrete act, such as a prayer, a written note, or a moment of worship, to remember that He is your peace.
exp.12:9:
The wife of Manoah, whom the Bible does not name, runs quickly to tell her husband that the man who came to her the other day has reappeared. "Quickly" means fast, and "tell" means she reports the news to him. The verse calls him simply "the man."

Manoah had prayed that the man of God would come back to teach them how to raise the promised child. God heard, and the messenger returned, but he found the woman alone in the field. She hurries to her husband because she wants him to meet the messenger as soon as possible. The child would be Samson, though here he has not yet been born.

When God answers a prayer, sometimes we are the ones who must move. This woman did not stay still or keep the news to herself. If God has given you an answer or guidance, share it with those you love and move forward promptly and humbly.
exp.20:24:
In those days Israel had no king to rule over the whole people. So each person decided what was right according to their own judgment. "Right" here means correct or just, and "what was right in his own eyes" means what seemed right to each one.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, and he closes the book with this sentence. He has just recounted episodes of violence and disorder among the tribes, and his final chapters show a people who had turned away from God. Many understand the sentence as pointing to the need for good leadership, and others understand the missing foundation as obedience to God. Both readings can be defended.

For today: before deciding something important, don't ask only "what seems good to me?" but "what does God say in his Word?" Ask him for wisdom and allow yourself to be corrected.
exp.11:1:
Jephthah answers the men of Ephraim by telling them that he and his people had a serious conflict with the Ammonites. He says that when he called for help, they did not rescue him from the hands of the enemy.

Jephthah, judge of Gilead, speaks to the people of Ephraim, who threaten to burn his house because they were not invited to the battle. He answers that he did call them. The book of Judges does not record that earlier call, so we do not know the details. What we do see is that Ephraim claims honor, while Jephthah points out that they did not help when help was needed.

For today: before claiming or reacting in anger, it is wise to ask what really happened and to speak truthfully and calmly. Many quarrels grow out of wounded pride and misunderstandings, and a calm answer can prevent greater harm.
exp.11:14:
This verse tells that Abdon, son of Hillel from Pirathon, died and was buried at Pirathon, his town, in the territory of Ephraim. It says he was buried "in the hill country of the Amalekites," a region that bears that name, though the Bible does not explain in detail why.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the narrator of the book of Judges. Abdon was one of the judges, leaders whom God raised up to guide Israel. The preceding text says he judged for eight years and that his family was large and well off, since they rode on donkeys. No battle is recorded for him, only the close of his life.

For today: not everyone will serve in very visible things. God also values a faithful and simple life, lived with responsibility in the place where we find ourselves.
exp.17:6:
These five spies from the tribe of Dan came to Laish and found a people who were living at ease, unworried and unguarded. "Quiet and unsuspecting" means they were calm and had no fear of danger, and "securely" means they felt safe. They lived like the Sidonians, yet they were far away from them and had no alliance with anyone, so no one would come to their aid. Nothing in the land was lacking, and no ruler pressed down on them.

The narrator describes how the Danites, who had not yet taken the land allotted to them, were looking for a place to settle. These five men had asked the priest of Micah for a word from God, and he gave them a reassuring answer. However, the book shows a time of great religious disorder, and it does not say that God approved of everything they did.

For today: let us not confuse an easy opportunity with the will of God. Before deciding, it is wise to pray, examine the Bible, and seek wise counsel.
exp.2:12:
Eglon, king of Moab, did not attack on his own. He joined forces with the Ammonites and the Amalekites, then attacked and defeated Israel. He then took possession of the City of Palms, which many identify as Jericho, although the text does not name it.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He explains that, after the death of Othniel, Israel again did what was evil, and God allowed Eglon to grow strong against them. It was a consequence of abandoning God. Eighteen years of oppression would follow, until they cried out and God sent Ehud.

For today: sin almost always brings consequences, and sometimes they pile up. But the account also shows that God listens when we cry out. If you have drifted away from Him, do not wait until you are oppressed. Return to Him today with sincerity.
exp.16:7:
This man, a young Levite, left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle wherever he could find a place. As he traveled, he came to Micah's house in the hill country of Ephraim. He was only passing through, heading toward some other place. The phrase "to settle where he could find a place" means he had no fixed destination.

It is the narrator of Judges who tells us this. The Levites were to serve in worship and live in the towns God had assigned them, but this young man wanders without direction. The book says there was no king and that everyone did what seemed right to them, and it shows how the lack of direction affected even those who served God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking only comfort or whether we are seeking God's guidance when we make decisions. Praying and asking for wise counsel helps us not to drift aimlessly.
exp.10:8:
Jephthah answers the elders of Gilead with a careful question: if he goes back with them, fights against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them into his hand, will he really become their leader? The phrase "take me back" means bring me again with you. "Gives them to me" means hands them over to me.

Jephthah had been rejected by his brothers and driven out of his father's house. Now Gilead was in danger from Ammon, and the same elders who had sent him away were looking for him. He does not accept their offer without more ado; he wants a clear promise. Notice that he recognizes that the victory depends on the LORD, not only on himself.

Today, when someone who hurt us comes looking for us out of need, we can ask for clarity and honesty without bitterness. And in any task, let us remember that success comes from God.
exp.9:9:
The people of Israel, oppressed and suffering, cried out to God for help. They admitted their guilt: they had abandoned their God and served the Baals, the false gods of the neighboring peoples, tied to rain and harvest. "Cried out to the LORD" means they called out to the LORD. "LORD" is the name of God.

The narrator of the book tells this after eighteen years of oppression by the Ammonites and the Philistines. Israel repeated a cycle: they turned away from God, suffered, cried out, and received help. Here the sin is confessed, but God's response in the following verse shows that He wanted to see a real change and not only words.

For today: when you feel your life is falling apart, come to God with sincerity. Acknowledge what you have put in His place and ask Him for help to truly change, not only to get out of the problem.
exp.8:39:
It says that Abimelech pursued Gaal, and Gaal fled before him. Along the way many Shechemites fell wounded, all the way to the entrance of the city gate. The phrase "pursued him" means that Abimelech followed closely after him. The description of those who fell refers to men who were wounded in the fighting.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Gaal had boasted that he could defeat Abimelech, and Zebul, the ruler of the city, stirred him up to come out and fight. Gaal went out and lost. It was the result of a violent struggle for power in Shechem, where many paid the price.

For today: proud words can leave us in trouble when the test comes. Before speaking arrogantly or looking for quarrels, it is wise to stop, be humble, and seek peace. As Proverbs 16:18 says, pride goes before a fall.
exp.7:30:
This verse tells us that Gideon had another son with a woman who lived in Shechem, and he named him Abimelech. The verse calls her a concubine, a secondary wife who had fewer rights than a wife. It says she "bore" him a son, meaning she gave birth to him.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks here. After Gideon's great victory, the account shows us his family life: many wives and seventy sons. Abimelech is mentioned because his story will turn painful later on. The verses that follow say that Israel returned to idolatry after Gideon died. The Bible does not approve of this family life here; it simply reports it.

For today: a good start in faith does not guarantee a good finish. A person's decisions, especially within the home, affect those who come after them. Take care with your relationships and your example, and ask God for steady faithfulness.
exp.4:15:
This verse asks the tribe of Reuben a question: "Why did you sit among the sheepfolds?" Sheepfolds are the pens or enclosures where sheep are kept. The whistling is the call that shepherds used to gather the flocks. The "great indecision" means that Reuben weighed the matter for a long time and kept going back and forth, but did not act.

Here Deborah sings, together with Barak, after the victory over the army of Sisera. In her song she praises the tribes that came to the battle and rebukes those that did not. Reuben had much debate, but stayed with its sheep. Some think the question is a serious criticism; others think it expresses sorrow.

Today, it is easy to stay with our comfort and talk about what we should do. God invites us to move from good intentions to concrete obedience. Ask yourself: what small step can I take today to help someone?
exp.13:15:
Here the wife of Samson weeps and accuses him of not loving her, because he will not explain the riddle to her. "You hate me" means "you have rejected me." To "explain" the riddle means to make its meaning known. Samson answers that he has not explained it even to his father and mother, so he sees no reason to explain it to her.

The speaker is the Philistine woman whom Samson was marrying, during the wedding feast. Her countrymen had threatened to burn her and her family if she did not find out the answer. She uses tears and guilt to pressure him. Samson resists, but afterward he gives in.

For today: true love is not proven by demanding everything or manipulating with tears or fear. We also must take care whom we trust with what matters to us. Let us ask God for wisdom to be sincere, but also firm, without giving in to pressure.
exp.10:39:
This verse says that in Israel it became a custom that each year the young women would go out for four days to mourn and lament for the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. "Lament" means to express sorrow for a person who has died or been lost. "Young women" refers to the young women of the nation.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Jephthah had made a rash vow to God, and his daughter, the first to come out to greet him, was the one caught up in it. The text does not clearly explain what happened to her: some believe she was sacrificed, others that she was dedicated to live alone in the service of God. Believers have debated this for centuries. What is certain is that Israel remembered her grief.

For today: let us think before we promise something, especially before God. And let us learn to remember with respect and compassion those who suffer because of other people's decisions, without forgetting them.
exp.5:14:
Gideon tells God that he does not feel able to save Israel. He asks, "how can I save Israel?", meaning with what strength or resources. He says that his clan is the weakest in Manasseh and that he is the youngest in his father's house.

Israel was suffering under the oppression of the Midianites because of its disobedience. The angel of the Lord had already called Gideon and told him to go in the strength he had. Gideon answers with doubt and humility, looking at his own limits. God does not argue with his weakness, but instead promises him: "Surely I will be with you."

Many times we feel small or poorly prepared for what God places before us. This story reminds us that what matters is not how much we have, but that God goes with us. We can take the step with humility, trusting in his company and not in our own strength.
exp.9:13:
God invites the Israelites to go and ask for help from the gods they themselves chose. The phrase "Go and cry out" means to go and call out loudly. The verse is written with irony: if those gods are so good, let them save you in your trouble.

The Lord speaks after Israel had turned away from Him and served other gods. He reminds them that He had already rescued them from Egypt and from other nations when they cried out to Him. Now He confronts them about their unfaithfulness. Then they admit their sin, put away their idols, and return to serving Him. The text says that God was grieved by the suffering of His people.

For today: let us not seek God only when we are in trouble. Let us examine what has taken His place in our hearts, such as money or success, and return to Him sincerely, for His mercy remains open.
exp.18:21:
This verse tells how a group of wicked men from the city surrounded the house where a traveler was staying. They pounded on the door and demanded that the old man who owned the house bring out the guest so they could have relations with him. The men are described as wicked, with no regard for right or for anyone else. Pounding on the door shows how forceful and threatening they were.

The narrator sets the scene in a dark time in Israel, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them. A Levite was traveling with his concubine, and an old man took them in so they would not have to sleep in the square. The violence of the city stands in sharp contrast with the old man's hospitality. The text reports what happened, but it does not approve of the response that follows, the offer of the women, which is unjust and terrible.

For today: when a society loses the fear of God, the most vulnerable suffer. We can defend and protect the weak, and practice hospitality with wisdom.
exp.18:12:
He says to his servant that they should keep going a little further and reach Gibeah or Ramah to spend the night there. "Come, let us try to reach one of these towns" is an invitation to press on toward one of these places, and "to spend the night" means to stay there and sleep there.

The Levite speaks while travelling back with his concubine and his servant. The day is already ending. The servant wanted to stay in Jebus, a city of foreigners, but the Levite preferred an Israelite city, believing he would be safer among his own people. What is sad is that in Gibeah no one receives them, and this sets up a very dark story.

For today: let us not assume that a place is safe just because it seems familiar or religious. It is wise to pray, to think carefully, and to practise hospitality, opening the door to someone who needs shelter.
exp.7:0:
The men of the tribe of Ephraim confront Gideon. They ask him why he has done this to them, since he did not call them when he went out to fight against Midian. "They contended with him violently" means that they argued with him fiercely and scolded him harshly.

The Ephraimites speak here, an important tribe in Israel. Gideon came from the tribe of Manasseh, and he called them to fight only after the first battle, to pursue those who were fleeing. It seems they felt ignored and wounded in their pride. Gideon answers them with humility, as seen in what follows, and the tension is calmed.

When someone feels offended or ignored, sometimes they confront us with anger. We can imitate Gideon: listen without fighting, acknowledge the good the other person has done, and respond with gentle words. As Proverbs 15:1 says, a soft answer turns away wrath.
exp.15:8:
While the men were hidden in her room, Delilah called out, "Samson, the Philistines are here!" He snapped the bowstrings as easily as a strand of yarn breaks when a flame touches it. So the Philistines still did not learn the source of his strength.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistine lords had asked Delilah to find out why Samson was so strong. Samson gave her a false answer, and she tested it. Even so, he kept playing with her and with danger.

For today: do not play with whatever can pull you away from God. Samson escaped this time, but staying close to temptation was wearing him down. Get away quickly from what tempts you, and guard the relationships that lead you into dishonesty.
exp.7:14:
Gideon arrives at Succoth and shows the men there Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian whom he had captured. He reminds them of how they taunted him. The word "taunted" means they mocked him with scorn and contempt. They had asked him whether he already had those kings in his hands, so that he could then give bread to his tired men.

Gideon speaks here after chasing the Midianite armies. Earlier he had asked the leaders of Succoth for food for his exhausted people, and they refused. They did not want to take a risk in case Gideon failed. Now, with the victory won, he returns to hold them to account. The text tells what he did, but it does not say that God approved of that punishment.

For today: when someone fights for a good cause, helping them is an act of faith and love, not a matter of calculation. And if we have been wronged, we should seek justice without letting revenge take control of us.
exp.0:15:
The explanation says that the descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up from the City of Palms together with the men of Judah. They went to the Wilderness of Judah in the Negev, near Arad, and went to live among the people there. The phrase "in the Negev" points to the southern region. Many understand the City of Palms to be Jericho, though some see it differently.

Context: it is the narrator of the book who speaks. Judges 1 describes how each tribe took its territory after the death of Joshua. The Kenites were not Israelites by birth, but they joined the people of God and shared their journey. The text names the Kenite as Moses' father-in-law; the Bible refers to him in several ways, and nothing more precise can be said.

For today: God opens a place for those who want to walk with his people. We can welcome with warmth those who come to our church or community from outside, and help them feel at home.
exp.9:14:
The Israelites say to God, "We have sinned." They make no excuses. They place themselves in his hands: "Deal with us as You see fit." Even so, they ask him to deliver them "today," that is, right now.

God had just reminded them that they had abandoned him for other gods, and he told them he would no longer deliver them. The Ammonites were oppressing them. So the people respond with confession. What follows shows they did not only speak: they removed the foreign gods and went back to serving the Lord. The text says that God was grieved over their suffering.

For today: when we fail, the best response is to confess honestly, without excuses, and to trust in God's mercy. True repentance also changes behavior, so we can ask ourselves what false god we should put away today.
exp.12:24:
This verse says that the Spirit of the LORD began to stir Samson when he was already a young man, at a place called Mahaneh-dan, between the towns of Zorah and Eshtaol. The word "stir" translates a Hebrew word that can also mean to push or to drive, so it describes a strong, active movement of God's Spirit within him.

The one telling this is the narrator of the book of Judges. Earlier, an angel had announced Samson's birth to his parents, and his mother trusted that God had a purpose for her son. Now the boy grew up, God blessed him, and He began to prepare him to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Zorah and Eshtaol were in the territory of the tribe of Dan.
