For today: God cares for and prepares His children from an early age, even before we see results. Trust that He is at work in your life and in the lives of your children, and ask Him to guide you by His Spirit.
exp.5:11:
This verse says that the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and told him that the LORD was with him. He called him "O mighty man of valor," which means a brave and strong man.

The one speaking is the angel of the LORD, the messenger who brings God's word. Israel was suffering under the oppression of the Midianites because they had turned away from God. Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding out of fear. Even so, God greets him as a valiant man, because He sees what God will do in him, not only his present fear. Gideon answered with doubts, and that shows he did not feel strong.

Today, God does not define us by our fears or failures. If you are discouraged, remember that His presence with you is what gives courage. You can take a step of obedience, even if you feel small.
exp.4:3:
It says that when God went out of Seir, that is, out of the land of Edom south of Canaan, all of creation responded: the earth trembled and the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water.

Here Deborah, together with Barak, speaks in a song of victory after defeating the army of Sisera. She begins by recalling how God acted in the past, near Sinai, to remind the people that the present victory comes from the same powerful God. Some think the rain also points to the storm that helped in the battle, but the text does not say this clearly.

For today: when you face something that seems too big, remember what God has done before. His faithfulness in the past encourages you to trust Him now and to give Him thanks.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that the Lord left some peoples in the land of Canaan to test Israel. "Test" here means to examine, to see what is in the heart. It applied to the generation that had not experienced the wars of the conquest.

The book of Judges introduces the narrator, who tells the story of Israel after the death of Joshua. The Israelites had not finished driving out the peoples of the land. The text says that God used that situation to test them and to teach them to fight. It also shows whether they would obey the commands of the Lord. Some peoples mentioned later are the Philistines, the Canaanites, and the Sidonians.

Today, trials are not always punishments; they can be opportunities to grow in faith and in dependence on God. When you face a difficulty, ask yourself: "Lord, what do you want to teach me here?" and seek to obey him step by step.
exp.17:8:
The explanation says that the five men who went out to explore returned urging their tribe to act at once. They tell the others that the land is very good, and they ask why the people would fail to act, urging them not to hesitate. The question "Why would you fail to act?" means that they are staying where they are and not moving, and "Do not hesitate" means do not be slow to act. "Take possession of the land" means to take it as one's own.

The five spies speak for the tribe of Dan. This tribe had not yet fully taken its territory and was looking for a place to settle. Laish seemed easy to conquer because its people lived in confidence and isolation. They say that God has given it into their hands, but note this: the story of the chapter also shows disorder, since earlier they had taken Micah's idols. For that reason the passage does not approve everything they do.

For today: do not confuse a good opportunity with God's approval. Before acting, pray, consult the Word, and ask yourself whether the way is just.
exp.1:22:
God allowed some nations to remain in the land of Canaan. He did not drive them out right away, and he did not hand them over to Joshua to be defeated. The phrase "right away" means immediately, without delay. The phrase "driving them out" means forcing them to leave the land.

This verse closes the narrator's comment in Judges 2. Earlier, God had said that he would no longer drive out those nations, because Israel had broken the covenant. God left them to test whether the people would keep to the path their fathers had walked. Some see discipline here and others see a test; both ideas appear in the text.

For today: the difficulties God allows can show us what is in our hearts. Instead of only asking why something remains, we can ask him for help to stay faithful to him in the middle of the trial.
exp.10:31:
This verse tells how Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and how the LORD delivered them into his hand. "Delivered into his hand" means the LORD gave him the victory.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Jephthah was a leader whom Israel sought out in the middle of oppression. Before the battle he made a rash vow, promising to offer to God whatever came out of his house first. The text says the victory came from the LORD, and it does not present the vow as something God had asked for. Scholars discuss how the fulfillment of that vow should be understood.

For today: God can work even when our words are clumsy. Let us learn to speak with him sincerely, but without haste or impulsive promises. Let us trust his help without trying to bargain for it.
exp.12:10:
Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he came to the man she had seen, he asked him whether he was the one who had spoken to her. The man answered, "I am." Here "man" means simply a man, and the wife had told her husband about the visit.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel of the Lord had told her that she would have a son, the future Samson. Manoah had prayed asking for more instructions, and God answered by sending the angel again. Manoah does not settle for hearing the news secondhand; he wants to confirm it for himself. Here he still sees the visitor as a man, even though the text calls him the angel of God.

For today: it is good to seek God with humility when we need direction, and also to listen to those whom He uses to speak to us, as Manoah did with his wife.
exp.15:18:
She had him fall asleep with his head resting on her lap. Then she called for a man, who cut off the seven braids of his hair. The braids are long strands of hair woven together. Cutting the hair that short means shaving it close to the head. In this way she began to overpower him, because his strength had left him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samson was a Nazirite, that is, set apart for God from before his birth, and his long hair was the sign of that vow. After much pressure, Samson revealed his secret to Delilah, and she betrayed him for money from the Philistines. His strength was not in the hair as something magical, but in the presence of God, who withdrew because of Samson's disobedience.

For today: let us guard what God has entrusted to us and not play with temptation. Small compromises can lead us far from God without our noticing.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that Jephthah sent messengers once more to the king of the Ammonites. The phrase "sent messengers again" is the verse's own wording, and it means he sent them a second time. "Messengers" are people who speak on behalf of someone else. The verse is short, but it opens Jephthah's second response.

The Ammonite king had just claimed that Israel took his land when they came up out of Egypt. Jephthah, who was a judge of Israel, did not rush to fight. First he sent messengers to talk and clarify the facts. In the verses that follow he explains Israel's journey through the wilderness. In this way he tries to avoid a war, although in the end peace is not achieved.

For today: before responding in anger in a conflict, try to speak calmly and truthfully. Dialogue does not always resolve everything, but it shows wisdom and respect.
exp.4:5:
According to the explanation, in the time of Shamgar and Jael, life in Israel came to a standstill because of fear. The main roads were left deserted, and travelers took the byways, the hidden side paths, instead of the open routes. The phrase "the highways were deserted" means that it was no longer possible to travel safely.

The speaker is Deborah, in the song she sings together with Barak after the victory over Sisera's army. She remembers how difficult the situation had been before: the people were oppressed by the Canaanites and could not move about freely. Shamgar appears as a deliverer in Judges 3:31, but the oppression continued. Scholars debate some details of this period.

For today: when fear makes us go around and hide, let us remember that God still delivers. We can ask Him for courage to take the next straight step He shows us.
exp.0:29:
It says that the tribe of Zebulun did not drive out the people living in Kitron and Nahalol. Instead, the Canaanites stayed among them and served as forced laborers. "Drive out" here means to force people to leave, and the picture is of a people who were never removed and ended up working for Israel.

The narrator of the book of Judges, whose author is not known for certain, reviews how each tribe settled in the land. God had commanded Israel not to live alongside the peoples whose practices led to idolatry. Yet tribe after tribe settled for a convenient arrangement: profiting from the Canaanites instead of obeying fully. This account prepares the explanation of Israel's later stumbling.

For today: sometimes we tolerate a small sin because it seems useful or manageable. Let us ask God for courage not to bargain with what pulls us away from Him, even when it costs us.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to Bochim and spoke to the people of Israel. He reminded them that God brought them out of Egypt, led them into the land he had promised to their fathers, and assured them that he would never break his covenant with them. To break or cancel a promise is what it means to annul it, and a promise made under solemn oath is what the text calls a sworn promise.

The one speaking is the angel of the Lord, who here speaks as God's representative. Some scholars think he is a special messenger of God, and others see in him an appearance of the Lord himself. He speaks after the death of Joshua, when the people had not fully obeyed. The name Bochim means "those who weep." That is why he begins by recalling God's faithfulness.

For today: God is faithful even when we fail. His faithfulness is not an excuse for carelessness, but a reason to obey him with gratitude and not to make agreements with anything that draws us away from him.
exp.18:28:
He says that when the Levite reached his house, he picked up a knife, took hold of his concubine, cut her limb by limb into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout the territory of Israel. A "concubine" was a wife of secondary rank, and "territory" here means the land and the areas belonging to Israel.

This is the end of a very dark story. The woman was handed over to a mob in Gibeah, in the tribe of Benjamin, and died after being abused. The narrator is not approving of the Levite's act; he shows how far Israel had fallen. The book repeats that there was no king and everyone did what seemed right to them. The twelve pieces were meant to shake the tribes into reacting. How to judge the Levite's conduct is left by the text for the reader to decide.

For today: let us not become accustomed to injustice or to violence against the vulnerable. When a society sets God aside, the weakest people suffer first. Let us defend and care for those who cannot defend themselves.
exp.2:24:
They waited until they became worried, because the door of the upper room still had not been opened. Finally they took the key, unlocked the doors, and found their lord lying dead on the floor.

The upper room is the room on the upper floor of the palace. The text does not say what the servants were doing during the wait, so this explanation does not add any detail beyond what the verse states.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Israel was under the rule of Moab, and God raised up Ehud as a deliverer. Ehud killed the king and left calmly, closing the doors behind him. The servants believed the king was resting or in the bathroom, and that delay gave Ehud time to escape and gather the people.

For today: God can use ordinary circumstances and people's patience to carry out his plans. Trust that he is at work even when everything seems still, and do not despair if answers take time.
exp.18:0:
In those days, when Israel had no king, a Levite was living in the remote hill country of Ephraim. He had taken a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah. A concubine was a woman with a lesser legal standing than a wife, which was common in that era. Living in a remote area means he lived apart from the centers of people and their support, a stranger in that land.

This is the start of a very painful story near the end of the book of Judges. The one speaking is the narrator, not a character. The phrase "when there was no king in Israel" appears in the book to show the moral disorder of those years, when people acted without guidance and without respect for God's law. Scholars understand that phrase in different ways, but all of them see a warning.

For today: when each person does what seems right to them, respect and care for others are lost. Ask yourself whom and what you are allowing to guide your life.
exp.18:11:
Here the Levite, who travels with his concubine and his servant, turns down the suggestion to spend the night in Jebus. He says they will not stop at a city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites. He decides to keep going on to Gibeah.

The Levite, who is the owner of the group, speaks to his servant, who suggested resting in Jebus because it was already late. Jebus was then a Jebusite city, which would later become Jerusalem. The Levite seeks safety among his own people. But the story shows something bitter: in Gibeah, an Israelite city, a great wickedness will take place. This climate of corruption in Israel is summed up in Judges with the statement that everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes.

For today: let us not blindly trust that a place or group is safe just because it carries the label "ours." Let us ask God for wisdom and examine real fruits with humility.
exp.12:11:
Manoah answers the man and says, "When your words come to pass." That is, he believes and accepts what he was told. Then he asks what the boy's rule of life and mission will be. Here "rule of life" refers to the way the child is to live and the purpose he is to serve.

Manoah is the husband of the barren woman to whom it was announced that she would have a son. She ran to tell him about the visit of the man, who later appears as the angel of the LORD. Manoah does not doubt the announcement, but he wants to know how to help the child fulfill his calling well. The child would be Samson, set apart for God from his birth.

When God entrusts us with something important, believing is not enough: it is also wise to ask humbly how to do it well. We can seek his guidance in prayer and in his Word before we act.
exp.18:8:
This verse tells us that the Levite had already got up to leave with his concubine and his servant. But the young woman's father urges him to stay one more night. He tells him that the day is already drawing to a close, that is, the sun is about to set, and he asks him to spend the night and let his heart be merry. He also says that the Levite can get up early the next morning and continue his journey home.

The one speaking is the father-in-law, who had already kept the Levite for several days with food and hospitality. He seems to want to enjoy his daughter's company a while longer and to take good care of his son-in-law. But the Levite refuses and leaves late, which leads him to look for lodging at night and into a very painful story. The Bible does not say that the father-in-law had bad intentions; his insistence seemed to be affection and courtesy.

For today: it invites us to think carefully about when to decide and when to set out. Hospitality is good, but it is also wise to make decisions with prudence, without rushing into situations that expose us to unnecessary risks.
exp.8:32:
He tells Abimelek to get up at sunrise and attack the city of Shechem. Gaal and his men will come out to meet him. "Attack" means to strike at the city, and "do whatever you are able" means: act however the situation allows once you see what is happening.

The one speaking is Zebul, the governor of Shechem, who secretly sends messengers to Abimelek. Zebul pretends loyalty to Gaal, but in truth he serves Abimelek. He advises a night ambush. It is a story of intrigue and violence, and the account does not present it as an example to imitate. It shows how ambition and betrayal destroy one another.

For today: let us not resolve conflicts with deceit or harmful cunning. Let us seek truth, peace, and justice, trusting that God sees what is hidden.
exp.2:28:
This verse tells that the Israelites struck down about ten thousand Moabite fighters, robust and valiant men, and that not one of them got away. "Struck down" means they defeated them in battle. "About ten thousand" is an approximate number.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. He has just described how Ehud, a judge whom God raised up, called Israel to fight against Moab, which had oppressed them. Israel seized the fords of the Jordan, that is, the crossing points of the river, and so cut off the enemy's retreat. The text presents this victory as the work of God, who gave the enemies into their hands. It is an account of warfare from that period, not a guide for resolving conflicts today.

For today: when you face something that weighs on you, such as a habit, a fear, or an injustice, trust that God can give you freedom. But act with courage and wisdom, like Israel, which followed its leader and closed off the enemy's escape routes.
exp.18:25:
At dawn, the woman went back to the house where her master was staying. She collapsed at the doorway and lay there until it was light. Here "concubine" means a secondary wife, and "master" means her husband or owner. The phrase "until it was light" means the sun had already begun to brighten the sky.

The narrator recounts one of the darkest episodes in Judges. Some men of Gibeah, in Benjamin, wanted to abuse a Levite who was a guest. Instead of protecting her, the man handed over his concubine, and she suffered violence through the night. The book repeats that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what seemed right to them. It is a condemnation of wickedness, not an approval of it.

For today: God calls us to protect the vulnerable, not to sacrifice them to save ourselves. Today we can listen, believe, and accompany those who suffer abuse, and defend their dignity.
exp.8:41:
The next day the people of Shechem went out into the fields, and this was reported to Abimelech. The report means that someone gave him the news. The verse does not say who did it or why.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Gaal had already been driven out of Shechem by Zebul, and Abimelech was waiting in Arumah. When Abimelech learned that the people had gone out of the city, he prepared a surprise attack. So the people were left exposed outside the walls, and the account shows how violence and rebellion led to more death.

For today: what seems like an ordinary day may be shaped by decisions made earlier. It is wise to seek peace, to avoid conflicts that grow out of pride, and to remember that our actions have consequences that reach other people.
exp.15:21:
It says that Samson's hair began to grow back after it had been shaved. "Shaved" means cut off very close to the head, so it is a brief detail, but a very important one in the story.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Samson had been set apart for God from birth as a Nazirite, and his long hair was a sign of that commitment. Delilah cut it while he slept, and the Philistines captured him. The text does not say the hair had magical power; it stresses that God had departed from him. By mentioning the hair growing back, the account shows that the story is not yet over.

For today: even when we have failed and feel we have lost everything, God can give a new beginning to anyone who turns back to Him with humility.
exp.5:17:
Gideon asks the visitor not to leave yet. He wants to go and bring his offering and set it before him. The visitor answers that he will stay until Gideon comes back.

Gideon is speaking with the angel of the LORD, who is calling him to save Israel from the Midianites. Gideon feels small and unsure, so he asks for a sign to be certain that it is really the LORD who is speaking to him. His offering is a way of honoring God and of testing what he is seeing. Then the angel uses that offering as the sign.

When we doubt, we can speak with God honestly and respectfully, without hiding our questions. He is patient with those who seek him. Even so, it is good to respond with humility, preparing our hearts to listen and obey.
exp.11:10:
After Ibzan, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel ten years. He was from the tribe of Zebulun and led the people for a decade. The word "judged" does not refer only to giving verdicts, but to guiding, defending, and governing the people.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, giving a brief record of the minor judges. About Elon's time no battle or deed is told, only his tribe, the years of his rule, and his burial. We do not know why so little was written, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is not famous and leaves no great stories behind. If today you carry out your work, your family, or your church with steadiness, your faithfulness does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.8:27:
Gaal says with contempt: "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him?" He points out that Abimelech is the son of Jerubbaal, and asks whether Zebul is not his officer. Zebul is the man Abimelech has placed in charge, so Gaal treats him as a subordinate. He proposes that the people serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem, instead. And he asks: why should we serve Abimelech?

Gaal is a newcomer who gains the trust of the people of Shechem. They were already angry with Abimelech, and after the feast the curses came. Gaal speaks in the middle of that atmosphere, and his speech aims to stir up a rebellion. Some think he appeals to the people's pride in their ancient roots, but the text does not fully explain this.

Speaking with pride and sowing division may seem like courage, but it almost always leads to more violence. Before following someone who criticizes harshly, it is wise to ask what they really seek and to look for peace.
exp.19:20:
This verse tells that the men of the tribe of Benjamin came out of the city of Gibeah and cut down Israelites on the battlefield on the first day of fighting. Twenty-two thousand Israelites died in that single day.

The narrator of the book recounts a war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. The Israelites wanted to punish a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, and Benjamin did not hand over the guilty men. Although Israel had a just cause and had gone to fight with a great number of men, it lost. Afterward they wept before the LORD and sought his counsel. The text does not fully explain why God allowed this defeat; some think Israel needed to humble itself and seek him with more seriousness.

For today: being in the right does not guarantee that everything will be easy. When something goes wrong, do not give up or rely only on your own strength; come to God with humility and sincerity, and ask him for direction.
exp.0:27:
When Israel became stronger, they pressed the Canaanites into forced labor, but they never drove them out completely. The phrase "forced labor" means the Canaanites were made to work for Israel rather than being removed from the land.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges, who summarizes how the tribes gradually took over Canaan, is speaking. God had commanded them to drive those peoples out of the land. But the tribes, such as Manasseh, Ephraim, and Zebulun, were content to profit from them. The text shows a beginning of disobedience that would later bring trouble.

For today: sometimes we tolerate a sin or bad habit because it benefits us, or because we think we have it under control to some degree. Ask God for strength to remove it at the root, not just to manage it.
exp.8:47:
Abimelech goes up with his men to Mount Zalmon. There he takes his axe, cuts a branch from the trees, and lifts it to his shoulder. Then he tells his men to hurry and do the same as he has done.

Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. Now the leaders of the tower of Shechem had turned against him and taken refuge in the stronghold of the temple of Baal-berith. Abimelech, as the military leader, sets the example so that his men will follow him. With those branches they will set the place on fire, and about a thousand people will die.

A leader draws others along by his example, for good or for evil. Before following someone, let us ask where he is leading us. And if we guide others, let us make sure our example brings them closer to God, not to violence.
exp.17:1:
This verse tells how the tribe of Dan sent five men from their own clans, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to scout the land and explore it for a place to settle. The men were brave, and their task was to look over the territory closely. On their way they entered the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah, where they spent the night.

The narrator of the book of Judges explains that in those days there was no king in Israel. Dan had not yet taken the land that had been assigned to them, so they were looking for another territory. What follows shows spiritual disorder: a Levite serving in a private house as a priest, which was not the order God had established.

For today: before making an important decision, it is not enough to investigate carefully and to have courage. It is wise to ask God and to examine his Word, so that our plans do not follow only what seems good to us.
exp.4:24:
Here it is told that Sisera, commander of the enemy army, asked for water, and Jael gave him milk. She also brought him curds in a magnificent bowl, a fine dish fit for an important guest. The curds were probably thick, curdled milk or heavy cream.

Deborah speaks together with Barak in a song of victory after defeating Sisera. Jael appeared to offer hospitality and protection, but it was a trap. The verses that follow tell how she killed him. Interpreters debate how to judge her act: the song celebrates it, but the text does not hold it up as a model of conduct.

For today: this passage invites us to think about generosity and hospitality. Today we do not imitate Jael's deceit, but we can offer others fair, sincere treatment without duplicity.
exp.4:8:
Deborah says that her heart is with the princes of Israel, that is, with the leaders who stepped forward freely for the battle, the volunteers among the people. At the end, she calls on everyone to bless the LORD. Here, "princes" means leaders, and "volunteers" describes those who gave themselves willingly, without anyone forcing them.

Deborah, a prophetess and judge, speaks in the song of victory that follows the defeat of Sisera's army. Before that, she describes a time of fear and neglect, when Israel had turned away from God. Now she acknowledges those who stepped forward and directs the praise toward God, not toward people.

For today: God delights in service given with joy. Think of a place where you can offer yourself willingly, in your church or your community, and do it wholeheartedly. When things go well, give thanks to God.
exp.18:13:
This verse tells how the Levite, his concubine, and his servant kept walking until the sun set as they neared Gibeah, a town in Benjamin. The phrase "the sun set as they neared Gibeah" means that evening overtook them on the road.

The one speaking is the narrator, who follows this Levite on his journey home. He had decided not to stay in a foreign city, because he thought he would be safer among his own people. So they continued on and drew near to Gibeah. The book of Judges shows a time of great moral disorder in Israel, and this story will end in a very painful way.

For today: an appearance of safety can be deceiving. Belonging to a group, a church, or a town does not guarantee that justice will be done. Let us ask God for wisdom, and seek to live and practice hospitality.
exp.0:22:
The explanation says that the tribe of Joseph (made up of Ephraim and Manasseh) sent spies to Bethel, a city formerly known as Luz. "Spies" here are men sent to observe a place in order to learn how to attack or enter it.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel is taking possession of the land after the death of Joshua. The text has just said that the LORD was with them, so it presents this plan as an action carried out with God's help. Bethel held a special value in the history of Israel, and the account recalls its older name, Luz.

For today: trusting God does not remove the responsibility to think and prepare. Before an important decision, we can pray, seek counsel, and gather good information, believing that God accompanies us in that process.
exp.18:6:
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law kept pressing him to stay. The word "persuaded" in this verse means he kept at him, urging him again and again. "So he stayed there that night" means that the Levite spent that night in the house once more.

The Levite had gone to Bethlehem in Judah to bring back his concubine, who had left his side. Her father welcomed him warmly and, day after day, kept encouraging him to stay. Here the father-in-law speaks, and he seems to want to enjoy more time with his son-in-law and his daughter. The text does not say whether he had other reasons. What is clear is that these delays would end up making the journey start late.

For today: kindness is good, but it is wise to know when to say "it is time for me to go." Let us plan with wisdom and not let the pressure of others make us postpone what is important.
exp.19:38:
The explanation says that the men of Israel pretended to retreat in the battle. The men of Benjamin pursued them and struck down about thirty men of Israel, and they became confident. They thought: "They are defeated before us, as in the first battle." The phrase "struck them down" means they hit them and killed about thirty of them. "Turned in the battle" means that the Israelites turned around to flee.

Context: the one narrating is the author of the book of Judges. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin for having protected the guilty parties of a terrible crime in Gibeah. Earlier, Benjamin had won twice. Now Israel used a trap: an ambush and a signal of smoke. Benjamin trusted in their past victory and did not see the danger behind them.

For today: yesterday's success does not guarantee today's. If we defend what is wrong, sooner or later it collapses. Let us seek humility, and examine whether we stand on the side of justice.
exp.8:51:
It says that Abimelech came to the tower of Thebez to attack it. He approached the entrance to set it on fire, because the people of the city had taken refuge inside. "Attack" means to assault it, and "set it on fire" means to set it alight.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. He had already destroyed Shechem in the same way, by burning its tower. Now he repeats his method at Thebez. The account shows how his violence leads him to an end he himself does not control, and the Bible presents it as a judgment from God (vv. 56-57).

For today: whoever trusts in force and pride to get their way may fall in the most unexpected manner. Let us seek to serve with humility and justice, and not with ambition.
exp.16:10:
The explanation says that the Levite agreed to stay and live with Micah, and that Micah treated him like a son. "Agreed" means he was willing to go along with the arrangement, and staying means living with him in his home.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Micah had in his house a shrine with idols, and he was looking for a Levite to be his priest. The young Levite was wandering without direction, looking for a place to live, and he accepted pay, clothing, and food. Judges repeats that in those days there was no king and everyone did what seemed right to them. So this scene shows a disorderly religion, shaped to suit each person.

For today: comfort and good company do not prove that something is right before God. Before accepting an opportunity, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to the Word of God or only meets your needs of the moment.
exp.2:22:
Then Ehud went out through the porch and closed and locked the doors of the upper room behind him. Here "upper room" is the cool room where King Eglon was, and "porch" is a Hebrew word that some scholars think may mean a vestibule or corridor; its exact meaning is not known with certainty.

The verse tells how Ehud, judge of Israel, had just killed Eglon, king of Moab, who oppressed the people. By locking the doors, he kept others from discovering the deed right away and gained time to escape. The story shows how God delivered Israel through an unexpected man, left-handed and of little renown.

For today: God can use people who seem ordinary to face great problems. This account describes what happened; it does not command us to use violence. What we can learn is to act with courage, wisdom, and trust in God when we face injustice.
exp.17:23:
Micah answers with grief and anger: the Danites carried off the idols he had made himself, along with the priest he kept in his house. He says he has nothing left. Then he protests: how can they ask him "What is the matter with you?" as if they did not understand his loss? The phrase "What else do I have?" shows how completely he feels stripped of everything.

Micah speaks to the men of Dan, who passed by his house during their search for territory. He followed them with his neighbors, but seeing that they were stronger, he went back home. His gods could neither defend themselves nor defend him; his religion depended on objects and a hired priest. The text shows the spiritual confusion of that time.

Today, the question is: what do I trust so much that, if it were taken from me, I would feel I had nothing left? Only God cannot be taken away. We should place our security in Him, and not in things we build ourselves.
exp.3:3:
This verse presents Deborah as the person who was leading Israel at that time. She was a prophetess, that is, someone through whom God spoke to his people, and she was married to Lappidoth. Here, "leading" means that she held authority and was judging, settling matters for the people.

The narrator of the book tells us that Israel had been oppressed for twenty years by Jabin, king of Canaan, and his commander Sisera, who had nine hundred iron chariots. The people had cried out to God. In that difficult moment, God had Deborah in a place of authority. The Israelites came to her to receive justice, and she would summon Barak to pass on the word of the Lord.

God can use whom He chooses, at the moment He chooses. When you face a difficult situation, seek His direction with humility and obey, no matter who brings it to you.
exp.14:2:
Samson says that this time he will not be to blame before the Philistines if he harms them. By "blameless" he means that no one can accuse him of wrongdoing, because they had first done him an injury. The phrase "doing harm to" them means causing them harm.

Samson speaks in anger and hurt. He went to visit his wife, and her father would not let him in, because he had given her to another man, believing that Samson had rejected her. Samson justifies himself before he acts, and right after this he sets fire to the Philistines' fields. The text tells what he did, but it does not say that God approved his anger or his revenge. Even so, the Bible shows that God was at work within this situation.

For today: when someone hurts us, it is easy to use the injustice we have received as an excuse for taking revenge. Before we react, it is wise to pray and ask God for self-control and wisdom.
exp.14:17:
Samson is very thirsty and speaks to God openly. He reminds God that he has just given him a great victory, which the Berean wording calls a "deliverance" accomplished through his servant. Then he asks whether he is now going to die of thirst and fall into the hands of the "uncircumcised," a way of naming the Philistines, who did not belong to the covenant people.

He is speaking as Samson, judge of Israel, right after defeating a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. He went from celebration to exhaustion. He acknowledges that the victory came from God, even though it was carried out through his own hand. God answers by bringing water out of the ground, and Samson is revived.

For today: after a great achievement, we still depend on God. When you are tired or in need, speak to him honestly, without pretending to strength. He cares for us not only in our battles but also in our daily needs.
exp.14:1:
Here Samson's father-in-law explains why he did not let Samson see his wife. He says he was sure Samson thoroughly hated her, so he gave her to one of the men who had come with Samson to the wedding. Then he offers the younger sister, saying she is more beautiful.

The speaker is the father of the Philistine woman. Samson had left angry after the wedding, when she revealed the riddle (chapter 14). Now he returns with a young goat as a gesture of reconciliation, and finds that she has already been given to another. The father acts on his own and treats his daughter as something that can be exchanged for another.

For today: before acting, it is wise to speak and confirm the facts. The father decided on assumption and caused a greater wound. Also, people are not interchangeable objects; they deserve respect and care.
exp.17:22:
Here, Micah and his neighbors call out to the men of Dan, who are walking away with his belongings. The Danites turn around to face them and ask him with irony: "What is the matter with you that you have called out such a crowd?" The phrase "called out after them" simply means shouting after someone.

The men of Dan had just stolen Micah's idols and taken his priest with them. Micah, together with his neighbors, pursues them. The Danites pretend not to understand, even though they know very well what they did. Shortly afterward they threaten him, and he is left with nothing. The book shows a time of disorder, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them.

For today: when our faith depends on things we can lose, such as possessions or people, it becomes fragile. Let us ask God to be our security, and to give us the honesty not to justify what we know is wrong.
exp.18:16:
This verse tells that an old man looked up and saw a traveler in the city square. Then he asked him: "Where are you going, and where have you come from?" The word "saw" matches the verse, and "asked" reflects how the verse describes the old man speaking to him. A "traveler" is a man passing through who is only visiting.

The speaker is an older man, from the region of Ephraim, who was living in Gibeah as a foreigner. He was coming back from work in the fields as evening drew near. The traveler and his companions had arrived in the city, but no one offered them lodging. That they were left to wait in the square shows the lack of hospitality in the place. The old man notices him and asks in order to learn his situation.

For today: do not walk past the one who is alone or without help. Sometimes a sincere question, asked with genuine interest, is the first step toward offering help, companionship, or a place to rest.
exp.8:45:
When the people of the tower of Shechem heard that Abimelech had destroyed the city, they ran to take refuge in the strongest part of the temple of El-berith. The inner chamber here is a fortified place, a safe hiding spot inside the temple.

The narrator tells this within the story of Abimelech, son of Gideon, who made himself king by killing his brothers. The leaders of Shechem had supported him, and then they rebelled against him. Now he attacks them. These people sought protection in the temple of El-berith (Judges 9:4), a false god. Scholars do not know exactly what that building looked like.

For today: when trouble comes, we tend to run to whatever is at hand, such as money, influence, or other things. But only God is a safe refuge. Let us learn to turn to Him first.
exp.17:3:
Here the young Levite explains how he came to be Micah's priest. He says that Micah "has done this and that for me," meaning that Micah made an arrangement with him, and that he "has hired me to be his priest." Being hired means that Micah employed him and paid him a wage.

The Levite and the five scouts from Dan speak together. They recognize his voice, perhaps because of his accent or because they already knew him, and they ask what he is doing there. He explains his situation. He is a priest hired to serve in a house with idols, something foreign to what God had commanded. Afterward the Danites ask him for counsel, and he answers with confidence, though the text does not confirm that God spoke through him.

Today, before accepting a job or a position, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it draws us closer to God or leads us to keep the truth silent for convenience. A religious voice is not always the voice of God.
exp.4:11:
The command is repeated with force: "Awake, awake, O Deborah! Awake, awake, sing a song!" Deborah is called to wake up and sing a song of praise. Barak is told to arise and take hold of the enemies who were captured. The phrase "sing a song" means to sing out loud. The captives are the prisoners of war.

This verse is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, sung after Israel defeated the army of Sisera. The one speaking is the song itself, which addresses Deborah and Barak as in a poetic call. Some think Deborah urges herself to sing; others think it is the people who invite her. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when God gives you a victory, do not stay silent or still. Stir your heart to thank him, and then rise up to keep obeying with courage.
exp.1:8:
This verse tells where Joshua was buried: in the land that was his own inheritance, at Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. "Land of his inheritance" refers to the territory that came to him as his share. Joshua is known to have received that town (Joshua 19:49-50), although today not everyone agrees on its exact location.

Context: the narrator of the book of Judges, whose author is not known for certain, summarizes what happened after Joshua's death. First he shows that the people remained faithful as long as those who had seen the works of God were alive. Then he announces that the next generation did not know the LORD and turned away. In this way he prepares the account of the cycles of sin and rescue that follow.

For today: faith is not passed down automatically. If we have known God's work in our lives, let us tell our children, grandchildren, and friends about it, and personally teach them to know him.
exp.15:14:
Delilah challenges Samson, asking how he can say he loves her when he does not trust her. She reminds him that he has already deceived her three times and still has not told her the source of his great strength. "To uncover" here means to reveal or tell.

The speaker is Delilah, the woman Samson loved. The Philistine rulers had asked her to find out the source of his strength so they could subdue him. She presses him with accusations and emotional pressure, and Samson had already deceived her with false answers. In the end, tired of her persistence, he tells her that his strength is tied to his Nazirite vow, and that for this reason he had never cut his hair.

For today: true love shows itself in trust and sincerity, not in pressure or manipulation. If someone keeps pressing us again and again to give in to what we know we should not do, let us ask God for wisdom to set boundaries and to care for what He has entrusted to us.
exp.15:15:
It says that Delilah pressed Samson daily with her words and would not leave him alone. She pleaded with him so persistently that Samson was worn down, pushed to a point of distress that he could barely bear. The verse describes her pressing him with constant pleading until he was sick to death, meaning that his spirit was worn down and exhausted to the point of despair.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Delilah, paid by the Philistine lords, wanted to learn the secret of Samson's strength. She had already tried three times, and now she uses emotional pressure: "How can you say you love me?" Samson gives in shortly afterward and reveals his Nazirite vow.

For today: constant pressure can wear us down and make us give in on what we know is sacred. It is wise to surround ourselves with people who respect us, to set limits in time, and not to hand our heart over to someone who uses it to harm us.
exp.0:4:
This verse tells how the tribes of Judah and Simeon found Adoni-bezek in a place called Bezek. There they fought against him and struck down the Canaanites and Perizzites, who were peoples living in that land. Here "found" means they came upon him, and "striking down" means they defeated them in battle.

It is part of the account in the book of Judges, which does not name its narrator. After the death of Joshua, Judah asked his brother Simeon for help to conquer the territory that had fallen to them. The text says it was the LORD who delivered these peoples into their hands. Adoni-bezek seems to have been a local king, and his story continues in the verses that follow.

For today: Judah did not want to fight alone, but asked his brother for help. In the same way, we do not have to face difficult tasks by ourselves. Let us seek the support of brothers and sisters in the faith, and trust that God works through our united effort.
exp.12:12:
The angel of the LORD answered Manoah that his wife must do everything he had already told her. The BSB wording "Your wife is to do everything I told her" makes clear that the instruction is for her to carry out what she was already given. The LORD, written in capitals, is the name of God, and the angel of the LORD is a messenger sent by Him.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a child, who would be Samson. The angel had already given instructions to the woman, and Manoah, concerned about raising the boy well, asked that they be repeated to him. The angel adds nothing new: he points back to what had already been said, and then explains the details, such as not drinking wine or eating anything unclean.

For today: when God has already shown us the way, we do not always need more information, but obedience. We can ask ourselves what God's Word has already told us and begin to put it into practice faithfully.

sum.1: An angel of God rebuked Israel at Bochim for not obeying, and the people wept. After Joshua died, the new generation forgot God and served Baal, so they suffered oppression. God raised up judges to rescue them, but the people returned to their wickedness, and God left those nations in place to test them.
sum.16: Micah, a man from Ephraim, returns to his mother the silver he had stolen from her, and she uses some of it to make an image and place it in his house. He sets up his own place of worship and hires a Levite as his priest, believing that this way God will bless him. The text shows the disorder of a people where "everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes."
sum.11: The men of Ephraim were angry with Jephthah because he had not called them to fight against the Ammonites, and they threatened him. Jephthah replied that he had called them, but they did not come to help. Then the Gileadites defeated them, and forty-two thousand Ephraimites were killed. After that, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon judged Israel.
sum.18: A Levite went to bring back his concubine, who had left him, and on the way home he spent the night in Gibeah of Benjamin. There some wicked men abused her until she died, and he cut her body into pieces and sent them throughout Israel. The chapter shows how dark wickedness had become when "there was no king in Israel."
sum.20: The people of Israel grieved because the tribe of Benjamin had nearly disappeared. Since they had sworn not to give their daughters to the Benjaminites in marriage, they looked for a way out. They attacked Jabesh-gilead and took four hundred young women. Then they allowed the Benjaminites to seize women at Shiloh. The chapter ends by showing the chaos of a people without a king, where everyone did whatever seemed right to them.
sum.4: Deborah and Barak sing to praise Jehovah for the victory over Sisera. They commend the tribes that volunteered to fight and rebuke those that stayed behind. They celebrate Jael, who killed Sisera, and the song ends by asking that those who love God be like the sun, and the land rested for forty years.
sum.5: Israel did what was evil, and God allowed the Midianites to oppress them for seven years, until they cried out to Him. Then God called Gideon, a humble and fearful man, and promised to be with him, and Gideon tore down the altar of Baal. Afterward he asked for a sign with the fleece of wool, and God answered him with patience.
sum.3: Israel again did what was evil, and God allowed Jabin, king of Canaan, to oppress them for twenty years; then they cried out to God. The prophetess Deborah encouraged Barak to fight, and God gave the victory over Sisera and his iron chariots. Sisera fled and died at the hands of Jael, showing that God delivers his people when they cry out to him.
sum.15: Samson falls in love with Delilah, and the Philistines pay her to find out the secret of his strength. After deceiving her three times, he gives in to her persistent pleading and reveals that he is a Nazirite; they cut his hair, capture him, and blind him. In the end, he calls out to God and, by pulling down the temple, dies together with many Philistines.
sum.17: The tribe of Dan was looking for land and sent out five scouts, who found the city of Laish quiet and peaceful. Then six hundred armed men set out, took the idols and the Levite priest from Micah's house, attacked Laish, burned it down, and renamed it Dan. It shows how, without faithful guidance from God, the people mixed violence with false worship.
sum.6: God reduced Gideon's army from thousands of men to only three hundred, so that Israel would know that the victory came from Him and not from their own strength. At night, with trumpets, clay jars, and torches, the three hundred surprised the enemy, who fled in confusion. Afterward, Israel pursued them, and they captured Oreb and Zeeb.
sum.2: God left some nations in Canaan to test whether Israel would obey him. But the people mixed with them and worshiped their gods. Because of this, Israel was oppressed. Each time they cried out to God, he sent deliverers such as Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar, and the land had rest.
sum.0: After the death of Joshua, Israel asks the Lord who should go up first to fight against the Canaanites. Judah, together with Simeon, goes up, and they win important victories. The Lord is with them. However, several tribes do not drive out the inhabitants of the land completely, and they live alongside them, which shows an incomplete obedience.
sum.14: Samson went to visit his wife, but her father had already given her to another man. Samson took revenge by setting fire to the Philistine fields. The Philistines killed the woman and her father, and Samson attacked them violently in response. The men of Judah bound him and handed him over. God gave him strength, and he killed a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey. Then God gave him water when he was thirsty.
sum.10: Rejected by his brothers, Jephthah is called by the elders of Gilead to lead the war against the Ammonites. With the Spirit of the LORD he wins the victory, but before the battle he makes a rash vow, and when he returns, the first to come out to meet him is his only daughter. The text tells of her grief and that she accepted the vow, and it does not clearly explain what happened to her.
sum.9: After Abimelech, Tola and Jair led Israel as judges. But the people went back to worshiping idols, and God allowed the Philistines and the Ammonites to oppress them. When they were in great distress, Israel admitted their sin, got rid of the false gods, and went back to serving God, who was moved by their suffering. Meanwhile, the leaders of Gilead were looking for someone to lead them in battle.
sum.19: All of Israel gathers at Mizpah to punish the crime committed at Gibeah, but the tribe of Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty men and goes to war. Israel loses two battles, weeps, fasts, and asks God for guidance, and in the third battle it wins through an ambush. The chapter shows the grief of a divided nation and the violence that spirals out of control.
sum.13: Samson wants to marry a Philistine woman, and although his parents object, God uses the situation to act against the Philistines who were ruling over Israel. At the wedding, Samson poses a riddle about the lion and the honey, but his wife betrays him, and he ends up angry, striking down thirty men in Ashkelon.
sum.12: Israel again did what was evil, and the LORD left them under the Philistines for forty years. Then the angel of the LORD announced to the barren wife of Manoah that she would have a son who was a Nazirite, and that he would begin to deliver Israel. Manoah and his wife offered a sacrifice to the LORD, and Samson was born, and God blessed him.
sum.8: Abimelech, the son of Gideon, killed his seventy brothers with the help of the people of Shechem and made himself king. Only Jotham, the youngest, escaped, and he warned the people of Shechem with a parable. After three years, violence and betrayal broke out between Abimelech and Shechem, and both ended up destroyed. The chapter shows that God holds people accountable for the evil they have done.
sum.7: Gideon calmed the men of Ephraim, pursued the kings of Midian, punished Succoth and Penuel for refusing him help, and killed Zebah and Zalmunna. He refused to be king, saying that the LORD is the Lord, but he made an ephod that the people worshiped. When he died, Israel forgot God.
